A memorial register read as ancestry: Highlander and our own elders, the ones the Cult of Compliance took, and why memory is labor owed forward. Carries Ira Socol and Page & Woodland in full, closing on “forgetting is a tool of white supremacy — memory is the work.” Eight spreads, five diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set. 8 spreads → Zine No. 17 The Nearest Body Stimpunks Zines Tides and co-regulation as star stuff. The Sun out-masses the Moon 27 million times, yet the Moon runs the tide — because tidal force falls off with the cube of distance, and nearness beats mass. So co-regulation is gravity: a safe-enough nervous system nearby pulls yours into rhythm, at a distance, without touching. Spring and neap tides as aligned or crossed pulls, parallel presence as tidal locking, meerkat mode as a sea that lost its moon, and the ecosystemic turn — the storm is in the weather, not the water. Grounded in the Stimpunks glossary (co-regulation, polyvagal theory, meerkat mode, ARLES, regulation-first), with a hydrofeminist thread carried inward from No. 14. Eight spreads, six diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set. 8 spreads → Zine No. 19 No Universal Now Stimpunks Zines Crip time, read through relativity — with a guest coda by Helen Edgar. Physics says there is no universal “now”: simultaneity is relative and clocks run at different rates by speed and gravity (your phone's GPS corrects for it). So the one true clock is a human invention — railway-and-factory standard time, a convention we mistook for a law and then began grading bodies and minds against. Crip time (Zola & Gill, Kafer, Samuels, Price) bends the clock back to fit us instead of bending us to it — the same move as Minor Worlds, now applied to time. Monotropic spiral time and felt time (Helen Edgar, Bergson, Deleuze) are their own real clock, measured in intensity, not minutes; Samuels' time travel, grief time, and broken time hold the hard edges too. The reading: no clock is master, and being “off the clock” is closer to the truth than fitting it. Nine spreads, seven diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set, and a closing coda by Helen Edgar on spiral time. 9 spreads → Zine No. 20 The Same Water Stimpunks Zines Fluctuating capacity, read through the physics of phase transitions. Water doesn't get gradually stiffer as it cools — it holds, then flips to ice all at once at a threshold. Same H₂O, different state, and the conditions (not the substance) decide which. So the exhausting question — why could you do it yesterday and not today? — has a clean answer: capacity is a state, not a trait, and you were near a boundary. The hardest part is the crossing itself (threshold anxiety is sensitivity to a real edge — broken thresholds, not broken people); you can be supercooled, held past your limit until one small thing tips everything at once; and recovery slows near the edge, because that's how systems behave. Nothing is fixed or broken — fluid adaptation and weather-bodies, re-adapting to a changed climate. Extends Minor Worlds: change the conditions, not the substance. Grounded in phase-transition physics, Cynthia Kim, Helen Edgar, and Stimpunks' own threshold anxiety. Eight spreads, six diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set. 8 spreads → Zine No. 21 Not a Line Stimpunks Zines The spectrum was never a severity scale — after Helen Edgar & Patrick Dwyer. “Spectrum” is the most misread word in our vocabulary: people hear a line from mild to severe. But a real spectrum isn't a ladder — split a star's light and every element signs its own pattern of lines, a fingerprint, which is the only way we know what stars are made of. And the sky's figure was never a line: it's a constellation. The zine follows the escalation from Helen Edgar's brand-new essay — the line of neuronormativity, to the spiky profile (better, but still a grid measured from a baseline), to a constellation of intensities: no rank, no norm, no line. Patrick Dwyer's autism constellation anchors it; the functioning-labels critique shows how the line gatekeeps support (“not disabled enough” vs “too disabled”). Held with care: refusing the line doesn't erase that some of us need far more support — need is not a rank; name it instead. Cashes in the rainbow motif on every page and hands off to the Constellation Field Guide. Eight spreads, spectrum-forward diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set. 8 spreads → Zine No. 23 Bodies of Water Stimpunks Zines Hydrofeminism as belonging, read through star stuff — after Astrida Neimanis. You are not a container of water; you are water, roughly 60% of you, briefly gathered into a shape. And none of it is only yours: it was rain, river, cloud, and the inside of other creatures first. Neimanis's gestationality (we each began inside another body's water) and Stacy Alaimo's transcorporeality dissolve the clean edge — we are all downstream of one another, permeable and borrowed. The crucial move, held with care: watery belonging is not dissolution into sameness. Where two rivers meet, the confluence runs braided for miles — one channel, two waters, still distinct. That's the neurodiversity paradigm in an image: the spiky profile survives the merge. A dedicated spread carries shared/collective flow — monotropism's deep channels can align into shared flow (Autistic Realms, Helen Edgar); a watering hole is where currents pool. So belonging is a current, not a border — build watering holes, keep the water moving. Much of Earth's water is older than the Sun. Eight spreads, six diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set. 8 spreads → Zine No. 24 Shared Air Stimpunks Zines The air we share, read through star stuff and solarpunk — a companion to Bodies of Water. There is only one air: a single, well-mixed body with no walls in it, so thoroughly circulated that your next breath very likely holds atoms once breathed by strangers and by trees across the world. It's a reciprocal breath — we exhale what plants inhale, and our oxygen is the exhaust of ancient cyanobacteria (the Great Oxidation Event, ~2.4 billion years ago), forged first in stars. Every room we share is a shared-air space (a term coined by Helen Edgar & Ryan Boren): in it we trade breath and co-regulate, nervous systems settling into a shared rhythm. The neurodiversity turn: many of us are the canaries of that room. Miners carried canaries because the birds felt the bad air first — not because they were weak, but because they were sensitive, and their alarm was information. Our sensitivity to fragrance, stale air, and fluorescent hum is an early-warning system, not a flaw: don't blame the bird, change the air — build it breathable for the canaries and it's breathable for all. Which raises the harder question: habitable, and for whom? The burden of shared air falls unevenly, so breathable air is a commons, not a private accommodation one person quietly manages. The response is solarpunk: clean air as infrastructure as resistance — open windows, plants, masks, DIY Corsi–Rosenthal boxes — mutual aid you can build in an afternoon. Move quietly and plant things. Nine spreads, seven diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set. 9 spreads → Zine No. 25 Shared Signal Stimpunks Zines Connection carried across distance, read through star stuff — a companion to Shared Air. The electromagnetic spectrum is one continuous field: radio waves and starlight are the same phenomenon at different wavelengths, and the same physics that carries a voice call carries a star's light. Shared-signal space — a term coined by Helen Edgar — is the counterpart to shared-air space: a call, a message, a voice note, a synthesised voice, carrying the rhythm on a signal instead of the air of a room. A voice note is breath, timestamped and sent; co-regulation crosses a screen too — thinner, but real (Porges; Streuber et al.). For many of us, text and AAC aren't a fallback from speech but the clearer channel — thinking time, structure, fewer sensory demands, a record to return to (Howard & Sedgewick) — and AAC is the real communication, not a workaround. Aversion to the phone is information, not fragility. Reachable, and for whom? Communication access is a commons; we build our own watering holes — the Autistic Rhizome (Edgar), Discords, AAC — sideways and underground, where lurking counts. The oldest signal of all is a dead star's light still reaching your eye: signal lets connection cross a gap touch can't, so no channel is the master channel (Milton). Stars We Grew Up On A Star Stuff collection · 2 pieces The other kind of star. Icons who made weird into a way of being, and let the rest of us find each other.

What holds these together Here “star” means the other thing, and we are naming that rather than letting it read as drift. These pieces are about icons who made weird into a way of being — Bowie, where unmasking is authorship rather than exposure and many selves are a freedom rather than a symptom; AURORA, the alien who came home by gathering a tribe of Weirdos instead of being cured into fitting. One of the reasons this project exists is that it is fun , and this is where the fun is loudest. We deliberately did not build a collection called “for fun,” because a bin labelled that way quietly labels everything else homework — and would become the one place where our verify-everything standard could slip. So the fun lives out in the open, in its own collection, held to the same ledger as the rest.

Its companions The L★S Playlist and the L★S Broadside belong to this collection in spirit and are one click away in the Sound and Print sections of the index . Not Not fandom standing in for an argument. Loving an artist is not evidence, and these pieces do not pretend it is. Not the superpower framing. Neither of these people is proof that difference pays off if you are talented enough. Belonging is not a prize for exceptional output — that is the extraction story, and we refuse it here as everywhere.

The pieces In the order they were made. The number records when ; the collection records what . Unmasking as authorship rather than exposure, the freedom of many selves, bringing the hidden to the front, and authenticity as our purest freedom. From “Changes” and Space Oddity to Blackstar, difference read as direction, not deficit. L★S · 001 The Stimmer formerly · Gemini · The Twins 07h 45m · +22° · mag 1.9 Seen for centuries as two identical figures standing side by side. The old charts missed what was actually there: two bodies in constant, purposeful, self-regulating motion. Not mirror images. Not twins. Each one moving exactly as they need to move. self-regulationmovementembodimentrhythm ▸ Field notes Field notes · The Stimmer Stimming is not a symptom. It is a technology — one of the oldest human technologies, and one of the most sophisticated. The body knows things the diagnostic manual doesn't. The Stimmer is one of the brightest constellations in the winter sky and one of the most misread. The old charts saw identical twins. The reclaimed chart sees what's actually happening: two bodies in dialogue with themselves and with each other, each one moving in the precise way that keeps the nervous system regulated, present, and intact. Every culture that has ever watched the sky has found patterns here. Every nervous system that has ever inhabited a body has found its own version of this too. The motion that looks like repetition from the outside is, from the inside, a conversation between the body and the world — one that the body is very good at having, if it's allowed to. The Stimmer rises in the northeast in late autumn and is best observed in winter. At its culmination it stands almost directly overhead for observers in mid-northern latitudes. L★S · 003 The Pattern Seeker formerly · Virgo · The Maiden 13h 25m · -11° · mag 0.97 The largest constellation in the zodiac, and for good reason: pattern recognition at this scale takes up a lot of sky. The old charts saw a figure holding a sheaf of wheat. The reclaimed chart sees what that figure was doing — finding the signal in the noise, which is what wheat is. Grain selected from grass by someone who noticed. pattern recognitionsystemizingsignal detectionclassification ▸ Field notes Field notes · The Pattern Seeker Pattern seeking is not obsession. It is one of the foundational cognitive capacities of the human species — the one that produced agriculture, mathematics, music theory, taxonomy, and astronomy itself. Every person who has ever looked at the sky and found a pattern in the stars was doing exactly what The Pattern Seeker does, all the time, about everything. The pathologizing of pattern-seeking is one of the stranger moves of the diagnostic tradition. The same capacity that lets a person memorize every train schedule in the metropolitan area, map the complete ecosystem of a backyard, or hear the harmonic structure in a piece of music is described, in the diagnostic literature, as a "restricted and repetitive" behavior. The frame is the problem, not the capacity. Spica, this constellation's brightest star, is a binary system — two stars so close together and moving so fast that they've distorted each other into egg shapes. The Pattern Seeker's brightest point is a system that has been deeply, structurally changed by its relationship with another pattern. Porrima is also a binary, famous among double-star observers for its beauty and its long orbital period. Two stars, each completing the other's picture of the sky. L★S · 004 The Flood formerly · Aquarius · The Water Bearer 22h 05m · -13° · mag 2.9 The old charts saw a figure pouring water from a jar — an image of controlled, measured, deliberate giving. The reclaimed chart sees what actually happens when a mind holds too much and the vessel finally tips: not a failure of containment, but a return to equilibrium. The flood is not the disaster. The flood is the water going where it needs to go. emotional intensityoverwhelmequilibriumrelease ▸ Field notes Field notes · The Flood The diagnostic tradition describes emotional intensity as dysregulation. The word "dysregulation" assumes a correct regulation — a factory setting from which the neurodivergent nervous system has deviated. But a nervous system that feels things deeply is not a miscalibrated nervous system. It is a nervous system doing exactly what nervous systems do, at a higher amplitude. The Flood is one of the oldest constellations in the sky. In Babylonian astronomy it was associated with the god Ea, who was, among other things, the god of wisdom — a figure who held all the water of the deep and who poured it out when it was needed. The pouring was not a loss of control. It was the wisdom itself. Sadalsuud — "the luckiest of the lucky" — was the star that rose with the first rains of spring. In cultures that depended on rain, this was not merely a meteorological event. It was the world coming back to life. What looks from the outside like the system being overwhelmed is often, from the inside, the system working — bringing the water where it needs to go, at last. L★S · 005 The Navigator formerly · Ursa Minor · The Little Bear 15h 44m · +77° · mag 2.02 The old charts saw a small bear — a diminutive, lesser version of the great bear nearby. The reclaimed chart sees what this constellation actually does: it contains Polaris, the pole star, the fixed point around which the entire sky appears to rotate. The smallest-seeming pattern holds the center. navigationorientationfixed pointsthe unseen anchor ▸ Field notes Field notes · The Navigator The Navigator doesn't move the way the other constellations move. While everything else in the sky wheels overhead in great arcs through the night, The Navigator holds still — or appears to. Polaris sits less than one degree from the celestial north pole and has been used for navigation for at least three thousand years. There are minds that work like this: that provide a fixed reference, a stable orientation point, for everyone around them. They may not be the most dramatic presence in the room. They may not move in the ways the culture expects. But when you need to know which way is north, you look for them. Kochab was the pole star before Polaris. Due to the slow precession of Earth's axis — a wobble that takes about 26,000 years to complete one cycle — the position of true north moves gradually through the sky. In 3000 BCE, Kochab was the star the navigators used. In 14,000 CE, Vega will take the role. The Navigator is a reminder that fixed points are real but not permanent. L★S · 008 The Forge formerly · Orion · The Hunter 05h 35m · +5° · mag 0.12 The most recognized constellation in the sky. The old charts saw a hunter with a raised club and a belt of three perfect stars. Cosmic Connections Three sites, one web. Nothing here was arrived at in a straight line, and none of it is anybody's alone. This is the page about the links — what travels between Stimpunks, More Realms, and Star Stuff, and why the connections are the content rather than the packaging. Cosmic Connections is Helen Edgar 's phrase for what this collection is doing, and it landed because it was already carrying two histories. The first is Connections , James Burke's BBC series, first broadcast in 1978. Ryan Boren grew up on it, and a good deal of how this collection thinks came from watching it young. Its method is the opposite of the tidy march of great men and eureka moments: Burke's argument is that you cannot understand any piece of the modern world in isolation, because the thing you are holding was assembled out of centuries of unrelated people solving unrelated problems for reasons of their own — profit, boredom, war, faith — none of them aiming at the outcome they produced. An episode starts somewhere medieval and arrives, by way of eight things that have no obvious business with each other, at the object on your desk. Burke went on making the argument across three more series, in 1994, 1997, and 2023. The second is The Cosmic Connection: An Extraterrestrial Perspective , Carl Sagan's 1973 book — the one where he first put the line in print that this whole collection runs on: we are made of star-stuff. Sagan's connection was between our bodies and the interiors of dead stars. Burke's was between a stirrup and a computer. They turn out to be the same move made at different scales: follow the thread, and the thing that looked separate turns out to be continuous with everything around it. Connection isn't a metaphor we apply to the material. It is how the material got made — and how we make it.

Three sites, one web There are three places, and they do different work. Calling them a collaboration is accurate but too flat; what actually happens is traffic. The three sites and what travels between them Stimpunks, More Realms, and Star Stuff drawn as three nodes of one web. Stimpunks sends glossary, patterns, and design method; More Realms sends essays, coinages, and speculative framing; Star Stuff sends both of them back finished, printable, citable artifacts. Every arrow runs in both directions. coinages · citations · corrections glossary patterns design method essays speculative framing felt time · relations STIMPUNKS the garden MORE REALMS the wandering STAR STUFF the flowering no source, no downstream — every edge runs both ways Figure 1 · Not a pipeline with an origin and an output. A web, where each site is upstream of the other two. What actually travels, with receipts From What moves Where it landed More Realms & Autistic Realms Essays, coinages, and the speculative framing — Why Difference Comes First , We Are Made of Relations , My Monotropic Galaxy , the constellation reading of the spiky profile, felt time, shared-air and shared-signal space No. 11 and the Difference-First Frame ; No. 21 ; No. 24 and No. 25 ; No. 29 ; No. 28 and No. 30 in her own voice Stimpunks the knowledge garden Glossary, pattern library, and design method — monotropism, crip time, co-regulation, meerkat mode, ARLES, the ecosystemic model of distress, Cavendish Space, regulation-first No. 17 reads almost entirely out of the glossary; No. 8 turns on Cavendish Space; No. 19 on crip time. Nearly every zine links a term back out. Star Stuff this site Finished artifacts — printable, citable, forkable — plus the fact-checks that go back and correct the sources they came from The ghost pipe entry pairs with Helen's Monotropa uniflora and Monotropism ; Field Guide No. 8 is the companion catalogue to her No. 30 ; every correction lands in the public changelog The Symbioses row is the one that shows the shape best. Helen wrote about Monotropa uniflora — the ghost pipe, which grows no chlorophyll and takes all its carbon second-hand from fungi — as a botanical expression of being monotropic. Monotropa means one turn : the same root as monotropism , the Autistic attention style named by Murray, Lesser and Lawson in 2005. A plant name from Linnaean botany, an attention theory from Autistic researchers, and a mutual-aid ethic about receiving without shame, all sitting on one etymology. Nobody planned that. It was found by following a link.

Why links, and not folders Stimpunks has kept its knowledge as a web of small linked pieces rather than a hierarchy of folders, on the argument that a web of notes with links between them is far more useful than a fixed hierarchical system — the design principle underneath both Tim Berners-Lee's original proposal for the web and Niklas Luhmann's card-index practice. The payoff is not tidiness. It's that connecting notes makes higher-level concepts appear that nobody wrote down , and connecting those makes larger categories appear in turn. The categories are outputs, not inputs. That is emergence , which Stimpunks glosses as the way complex systems and patterns arise out of a multiplicity of relatively simple interactions. It is the same principle physics states as more is different — that a large enough collection of parts obeys laws you cannot read off the parts themselves — and the same one adrienne maree brown builds organizing practice from in Emergent Strategy : small actions and connections create complex systems. Link density and emergence Three panels. In the first, eight notes sit unconnected in a grid — a filing system. In the second, a few links appear between them. In the third, the links are dense enough that a higher-level concept, drawn as a ring around a cluster, has formed without anyone writing it. FILED eight notes, no edges LINKED edges start doing the work EMERGENT a concept nobody wrote Figure 2 · The dashed ring is the point. It is not a folder somebody made; it is a pattern that appeared once the links got dense enough, and it can be named afterward. This is why the collection is built the way it is — every zine cross-linking its siblings, every term linking back out to the glossary, search that indexes down to the individual spread rather than the page. The link density is the argument. A collection where each piece sat in its own folder would make all the same claims and none of the same connections.

Accumulated, not authored The part of Burke that stuck hardest is the timescale. His chains run for centuries, and no single link in them is a breakthrough. Each is a small competent adjustment by someone who could not have known what it would join up with. Progress in Connections is not a person; it's an accumulation. Stimpunks calls this iteration and treats it as the working method rather than a phase: as Cornelius Minor puts it, learning is a series of iterations — not linear, and needing deliberate room made for revision and failure. Which is also why this site publishes its own errors. The changelog and the fact-check ledger are the iteration made visible: what we got wrong, what's right, who caught it. A living document that never shows a correction is just a document making a claim about itself. Everything is a remix The phrase is Kirby Ferguson 's, from his video series Everything Is a Remix (2010–2012, with a fifth part in 2023) — the argument that copying, transforming and combining is not a failure of originality but the mechanism of creativity itself. Stimpunks' license page puts the same thing in the house register: “Nothing comes from nowhere. Punk understood this. So did bricoleurs, rhizome thinkers, and every neurodivergent kid who built something strange and new out of whatever was at hand.” That is why everything here is CC BY-SA 4.0 and made to be printed, forked and passed on. A collection that argued for interdependence and then locked its own doors would be arguing against itself.

The refusals Not: Not a genealogy of geniuses. Burke's whole point is that nobody in the chain saw the end of it, and we are not adding ourselves to a lineage of great minds. Not “everything is connected” as mysticism. Specific links, named and checkable, or it doesn't go on the page. Not interdisciplinary as tourism — borrowing a physics word for its glamour and leaving the physics behind. Not connection as extraction. Crediting the source is the connection; taking the idea and dropping the name is the opposite of one. Not a shared masthead standing in for a shared byline. Where a piece is Helen's, it is hers and says so. Held honestly Emergence is a real property of complex systems, and the physics of more is different is well established. It does not follow that any particular web of notes will produce insight, that our three sites are a complex adaptive system in the technical sense, or that link-density guarantees anything. Burke's chains are also a storyteller's selection: he picks the path that arrives somewhere, and the unchosen paths that went nowhere don't get an episode. We are noticing a rhyme between how knowledge accumulates and how we work, and using it as a method. That's a good reason to link generously. It isn't a proof. So: follow the links. Read a zine, hit a term you don't know, land in the glossary, come back by a different door than you left. That route through the material is not a failure to organize it. The Design System One typeface chosen for legibility, five accents held at near-uniform lightness, and body text that never fades. The visual language of this collection is itself an argument about access — so here it is, with its numbers and its receipts. Every artifact here is a single self-contained HTML file with no dependencies beyond Google web fonts — no build step, no framework, no JavaScript required to read a word. That constraint is the first design decision, and most of the others follow from it. A zine should be one file you can save, print, fork, or hand to someone. Accessibility isn't a layer applied at the end. It is the thing that decides the palette.

Typeface The collection sets its prose in Atkinson Hyperlegible , released free by the Braille Institute in 2019 and named for its founder, J. Robert Atkinson. It was drawn for readers with low vision, and its whole argument is letterform distinction — making characters that are commonly confused resolve differently from each other rather than merely look handsome together. The disambiguation problem I l 1 | 0 O o r n m a e s Look at the tail on the lowercase l , the slashless but narrowed 0 , the distinct apertures on a , e , and s . In a face built for elegance these converge; here they are deliberately pulled apart. For a collection about not being sorted into a norm, a typeface designed by and for people the standard face failed is not a neutral choice. Display · Atkinson Hyperlegible Next Bold The universe doesn't pathologize its own variation. Body · Atkinson Hyperlegible, 1.02rem / 1.75 Almost every atom heavier than helium was forged in stars and their deaths. The calcium in your bones and the iron in your blood came from stars that died before the Earth existed. Labels & counters · Space Mono STIMPUNKS FOUNDATION · ZINE NO. 1 · SPREAD 3 / 7 Two other faces earn their place. Space Mono carries every eyebrow, label, page counter, and colophon — a monospace voice for the machinery around the text, deliberately unlike the prose so it never competes with it. Fraunces appears where a piece needs an editorial register rather than a documentary one; Bone Song , Underground , and You Were Never One Thing are set in it with Space Mono, and use no Atkinson at all. The migration, and the bug it uncovered The collection ran on two versions of the face for a while: 18 pages on Atkinson Hyperlegible Next (the 2025 release, which adds five weights, a variable format, and support for over 150 languages), 26 still on the original, and 3 — the Fraunces-set trio above — on neither. All 44 Atkinson pages now load Next. Switching cost nothing in layout: the same measuring string set at 16px came out 286.97px before and 286.78px after, and across 126 measured text blocks not one changed height, width, or line count. The sweep turned up something worse than a split. Every page requesting Next asked Google Fonts for a 200..900 weight range — but Next only publishes 200–800 , so the request returned HTTP 400 and no @font-face rule at all. Those pages had been quietly falling back to system-ui for every visitor who didn't happen to have the font installed locally, which is to say almost all of them. A typeface picked specifically because it was drawn for readers the standard face fails was not reaching those readers. Corrected to 200..800 ; the woff2 now actually downloads.

Palette The canonical tokens live in starstuff.css as :root { --sp-* } — one source of truth for every recurring color. Each page aliases them inline ( --purple: var(--sp-purple) ), so a palette change happens in one place instead of forty-seven. A new shared color means a new --sp- token, never a hex pasted across pages.

Grounds --sp-void-deep #07070f L* 2.1 --sp-void #0a0a14 L* 3.0 --sp-deep #0d0d1a L* 4.0 --sp-page #0f0f1c L* 4.8 --sp-card #0f0f2a L* 5.5 None of them is black. Each carries a violet cast — #0a0a14 sits at hue 290° in CIELAB — so the ground reads as night rather than as absence. --sp-card is the most saturated of the five, which is what makes a card lift off the page without a border or a shadow doing the work.

Accents --sp-purple #a78bfa L* 64.6 · 7.24:1 --sp-pink #f472b6 L* 65.5 · 7.44:1 --sp-gold #fbbf24 L* 80.7 · 11.80:1 --sp-cyan #22d3ee L* 77.9 · 10.90:1 --sp-green #4ade80 L* 79.2 · 11.30:1 Five accents, all of them clustered between L* 64.6 and 80.7 — a spread of 16 points across the whole set. That tight band is the discipline: any accent can replace any other on a given page without changing how heavy the page feels. It's why each zine can be tinted differently (cyan for water, green for aurora, gold for bone) and still be recognizably the same collection. The lowest-contrast accent on the darkest ground still clears 7.2:1 .

Text & neutrals --sp-white #f9fafb L* 98.2 · 18.84:1 --sp-white-soft #f4f2fb L* 95.9 · 17.76:1 --sp-secondary-soft #d4d0e4 L* 84.3 · 13.07:1 --sp-muted #c4b5d4 L* 75.8 · 10.23:1 --sp-secondary #b8aed0 L* 72.9 · 9.38:1 --sp-dim #8a86a0 L* 57.1 · 5.62:1 --sp-dim-soft #807d98 L* 53.5 · 4.97:1 Note what the ladder does not do: it never dips below full opacity to make text quieter. "Muted" here means a different hue at high contrast, not the same hue at 60% alpha. Every value above clears WCAG AA for body text against --sp-void — the dimmest by the smallest margin, and only after being lifted for exactly that reason. The one that failed, and what it cost to fix --sp-dim-soft used to be #63607a — 3.27:1 , under the 4.5:1 AA floor. It styles page counters, series numbers, colophons and refs at 0.5–0.55rem, so it is small text and gets no large-text exemption; publishing a contrast table with that in it was the thing that made it obvious. Raised to #807d98 : same CIELAB hue and chroma, L* 41.9 → 53.5, now 4.97:1 on the void and 4.73:1 on the lightest ground, still visibly softer than --sp-dim . Auditing every text element against its own composited background then turned up four more: an accent pink on a tinted card that came to 4.43:1, three runs of alpha-faded cream on the broadside — the exact "faded gray" this system claims to refuse — and two links left unstyled, falling back to the browser's default blue at 2.11:1 on near-black. All fixed. All 47 pages now pass AA on screen.

Palette lineage The palette began as a Solarized dark variant. That happened before this repository existed, so there's no commit to point at — and it matters less than it sounds, because none of Solarized's sixteen values survive anywhere in the collection. The accents are Tailwind CSS v3's 400-weight ramp, exactly: --sp-purple is violet-400, --sp-pink is pink-400, --sp-gold is amber-400, --sp-cyan is cyan-400, --sp-green is green-400, --sp-white is gray-50. The grounds are ours; no Tailwind gray is that violet. What we kept from Ethan Schoonover is the method , and it's worth naming precisely because the method is the valuable part: A small, fixed, named accent set used as semantic tokens rather than color picked per occasion. --sp-* is that idea. Accents pinned to a narrow lightness band, so substitution doesn't disturb the page. Ours sit at L* 64.6–80.7; Solarized's at L* 49.1–60.1. A ground that refuses pure black and commits to a hue. Solarized's #002b36 leans cyan at hue 230°; our #0a0a14 leans violet at 290°. Warm cream instead of white for paper — --paper: #f5f0e8 in the broadside, --bone: #e8dfc8 in Bone Song , both close cousins of Solarized's base3 #fdf6e3 . And then we threw out its central move. Solarized's stated goal is to reduce brightness contrast while keeping hue separation. We push contrast as high as it goes: Body text against its own ground Scheme Text Ground Contrast Star Stuff #f9fafb #0a0a14 18.84:1 Solarized dark #839496 #002b36 4.75:1 Solarized dark (emphasis) #93a1a1 #073642 4.86:1 "Full-opacity body text, no faded grays" is a direct repudiation of the scheme this palette started from. A low-contrast colorscheme is a lovely thing in a code editor at 2am and the wrong thing entirely for a document meant to be readable by people with low vision, printed on a cheap printer, and handed across a table. Accessibility-first won the argument. Credit Solarized for the discipline, not for the colors.

Principles Full opacity Text is never dimmed with alpha to signal hierarchy. Hierarchy comes from size, weight, and hue at full strength. Generous leading Body copy runs 1.75 line-height. Long measure is capped around 36–38rem so lines stay trackable. 8px radius Cards round at 8px — soft enough to read as an object, tight enough to stay documentary. 3px left border A colored left rule marks anything set apart: claims, callouts, specimens, cards. The system's most reused gesture. Pure-CSS starfield Stars are layered radial-gradient stops on body::before , plus a few absolutely-positioned twinkling dots. No images, no canvas. Spectrum rule A 2px gradient through all five accents, used once per page as a signature — the palette introducing itself.
Motion, and the option to refuse it

Motion, and the option to refuse it The starfield twinkles from one shared @keyframes twinkle-anim in starstuff.css — it used to be copy-pasted into some twenty-five pages. Anyone whose system asks for less motion gets none: a global prefers-reduced-motion block collapses every animation and transition to 0.001ms and disables smooth scrolling, across every page at once. Motion here is decoration, and decoration must be declinable.

The refusals Not: Not low-contrast because low-contrast looks sophisticated. Not gray text on gray backgrounds to signal "secondary." Not a framework, a build step, or a bundle to read one page of prose. Not a design system that can't survive being printed in black and white. Not accessibility as a compliance checkbox added after the visual design was settled.

Print These are meant to be printed and handed to people, so paper is a first-class target rather than an afterthought. starstuff.css strips the site navigation and paging chrome from every printed page — that chrome is never content. On paper the whole collection inverts: white sheet, near-black type, decoration dropped. Because every page aliases the --sp-* tokens, the shared stylesheet inverts them once inside @media print and all forty-seven pages follow. Accents become ink there too — gold #fbbf24 on white is 1.6:1, so an accent that carries meaning as text has to give up its color to stay readable. The one exception is the spectrum rule, a 2px sliver kept in full color with print-color-adjust: exact , which survives the browser's background-graphics setting. Diagrams inherit the same treatment: SVG paints with fill and stroke rather than color , so labels and line art are inverted separately — the diagrams are content here, not ornament. Paged zines also turn inside out for paper. On screen a zine shows one .spread at a time; a single Cmd/Ctrl+P reveals every spread and starts each on its own sheet, so you get the whole zine rather than the visible page. This was broken until it wasn't Worth recording plainly, because the failure is more instructive than the fix. Browsers leave "Background graphics" off by default. For most of this collection's life, no page inverted its colors for print — so a light-on-dark zine sent near-white type to a white sheet and printed blank . Measured with print media emulated, 44 of 46 pages printed illegibly . On one, no pixel anywhere on the sheet was darker than mid-gray. The Bone Song poem — a piece built to be printed and handed to someone — came out as an empty page. Only the changelog was correct. The L★S broadside was half-right: its recto prints as designed, but its verso carried the poem in cream on near-black and vanished too. All forty-seven pages now print legibly, verified two ways — computed text contrast against white for every text element, and pixel sampling of the rendered sheet. A stated principle nobody measures is a wish.

Shared assets What every page pulls in File Carries starstuff.css The --sp-* palette tokens, the .ss-nav site navigation, the shared twinkle keyframe, the reduced-motion block, the print rules, and the injected spread-footer nav styles. starstuff.js Per-spread prev/next controls and #spread-N deep linking for paged zines. A safe no-op on any page that isn't one. favicon.svg The L★S mark. og-card.jpg The 1200×630 link-unfurl card shared by every page. Everything is linked by relative URL, which is what lets any page be saved, moved, or served from a subdirectory without breaking. Each page tints the shared nav by setting one custom property — --nav-accent — on the nav element, which is the whole theming API. Reuse it This system is CC BY-SA 4.0 , like everything else here. Take the tokens, take the contrast floor, take the refusals. If you build something with it, the only ask is that you keep it free and pass it on. Solidarity, not charity. Every correction to this page, and to every piece in the collection, gets published in the changelog — our own errors included. The Difference-First Frame A summary of Helen Edgar's essay Why Difference Comes First (Autistic Realms · More Realms), shared with Stimpunks and used with her blessing. Reference notes behind Love You Down To Your Star Stuff — for a funder, researcher, or skeptical parent who asks why difference gets to be the starting point. A resonant frame, not a proof. What this is, and isn't This is not physics or philosophy proving that our ethic is true. Experts disagree about much of what follows, and relational quantum mechanics in particular is one interpretation among several, not settled consensus. What this is: a resonance — three fields, working independently at wildly different scales, keep arriving at the same shape of idea. That convergence is worth having in our back pocket. It is not evidence, and we will not present it as evidence. Zine No. 9, The Lines We Drew , warns against precisely the move we must avoid here: dressing a human value up as a law of nature, the way the bell curve was recruited to make "normal" look like physics and eugenics followed. So we say it plainly, up front. The atoms do not owe us this conclusion. We are noticing a rhyme, not collecting a proof.

The claim, in one line Sameness is the fragile or fabricated thing. Difference isn't a deviation from a baseline — it's the condition anything real, including a self, gets made from. One clarification keeps that line honest, because it braids together two different mechanisms that happen to teach the same lesson. At the cosmic scale, sameness is fragile : near-uniformity was simply the early universe's default, and it was unstable — the smallest unevenness grew into everything. At the social scale, sameness is fabricated : the "typical profile," the flat baseline, is manufactured and then treated as ground truth. Two mechanisms. One moral. We should never blur them into a single tidy slogan, because the precision is where the argument holds.

Three scales, one shape Cosmology · the strongest leg The early universe was almost perfectly uniform: the cosmic microwave background — the oldest light we can see, the Big Bang's afterglow — varies in temperature by only about one part in 100,000 across the whole sky. A truly uniform cosmos would have stayed a dead, featureless fog forever: nothing dense enough for gravity to gather, no stars, no us. Everything that exists, exists because that near-sameness broke. The tiny perturbations are not noise on top of the story; they are the story. This part is well established (Penzias & Wilson 1965; mapped by COBE, WMAP, and Planck). Philosophy · the core Gilles Deleuze argued that Western thought habitually treats difference as secondary — judged by a thing's identity to a concept, its opposition to a contrast, its analogy to a standard, its resemblance to an ideal. All four smuggle in the same assumption: that a fixed baseline exists first, and difference is only the distance from it. Deleuze reverses it — identity is produced out of a prior field of difference, not the ground difference strays from (Deleuze 1994). That is exactly what a diagnostic model does to Autistic people: it measures us against identity, opposition, analogy, and resemblance to a "typical" profile that was never the ground truth to begin with. The flat line is the construct. Difference is what's actually there. Damian Milton's work on the ontological status of autism (Milton 2012) makes a kindred point from inside autism studies — the neurodivergent "spiky profile" gets read as deviation from a flat, typical baseline that was never the ground truth. Quantum physics · the most speculative, most hedged At the opposite end of every scale, Carlo Rovelli's Relational Quantum Mechanics proposes that particles don't carry fixed, standalone properties — what a thing is only becomes determinate in relation to another system (Rovelli 1996). Reading Rovelli from the inside, Helen describes not being a fixed, bounded thing moving through the world but something that emerges in and through its relations and encounters (Edgar 2026). We flag this leg as the shakiest: it is interpretation, offered as rhyme, not as physics settling a question about people. (A related move we add here, not in Helen's essay: Karen Barad's agential realism holds that it is relationships, not pre-given separate objects, that come first — Barad 2007.)
One term we have to handle carefully

One term we have to handle carefully Deleuze's "smooth space" (Deleuze & Guattari 1987) does not mean uniform. It means a field of ungridded, intensive variation — the opposite of striated space, which is fixed, measured, gridded. So the CMB's uniform fog is not "smooth" in Deleuze's sense; it's a pre-individual field, prior to both. The useful move is not "the universe was smooth and that's good." It's that diagnostic categories are the striation — the grid laid over a field that was full of ungridded variation before the grid arrived — and what LYDTYSS protects (the spiky profile, ★stuff, no-wrong-configuration) is the ungridded variation the grid keeps trying, and failing, to fully capture.

The bridge: ethodiversity Between the cosmic argument and the single nervous system sits a middle layer, and it keeps the whole thing from being merely personal or merely abstract. Ombre Tarragnat's ethodiversity — the variety of ways of being and behaving across humans and other animals — makes the same claim at the scale of behaviour, and locates it precisely: not inside one organism, but as a property of a relational field , the way biodiversity belongs to an ecosystem rather than any single species in it (Tarragnat 2025). Its opposite, ethonormativity — the unspoken grid of which ways of being are allowed to count — is functionally striation applied to behaviour: a grid laid over a field that was varied before the grid arrived. Stimpunks keeps this in the ethodiversity glossary ; the term also has earlier roots in conservation biology (Cordero-Rivera 2017), which we note as a Stimpunks aside rather than part of Helen's essay. So the chain runs: CMB perturbations, quantum relation, Deleuzian difference-before-identity (why difference is fundamental) → ethodiversity (the same claim, scaled to behaviour and species) → the spiky profile and LYDTYSS (the same claim again, scaled to one bodymind). Ethodiversity is what lets the cosmic-scale idea land as something ecological and communal, not only intimate. Zine No. 8, The Universe Runs on Difference, already carries this layer.
What it gives LYDTYSS — and how to use it

What it gives LYDTYSS — and how to use it It doesn't make the phrase heavier. LYDTYSS should stay exactly as unadorned as it is; the page works because it stays intimate, not academic, and this material must never be folded into it. What it gives us is an answer , ready when someone asks why difference gets to be the starting point rather than a thing to explain or excuse: because that's the shape reality takes wherever we've actually looked, from the CMB to a nervous system. Not despite the mess — because of it. Hold this as backing material: something to draw on if a funder, researcher, or skeptical parent asks us to justify the framing. Physics and philosophy have been implicit in the zines already; if this becomes a future zine, its distinct claim must stay clear of No. 8. No. 8's point is one of breadth — variety beats monoculture. This page's point is deeper and different: difference is ontologically prior — identity is produced out of a field of difference, not the baseline it deviates from. "Difference comes first," not merely "difference is good." Framed that way, it's a genuine addition, and the ontological floor under both No. 8 and No. 9. If it becomes a zine, it should keep Helen's first-person voice and byline — the essay's intimacy is the point, and flattening it into institutional "we" would lose exactly what makes it land.

On the CMB, for the curious The cosmic microwave background is the oldest light we can observe — the Big Bang's afterglow. For about 380,000 years the universe was too hot and dense for light to travel freely; once it cooled enough for atoms to form, light was released to travel in straight lines, and it has been arriving ever since as faint microwave radiation from every direction. Two things matter here: it is extremely uniform (about one part in 100,000), and the tiny variations that do exist are everything — gravity grew them into galaxies, stars, and us. H L★S · 001 The First Light Hydrogen · H Z 1 · 1.008 u · ~10% of you The oldest thing in your body. Nearly all your hydrogen was made in the first minutes of the universe, before there were any stars to make anything. You carry the Big Bang around in every drop of the water you mostly are. oldestwaterthe big bangeverywhere ▸ Field notes Field notes · Hydrogen Hydrogen is the one element in you that no star ever made. It condensed out of the cooling universe in the first minutes after the Big Bang and has been around ever since — roughly 13.8 billion years. Every other atom in you is younger. You are mostly water, and water is mostly hydrogen by count, so the oldest material in the cosmos is also the most intimate. It's in your blood, your cells, the tears on your face. By sheer number of atoms, you are mostly the early universe. The humble hydrogen bond — weak, temporary, endlessly re-formed — is what lets water behave the way it does and lets the two strands of your DNA hold hands and let go. The oldest atom makes the most provisional, most relational bonds. That feels about right. The most abundant thing in you is a gift from stars that had to die to make it. So the reframe is simple arithmetic: you are two-thirds inheritance, by weight. Before it was ever your breath, it was starlight's ash, drifting for ages until gravity gathered it into an ocean, and the ocean into you. C L★S · 003 The Scaffold Carbon · C Z 6 · 12.011 u · ~18% of you Every large molecule in you hangs on a carbon frame — proteins, fats, sugars, DNA. It is built inside aging stars by a fusion trick so improbable that its discovery reads like the universe leaving a note. backbonethe scaffoldred giantslife's frame ▸ Field notes Field notes · Carbon Carbon is the element life is strung on. With four bonds to offer, it links into rings and chains long enough to carry all the information and machinery a body needs — the backbone of proteins, fats, sugars, and DNA alike. It is made in aging stars by the triple-alpha process, three helium nuclei fusing almost at once. The step is so unlikely that Fred Hoyle famously predicted carbon must have a specific internal resonance to make it work at all — reasoning backward from the fact that carbon-based observers existed to ask the question. The resonance was there. The frame you're built on exists because of a coincidence delicate enough to be mistaken for intent. We won't claim intent. We'll just note that the scaffold holding you up was hard to make, and got made anyway. Umwelt · the sealed world No view from nowhere A century ago, the biologist Jakob von Uexküll asked a strange question: what is the world like for a tick? The answer is almost nothing — and yet complete. She waits, blind and deaf, for three signals: the warmth of a mammal, the smell of butyric acid, the touch of skin. On those three her whole life turns. That is her Umwelt — not a poorer version of our world, but her entire sky. This is the move that changes everything. Each creature lives within its own perceptual world, and each world is whole — not a partial glimpse of one true reality waiting underneath. There is no underneath. There is no view from nowhere. But whole is not the same as walled: a sky is a soap bubble, not a fortress — permeable, kept aloft by encounter, and never guaranteed. The "real world" — neutral, default, the one we assume we all share — no one has ever sensed it. The variety of minds No two alike Nervous systems are roughly 550 million years old, and life has been improvising them ever since — into shapes almost nothing like ours. An octopus keeps most of its neurons in its arms, so each arm half-thinks for itself. A jellyfish has no brain and no centre at all — just a net of nerves ringing its body. A nematode worm runs an entire life on exactly 302 neurons, every connection mapped. No two of these are the same — and no two within a kind are, either. Every nervous system is a one-off, tuned by body and history and the particular world it grew up sensing. So read neurodiversity at face value and it can't mean only us. It means the whole living spread of ways to have a nervous system. There is no standard nervous system, any more than there is a standard mind. The grid over behaviour The rule that says behave If ethodiversity is the field, ethonormativity is the grid laid over it: the unwritten, humanist rule about which behaviours are allowed and expected in a given animal — human or not — in a given room. And the grid has teeth. The horse who refuses the rider; the frightened or depressed cat who resists being petted and lashes out — for departing from the script, Tarragnat notes, animals like these "are often abandoned or euthanised." The reframe is the one this whole collection keeps making. The behaviour read from outside as a malfunction is, from inside, a subjective response that makes sense. Neurodivergent people are so often pathologised precisely by being animalised — cast as less-than-human, machine-like, without an inner life. A story that travels with an animal

The claim A story that travels with an animal Most claims about connection are wishes. This one is a range map. In Sand Talk, Tyson Yunkaporta — Apalech clan, Wik — sets out to tell part of a big story, and marks plainly whose it is and that it was given to be given away: "I will tell parts of a big story, a metastory that connects and extends all over Australia through massive songlines in the earth and sky, a Star Dreaming that Juma Fejo from the Larrakia People wants to share with all peoples. It goes everywhere that turtles go—and there are turtles all over the world, even in desert country, so it connects everybody." Tyson Yunkaporta, Sand Talk (2019), p. 15 Read quickly, that last sentence sounds like a lovely figure of speech. It isn't one. It is a testable statement about where an animal lives, and the reach of the story is pinned to the reach of the turtle. So we did the obvious thing and checked. The sentence holds. What follows is what we found on the way — including two places where the turtle's own biology turns out to say the opposite of what everybody assumes. A path that meanders is not a path that failed. The range Every continent but one Roughly 357 living species of turtle, and they are almost everywhere you are. Sea turtles in every warm ocean. Freshwater turtles in rivers, lakes, billabongs, ditches, drainage canals and city ponds on six continents. Tortoises on land from the Mojave to Madagascar to the Aldabra atoll. Softshells buried in river mud. The only continent without them is Antarctica — and the only reason is the cold. They are also old. The turtle body plan has been recognisably itself for more than 200 million years. It has crossed oceans, watched continents split, and outlasted the animals that were supposed to be the story. Yunkaporta's sentence works because of a fact about the world, not a fact about language. If you want one animal that nearly every human community on Earth has had to live alongside, look at your options. There are not many. The turtle is one of them. Even in desert country The ones who wait underneath "Even in desert country" is the part of the sentence that sounds like a stretch. It is the part that is most literally true. In the Pilbara and Gascoyne of Western Australia, Chelodina steindachneri lives in pools that can dry up and stay dry for a year or more. It does not leave and it does not die. It digs into the riverbed or bank and waits, and comes back to the surface after heavy rain. Across the world in the Mojave, the desert tortoise Gopherus agassizii spends up to 95% of its life underground, in burrows, out of a heat that would kill it in the open. And here is the part that makes it more than trivia: those burrows are not only the tortoise's. Other animals shelter in them. The desert tortoise is a keystone species — the one who dug itself a survivable place made a survivable place for everybody else. The reversal The shell was a shovel Everyone knows what a turtle shell is for. Everyone is wrong about how it started. It did not begin as armour. In Eunotosaurus africanus, an early relative on the turtle stem line from the South African Karoo, the ribs broaden long before there is anything shell-like to hide inside. Lyson and colleagues (Current Biology, 2016) put the case plainly: broadened ribs on their own provide little protection, and they cost you — a stiffened trunk shortens your stride and slows you down, and it gets in the way of breathing. What broad ribs are good for is digging. A rigid trunk is a stable base to swing a powerful forelimb against. The shell starts as the anchor for a shovel. Protection is an exaptation — a use the structure was not built for, discovered later, and now the only use anyone remembers. Read it back onto spread 4 and the sentence closes: the animal that got everywhere, including desert country, got there by first learning to go down. They had to invent a new way to breathe

The cost They had to invent a new way to breathe Every adaptation is a bargain, and in turtles you can read the receipt. Almost every land vertebrate breathes with its ribs. The ribcage expands, the lungs fill. Mammals, birds, crocodilians, lizards — all of us, all the time, without thinking about it. Lock your ribs into a shell and that door closes. It is not a small inconvenience; it is the removal of the standard mechanism for staying alive. And Lyson and colleagues (Nature Communications, 2014) found the stem-line evidence for exactly this trade already in place: a rigid ribcage, the inferred loss of the muscles between the ribs, and the bony signatures of a different system taking over. What took over is a sling of abdominal muscle wrapped around the lungs and organs — a division of labour in which the ribs gave up ventilation and the belly muscles picked it up. No other animal breathes this way. So: they lost the ordinary way, and they are not diminished. They are a turtle. Two ways to put a neck away

Two answers Two ways to put a neck away Once you have a shell, you have a head problem. There are two solutions alive today, and neither is the right one. The hidden-necked turtles — Cryptodira — fold the neck vertically, in an S, and pull the head straight back under the front of the shell. Sea turtles, tortoises, snappers, sliders, softshells. They are the ones most people picture. The side-necked turtles — Pleurodira — do not pull back at all. They lay the neck sideways along the shell's edge, tucking the head in under the rim. Every living one lives in fresh water in the southern hemisphere: South America, Africa and Madagascar, and Australia. Their map is a map of Gondwana, the supercontinent that broke apart beneath them. These are not a good version and a poor version. They are two lineages that met the same constraint and answered it differently, and both are still here, hundreds of millions of years on. The turtle a reader in Sydney pictures and the turtle a reader in Ohio pictures fold their heads away by different means. Sex is not in the genes

The sand decides Sex is not in the genes In most turtles, nothing in the egg says what sex the hatchling will be. The nest says. It is called temperature-dependent sex determination. Cooler sand, one outcome; warmer sand, the other; and a narrow pivotal temperature between them where a fraction of a degree decides. The machinery is now partly known: the enzyme KDM6B strips a silencing mark from the male-determining gene Dmrt1 and switches the male path on, and at warmer, female-producing temperatures a signalling protein binds the Kdm6b locus and shuts it down. And it is not even tidy across the group. In the Asian yellow pond turtle, researchers found XY chromosomes and temperature sensitivity in the same animal, working together. The neat binary of "genetic or environmental" was ours, not the turtles'. Which brings us to the philosophers of the Discworld. In Terry Pratchett's novels, the great turtle Great A'Tuin carries the world, and the learned spend enormous effort trying to determine A'Tuin's sex. They never manage it. The joke is better than they knew. They were looking in the wrong place. In a real turtle the answer is not written in the animal at all. It is in the temperature of the sand where somebody laid it. what the nest decides cooler warmer pivotal temperature a fraction of a degree KDM6B on Dmrt1 switched on pSTAT3 represses Kdm6b · male path off and in some species, XY chromosomes as well — both at once temperature-dependent sex determination the binary was ours, not theirs Everywhere That Turtles Go · Stimpunks
A map made of the planet

Finding the way back A map made of the planet A sea turtle hatchling crosses the beach once, in the dark, weighing less than a bar of soap. Decades later it comes back to lay its own eggs on the same stretch of coast. How? Earth's magnetic field varies from place to place, and every stretch of coastline carries a slightly different signature. The evidence is that a hatchling learns the field of its natal beach and holds onto it — geomagnetic imprinting — then uses it to navigate home across an ocean. Brothers and Lohmann (Current Biology, 2015) tested this against nineteen years of nesting records along 600 km of Florida coast. As the field drifted, the nesting drifted with it. Where two stretches of coast came to share a signature, turtles crowded in; where the signatures pulled apart, nesting thinned. They are carrying a route in the body, learned once, held for a lifetime, and read against a planet that keeps quietly moving underneath it. A route held as knowledge, carried across a life, tying a people to a country. That is a rhyme with what a songline does — and a rhyme is all it is. The Larrakia story is not turtle magnetoreception, and turtle magnetoreception is not a songline. The pattern in the shell One, two, three, five, eight Yunkaporta records Oldman Juma Fejo giving the sequence in the shell, and then records their own reaction to it: "I couldn't believe it when Oldman Juma told me the sequence—one became two, then three, then five in a row along the center of the shell. Then, at the eight points where each part met, eight new parts formed. The sequence goes: 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, and so on." Tyson Yunkaporta, Sand Talk (2019), pp. 225–226 Here is what is on an actual carapace. The keratin plates — scutes — are laid out to a plan: a small one at the neck, then five down the midline, flanked by four pairs at the sides and about twelve pairs around the rim. Five in a row along the centre of the shell is not a poetic flourish. It is what you count when you look. And we will say plainly where the passage stops being biology. Yunkaporta goes on to call this the golden ratio "that all nature is built upon, from flowers and trees to your body and even DNA." That last step is not supported. The golden ratio is not a general law of living form, and it is not in the structure of DNA. Both things are true at once, and we are not going to collapse them. A knowledge system that counts a real pattern in a real animal is not made better by a modern number, and not made worse by that number turning out to be over-claimed. The thesis Not the same turtle Because turtles are almost everywhere, almost everybody had to think with one. What they thought is not the same thought. In Haudenosaunee and Anishinaabe accounts, Sky Woman falls, animals dive for earth, the muskrat surfaces with mud in its claws, and the land is spread on a great turtle's back. This is why Turtle Island is a name for the continent — not a metaphor for it, a name. In the Chinese Huainanzi, the four poles of the world collapse, and Nüwa cuts the legs from the great sea turtle ao to prop the sky back up. The turtle is not a foundation; it is a repair. In the Hindu texts, Kurma is Vishnu's tortoise form, a pivot on the seabed so a mountain can be used to churn the ocean. Kurma is not carrying the world. The world-on-a-turtle's-back story is not this story, and the conflation is a Western habit. And in Terry Pratchett's Discworld, Great A'Tuin — Chelys galactica — swims through space with the world on its back, and nobody knows where or why. Here is the connection, and it is not that these are one story. They are five peoples who met the same animal and each made something different of it. The turtle didn't unify anybody. It gave everybody something to think with, and then let them think. A note we owe you: "turtles all the way down" is not William James and not Bertrand Russell. James wrote it with rocks, in 1882. The turtle version was hung on him in a 1967 thesis and has been repeated ever since. Its earliest printed appearance is from 1854. four turtles, drawn four ways, on purpose turtle island the land itself ao · huainanzi legs as pillars — a repair kurma a pivot for churning not a world-bearer great a'tuin chelys galactica and the star dreaming larrakia · told by its own people the connection is the meeting, not the matching five peoples, one animal, five thoughts not versions of each other Everywhere That Turtles Go · Stimpunks

What it costs to say this The shell is bone One last fact, and then the thing we actually came to say. A turtle shell is not a house it climbed into. The carapace is the animal's ribs and vertebrae, grown wide and fused. It is bone. And bone, as Iwao Yasuda found in the 1950s, is piezoelectric: press it and it answers with a small electrical charge. That is where this whole collection started, on page one of Bone Song. So the shell is not inert cover. It is a living structure that turns pressure into signal — the part of the animal that responds when the world leans on it. Which is why the phrase grates. "Come out of your shell" is said to quiet kids, to Autistic kids, to anyone whose way of being in a room is read as absence. It assumes the shell is a hiding place, and that the real person is elsewhere. In the animal that gave us the phrase, the shell is the skeleton. There is no coming out. There is no one in there behind it. The shell was never armour. It was how somebody got underground, and stayed alive, and then went everywhere. And the ones who did all that are in trouble. Around 75% of the testudine species studied show slow or negligible senescence — most of them age more slowly than we do, and some barely age at all. A lineage that largely does not die of being old is being killed anyway: roughly half of all turtle species are threatened. Deep time is no protection from a net, a road, or a bought beach. ~75% of studied testudines age slowly or not at all ~48% of all turtle species are threatened NotNot "come out of your shell." The shell is the skeleton. There is nobody hiding behind it. NotNot one world turtle. Five traditions are not five drafts of one story, and treating them that way is how a knowledge system gets flattened into a motif. NotNot a proof. Turtles rhyme with what we want to say about difference. The ethics do not rest on the rhyme; difference would deserve welcome in a universe that made only one shape. NotNot a mascot. Borrowing the animal for a metaphor is not the same as leaving it a beach to come back to. NotNot deep time as comfort. Surviving the Permian does not survive us. Everywhere That Turtles Go is Zine No. 35 in the Stimpunks Star Stuff series. We quote that published account and do not retell the story in our own voice; it is not ours to narrate. Three things we are flagging rather than smoothing. One: Yunkaporta's Fibonacci passage extends to the claim that the golden ratio is what "all nature is built upon, from flowers and trees to your body and even DNA." The five vertebral scutes down the midline of a carapace are real and countable; the general golden-ratio-in-nature claim, and specifically the golden ratio in DNA, are not supported, and we say so on spread 10 rather than quietly omitting it. Carrying a knowledge system faithfully includes not laundering an empirical claim through it. Two: the resemblance between natal homing and songlines is a rhyme. A route held in the body across a lifetime is not the same kind of thing as a route held in law, song and country by a people, and we are not claiming it explains anything about the other. Three: the Didactylos passage shipped as unconfirmed — attribution to Small Gods was solid but the wording had come from quote aggregators, which this house treats as leads and not as citations. Ryan then checked it against the book. It is verbatim, including the italic on the final Moves, so the zine now quotes the whole run rather than a fragment. We are leaving this note in rather than deleting it: the point is not that we were right, it is that we did not know we were until somebody opened the page. See the changelog, where corrections and closures are published rather than buried. And the standing one: as about.html puts it, we are noticing a rhyme, not collecting a proof. That variation persists in nature is not why difference deserves welcome. The star stuff is Carl Sagan's, and the SN 1006 remnant on every Stimpunks page. The universe doesn't pathologize its own variation. It just keeps making animals that go everywhere, and letting them go. The pattern Everything keeps becoming a crab Give the ocean enough time and it keeps arriving at the same animal. A wide flattened shell, a tail tucked under, legs out to the sides. Crustaceans have found that body over and over, from ancestors that looked nothing like each other and were never trying to match. The zoologist L. A. Borradaile named it in 1916 — carcinization, which he called one of the many attempts of Nature to evolve a crab. It happened at least five times: once or twice among the true crabs, and at least three times among the false ones — porcelain crabs, hairy stone crabs, king crabs. King crabs are not crabs. They came up out of hermit crabs and arrived at the shape anyway. And it isn't only crabs. Camera eyes evolved separately in us and in octopuses. Echolocation in bats and in whales. Flight in insects, pterosaurs, birds, bats. Convergence is real. We're not here to debunk it — it's one of the most striking things biology has found. We're here for what happens next, when a real pattern gets read as a verdict. five separate arrivals, one silhouette spongecrabs eubrachy-urans porcelaincrabs hairy stonecrabs kingcrabs nobody was copying anybody carcinization · borradaile 1916 at least five times over Five Times a Crab · Stimpunks

The part nobody quotes And lost seven times The crab body plan was gained at least five times. It was lost at least seven. Biologists have a word for that too: decarcinization. Wolfe, Luque and Bracken-Grissom, reviewing the whole field in 2021, count the losses as well as the gains — and add that there were likely several other losses besides, among fossil and living lineages both. Read the tally again, because the headline never does. Leaving the crab form is the more common event. Lineages roll down into that valley and then climb back out of it, over and over, across hundreds of millions of years. Which settles something. If the crab were the answer — the optimum, the ultimate form, the place complexity is trying to get to — then nothing would ever leave. Inside the basin Convergence is not sameness Here is the thing the word "converge" hides. They did not end up alike. Crab-shaped lineages live in nearly every habitat on Earth — bright coral reefs, sealed marine caves, abyssal plain, mountain streams, dry land. Their bodies run from millimetres to metres. Reviewing that range, Wolfe and colleagues reach for Darwin's last line in the Origin and call it endless forms most beautiful. So five lineages converged on a description — wide, flat, tucked — and then diversified wildly inside it. The attractor isn't a point. It's a neighbourhood, roomy enough to hold a pea-sized cave dweller and a metre-wide giant and count both as the same solution. We already know this shape of argument. Sharing a category never made anyone identical, and the spiky profile survives the merge. Two rivers meeting run braided for miles. Arriving at the same name is not arriving at the same shape. one basin · millimetres to metres marine cave coral reef abyssal plain same solution · endless forms the attractor is a neighbourhood not a point Five Times a Crab · Stimpunks

The route Same window, different wiring Our eye and the octopus's eye are the showpiece of convergence: lens, iris, retina, a chamber that throws an image. Built independently. Built backwards from each other. In our retina the light-sensing cells face away from the light, and their nerve fibres run back across the retina's inner surface and bundle out through it — which punches a hole in our field of view. You have a blind spot because of how yours is wired. The octopus's photoreceptors face the light, and the nerves leave from behind. No hole. Same outcome. Opposite construction. The function converged; the machinery never did. Now say it about people. A system that grades the route instead of the outcome will mark a different route wrong — and a body that got there another way looks like a malfunction rather than an eye. two camera eyes, wired opposite vertebrate nerves cross the retina → a blind spot octopus nerves leave from behind → no blind spot the outcome matched the route never did grade the route and you'll fail an eye convergent function, divergent build ours is the one with the hole in it Five Times a Crab · Stimpunks

The terrain The valley, not the virtue Why does anything converge? Because the ground slopes. The embryologist C. H. Waddington drew the picture in 1957: development as a ball rolling down a landscape of branching valleys, its path canalized — a word he'd coined in 1942 — by the shape of the terrain rather than aimed at a target. Deep valley, reliable outcome. Same ball, different landscape, different animal. "Attractor" is a real term, borrowed here. It comes from dynamical systems — Lorenz found his in 1963 — where it means a state a system settles toward. Applied to evolution or to culture it is a metaphor, a good one, doing analogical work. We should say that out loud, because the metaphor is what makes the overreach feel rigorous. And the honest state of the flagship case: reviewing all of it, Wolfe and colleagues report that the reasons for the repeated evolution of the crab-like body plan remain a mystery. They add that nobody yet knows whether it's true convergence or a shared inheritance being switched back on. So the crab is not a proven optimum. It's a place the ground happens to slope toward, for reasons still being worked out. Convergence is evidence about terrain — the constraints, the pressures, the materials at hand — and not about the merit of whatever lands in the bottom. waddington's landscape the slope decides, not the destination canalization · waddington 1942, 1957 a valley is not a verdict Five Times a Crab · Stimpunks

Ripeness Ideas ripen too Discovery converges the same way bodies do, and for the same reason. Newton had calculus by about 1666; Leibniz built it independently in the 1670s, and they spent years fighting about it. That story gets told as an anomaly. It isn't one. In 1922 Ogburn and Thomas assembled a list of 148 inventions and discoveries made independently by two or more people — sunspots four times over in 1611, conservation of energy four times in 1847, the telescope claimed by nine. Reviewing the same phenomenon decades later, Robert K. Merton concluded that these "multiples" are the dominant pattern in science, and the lone singleton the exception. It's faster now. In November 2022 Terence Tao logged what he called maths at internet speed: Justin Gilmer posted a breakthrough on the union-closed sets conjecture on the 16th, Gil Kalai blogged it the next day, and four days after that three independent groups had sharpened the same argument to the same constant. Ripeness is not inevitability, though. In 2025 Hannah Cairo, then 17, disproved the Mizohata–Takeuchi conjecture — roughly four decades of people trying to prove it, undone by one person going a different way. The field was ready. It still took her. There is a name for what ripens, and it isn't the individual. In the mid-1990s Brian Eno — fed up with the art-history idea of genius, where gifted individuals turn up out of nowhere to light the way for the rest of us — coined scenius. In his own words it "means ‘the intelligence and intuition of a whole cultural scene’. It is the communal form of the concept of genius." He set it against the "Big Man" theory of history, and preferred a world constantly remade by all its inhabitants — a cooperative enterprise. His own list of scenius moments runs through Dada, the American experimental music scene, and punk, 1975–8. Eno then guards the flank we would guard. He says plainly that it would be foolish to pretend everyone's contribution is therefore equal, and he would never claim it. Scenius doesn't dissolve the person who did the work — it moves the unit, from the lone mind to the scene that made the answer findable.
