An attractor is not a mandate

The turn An attractor is not a mandate In the ocean, the crab basin permits everyone who never rolls into it. Most decapods are not crab-shaped. Shrimp, prawns, lobsters, crayfish — millions of individuals living entire successful lives outside the famous attractor, and nothing in the water enforces anything. The slope is just a slope. Non-crabs are not failed crabs; the category doesn't exist. Engineered systems are different, and this is where the metaphor stops being charming. In a designed system, somebody picks the slope. Every platform converged on short vertical video. Not because that is the optimum of human expression — because engagement was chosen as the objective, and everything downhill of that objective rolled to the same place. The convergence is real, and it is also somebody's decision, and the two facts are usually presented as one. School does it more bluntly: one route to the answer, one pace, one accepted way of showing your work. Then the other routes — the ones that arrive by a different wiring and get there fine — collect a diagnosis. That isn't the terrain sloping. That's a wall, and someone poured it. This is the Cavendish banana: uniform, efficient, one blight from collapse. The answer is Cavendish Space — environments built for caves and campfires and watering holes, for dandelions and tulips and orchids. Deliberately re-graded ground. In Stimpunks' ARLES terms, this zine lives at the top two rungs — Environment and Systems. Change the terrain and the attractors move. They always did. If it's not working, it's not the person. It's the environment, the relationships, or the system. — Stimpunks · ARLES a slope, and a wall found terrain the ones who never rolled in are fine poured terrain the ones who don't get a diagnosis nature permits · institutions require someone chose the second slope · it can be re-poured arles · environment & systems change the terrain, not the person Five Times a Crab · Stimpunks

The live argument Gould's tape, Conway Morris's constraint Biologists have not settled this, and we should not pretend otherwise. Stephen Jay Gould, in Wonderful Life (1989), argued that history is contingent: rewind the tape of life, play it again, and you get something else. We are here by accident, not by arrival. Simon Conway Morris, in Life's Solution (2003), argued the opposite from the same evidence: convergence is everywhere, the channels are narrow, and outcomes — up to and including intelligence — are close to inevitable. It's a genuine disagreement between serious people, and this zine does not resolve it. Both readings are compatible with five crabs and seven un-crabbings. What we refuse is the thing that gets smuggled in when the second is read loosely: that because a form recurs, it is the form things ought to take. Convergence is a description of what happened. It licenses nothing about who belongs. replay the tape Gould 1989 different every time Conway Morris 2003 the same, near enough unresolved — and either way, recurrence is not permission a rhyme, not a proof we are not settling this here Five Times a Crab · Stimpunks

Held with care What we are not saying Convergence is a beautiful finding sitting one inch from an ugly argument. Here is the inch. Notconverge or lose. Most decapods aren't crabs and are doing fine. A shape that recurs is not a shape that's required. Notoptimality. The reasons for the crab's recurrence remain a mystery in the literature, and it's been abandoned more often than adopted. "Recurring" and "best" are different words. Notone right shape. The basin holds millimetres to metres, reef to abyss. Convergence never produced sameness, and belonging doesn't either. Notbiology proving a politics. A rhyme, not a proof. That a pattern recurs in nature says nothing about what we owe each other — deriving an ought from an is is a fallacy we'd rather name than commit. Not"you're a crab too." Belonging that requires you to have arrived at the same form isn't belonging. It's a membership test with better manners. Nota counsel of despair about design. Attractors move when terrain changes. That's the whole reason to bother building anything. the same forms, arranged two ways not a ladder one level different sizes, same standing no ticks · no crosses · no rungs variation is a spread, not an order a spread, not an order the universe doesn't pathologize its own variation Five Times a Crab · Stimpunks

Closer to home Ours was a multiple too The word you are reading this collection through is itself a case of ripeness. "Neurodiversity" is not one person's coinage. Following Botha, Chapman, Giwa Onaiwu, Kapp, Stannard Ashley and Walker (Autism, 2024), "neurological diversity" and "neurodiversity" reached print in 1997 and 1998 through the journalist Harvey Blume — who attributed them to the online Autistic community — and the concept and its theory were developed collectively by neurodivergent people. The terrain was ready. Jim Sinclair's "Don't Mourn For Us" (1993) and Autism Network International had done the ground work. Martijn Dekker's InLv list opened in 1996 and gave a scattered community one room. Kassiane Asasumasu coined neurodivergent in 2000. Nick Walker named the paradigm and the pathology paradigm it replaces. Several people, arriving at the same words at nearly the same time, under a shared pressure none of them chose — and the pressure was the thing worth naming. That is a multiple, in our own history, about our own lives. So both facts sit together, and neither cancels the other. Convergence happens. And nobody has to be a crab. Five times into the valley. Seven times back out. The ground is ours to re-grade, and it always was. a word arriving collectively neurodiversity inlv 1996 · print 1997–98 · developed collectively no single author · botha et al. 2024 ripeness, in our own history a community is a terrain too Five Times a Crab · Stimpunks

Five Times a Crab, Seven Times Not is Zine No. 31 in the Stimpunks Star Stuff series. It was written after Brett D. Wick's essay When Everything Becomes a Crab: The Strange Phenomenon of Convergent Evolution in Nature, Mathematics, and Human Systems (Washington University in St. Louis, 2026), which supplied the frame — convergence as attractors in possibility space, across biology, mathematics and technology — and the mathematical cases. Wick is not part of this collaboration and this reading is not his; the turn the zine makes, and the three findings it turns on, come from the primary crab literature rather than from the essay. (2021). How to become a crab: Phenotypic constraints on a recurring body plan. BioEssays, 43(5), 2100020 — read in the primary; source of the counts (carcinization "has evolved at least five times, and has been lost at least seven times," with likely further losses), of the statement that the reasons "remain a mystery," of the unresolved parallelism-versus-convergence question, and of the habitat and millimetre-to-metre range. "Endless forms most beautiful" is Darwin's closing line in On the Origin of Species (1859), which Wolfe and colleagues borrow. Borradaile, L. A. (1916) coined carcinization. Waddington, C. H. (1942). Canalization of development and the inheritance of acquired characters. Nature, 150, 563–565; and The Strategy of the Genes (1957), where the epigenetic landscape appears. Lorenz, E. N. (1963). Deterministic nonperiodic flow. Journal of the Atmospheric Sciences, 20, 130–141 — the attractor as a term of art. Ogburn, W. F. & Thomas, D. (1922). Are inventions inevitable? Proceedings of the American Philosophical Society, 105(5), 470–486. Scenius is Brian Eno's, coined in the mid-1990s and set down in A Year with Swollen Appendices (Faber, 1996) in a letter to Dave Stewart among the appendices — quoted here from that primary, along with the “Big Man” theory of history, the cooperative-enterprise passage, his list of scenius moments (Russia 1905–15, Dada, the American experimental music scene, the Anglo-American psychedelic sixties, punk 1975–8), and his own caveat that it would be stupid to pretend everyone's contribution is therefore equal. A note on the wording: the version of the definition in wide circulation — “Scenius stands for the intelligence and the intuition of a whole cultural scene. It is the communal form of the concept of the genius” — is not what the book says. It entered circulation through Kevin Kelly's “Scenius, or Communal Genius” (The Technium, 10 June 2008), which presents it as Eno's exact words; Eno's actual text reads “it means ‘the intelligence and intuition of a whole cultural scene’. It is the communal form of the concept of genius.” We follow the book. Kelly's four conditions for a ripe scene — mutual appreciation, rapid exchange of tools and techniques, network effects of success, local tolerance for novelties — are Kelly's own, from the same post, and are the reason he is credited on the figure. On the eyes: cephalopod retinas are everted, with photoreceptors facing the light and axons exiting behind, so there is no blind spot; vertebrate retinas are inverted, which is why ours has one. TEMPERATURE150°−272°usthem L★S · 001 The One Who Waits Tardigrade · water bear −272°C to 150°C · vacuum · at rest Half a millimetre long, and able to outlast vacuum, radiation, and years without water — not by toughing it out, but by stopping. It dries into a suspended grain called a tun, near-zero metabolism, and waits for conditions to change. dormancyrest is a strategyvacuumthe tun ▸ Field notes Field notes · Tardigrade The tardigrade is famous for surviving things that would kill almost anything — the open vacuum of space (it was among the first animals shown to survive it, on an orbital experiment in 2007), radiation at a thousand times a lethal human dose, temperatures near absolute zero. It is usually filed under "toughest animal alive." But look at how, because the how is the whole point. It does none of this while active and striving. It survives by drying into a tun — expelling most of its water, folding down to almost no metabolism, and going still until the world becomes livable again. It doesn't power through. It pauses. That is worth sitting with. The most durable animal we know of endures by resting — by treating dormancy as a legitimate state of being, not a failure to keep going. Not every survival is a fight. Some is knowing when to stop the clock and wait for a better day. MOISTUREsoakedvacuumusthem L★S · 002 The Partnership Lichen · fungus + alga bare rock · desiccation · even open space Not one organism but at least two — a fungus housing an alga or cyanobacterium — living so closely they were mistaken for a single species for centuries. Together they colonize bare rock, and have survived unprotected exposure to space. symbiosisnever one thingbare rockinterdependence ▸ Field notes Field notes · Lichen A lichen is not a thing; it is a relationship. A fungus provides structure and water-holding; a photosynthesizing partner — a green alga, a cyanobacterium, sometimes more than one, and often a yeast nobody noticed until recently — provides food. Neither could live on bare rock alone. Together they are one of the toughest, most patient colonizers on Earth. They tolerate near-total desiccation by simply going dormant when dry, and reviving when wet. In European Space Agency experiments, lichens were bolted to the outside of a spacecraft and exposed to raw space — vacuum, radiation, the works — and came back alive. This is the point You Were Never One Thing keeps making, written across a rock face: the resilience isn't in any single organism. It's in the partnership. What looks like one hardy individual is a collaboration that decided not to face the impossible alone. SUNLIGHTfull sunno lightusthem L★S · 003 The Sunless Economy Riftia · vent tubeworm no light · crushing pressure · sulfide Two metres tall, rooted around deep-sea vents in total darkness, with no mouth and no gut. They farm bacteria inside their own bodies that turn the vent's toxic chemistry into food — an entire ecosystem that owes nothing to the sun. chemosynthesisthe unseen economydeep seasymbiosis ▸ Field notes Field notes · Vent tubeworms Until 1977, textbooks agreed that all life ultimately ran on sunlight. Then a submersible reached the Galápagos Rift and found dense gardens of giant tubeworms crowded around hydrothermal vents in total darkness, kilometres below any sunbeam. The rule was simply wrong. An adult tubeworm has no mouth and no digestive tract. Instead it houses billions of bacteria inside a special organ and feeds them the hydrogen sulfide venting from the seafloor — a compound that is lethal poison to us. The bacteria turn that chemistry into food; the worm's blood-red plume is packed with a special hemoglobin that carries both oxygen and sulfide at once. An entire thriving economy, running on an energy source and an infrastructure the surface has never seen and does not depend on. Not a lesser life for lacking the sun — a whole different, self-sufficient world, getting on fine in the dark. The One That Eats the Poison

RADIATIONreactorbackgroundusthem L★S · 004 The One That Eats the Poison Radiotrophic fungi · Chernobyl grows toward radiation · reactor walls Black, melanin-rich fungi found thriving on the walls of the Chernobyl reactor — and apparently growing toward the radiation. Evidence suggests they use melanin to turn ionizing radiation into usable energy, the way plants use chlorophyll for light. radiotropismone's poison, another's foodmelaninreclamation ▸ Field notes Field notes · Radiotrophic fungi Inside one of the most radioactive places humans have ever made, something was growing. Black fungi coat the walls of the Chernobyl reactor, and studies found some strains grow toward radiation sources — a behavior researchers named radiotropism. The leading hypothesis is radiosynthesis: that the fungi use melanin, the same pigment that darkens our skin, to capture ionizing radiation and convert it into chemical energy, roughly the way a leaf uses chlorophyll to capture light. The mechanism is still debated and being studied — but the fungi are unmistakably at home where we cannot go. The reframe writes itself: what is poison to one living thing can be food to another. "Harmful" is not a property of a place alone; it's a relationship between a place and a body. A ruin to us can be a habitat — even a feast — to someone built differently. SALINITYbrinefreshusthem L★S · 005 The Salt Dwellers Halophiles · Halobacterium saturated brine · 10× seawater Microbes that need brine so concentrated it would sterilize almost anything else — the Dead Sea, salt flats, the pink evaporation ponds. That vivid pink is not lifeless water. The pink is them, in the millions, exactly where they belong. salt-lovingthe word "should"brinethe pink lakes ▸ Field notes Field notes · Halophiles Extreme salt kills most life by pulling the water straight out of it. So high-salt places "should" be sterile. That word — should — is doing an enormous amount of quiet work, and halophiles spend their whole lives contradicting it. They thrive in brine up to ten times saltier than the sea, in the Dead Sea and the salt flats and the industrial evaporation ponds. They balance the osmotic pull by loading their own cells with salts to match, so nothing gets drawn out. The startling pink of those waters — the color that reads to us as chemical and dead — is the organisms themselves, pigment and all, packed in by the million. "Should" is a statement about a default, dressed up as a law of nature. The places we're sure are lifeless are, often, simply full of a life we weren't the measure for. TEMPERATURE100°Ccoolusthem L★S · 006 The Gift from the Boiling Spring Thermophiles · Thermus aquaticus thrives near boiling · ~70°C optimal Microbes at home in near-boiling hot springs — water we could not touch. One of them, pulled from a Yellowstone pool a scientist was told held nothing worth studying, gave molecular biology the enzyme that makes DNA testing possible. heat-lovingthe margin is foundationalhot springsPCR ▸ Field notes Field notes · Thermophiles Hot springs were long assumed too hostile to bother studying. Then, in the 1960s, Thomas Brock started looking closely at the boiling pools of Yellowstone and found them teeming — including a heat-loving microbe he named Thermus aquaticus, happiest around 70°C. Decades later, that organism's heat-stable enzyme — Taq polymerase — became the engine of PCR, the technique that copies DNA and underpins modern genetics, forensics, and the tests that tracked a global pandemic. A creature from a pool everyone had written off turned out to be foundational infrastructure for the whole field. There's a pattern here worth naming. The margins — the places and beings the mainstream dismisses as too fringe to matter — are, over and over, exactly where the essential things turn out to have been waiting. TEMPERATUREwarm−2°Custhem L★S · 007 The Clear-Blooded Psychrophiles · Antarctic icefish −1.9°C seawater · antifreeze · no hemoglobin Fish that live in water cold enough to freeze their blood — so they make their own antifreeze. The icefish among them went further and abandoned red blood cells entirely: clear-blooded, a body plan that would be fatal anywhere warmer, and works perfectly here. cold-lovinga different body planantifreezeclear blood ▸ Field notes Field notes · Icefish The water around Antarctica sits at about −1.9°C, below the point where ordinary blood would freeze solid. The fish that live there make antifreeze glycoproteins that bind to tiny ice crystals and stop them growing — a chemistry evolved precisely for a place we'd call unlivable. The icefish took it even further. They are the only vertebrates known to have no hemoglobin — no red blood cells at all. Their blood runs clear. By any warm-water standard this is a catastrophic defect; a body simply should not be able to do that. But in freezing, oxygen-rich water, with big hearts and oxygen absorbed straight through the skin, it works. Read cold, the icefish is broken: it's missing the thing every textbook says a vertebrate needs. Read in its own home, it is fitted — a different design for a different world. The deficit was never in the fish. It was in judging it by someone else's conditions. METABOLIC PACEfastmillenniausthem L★S · 008 The Slow Ones Endoliths · rock-dwellers inside solid rock · millennia per generation Microbes that live inside solid rock, deep underground, on almost no energy — some may take centuries or millennia between generations. Barely metabolizing, easy to mistake for non-living, they are among the best models for where life might hide on Mars. deep biospherea different tempoinside rockastrobiology ▸ Field notes Field notes · Endoliths Kilometres down, inside what looks like solid stone, life persists in the pore spaces of the rock. With almost no energy and almost no water, these microbes run their chemistry so slowly that some estimates put centuries or even millennia between one generation and the next. Barely ticking over, they can be hard to tell apart from the non-living rock around them. But slow is not the same as dead. They are metabolizing, repairing, persisting — living, just on a clock scaled to geology instead of to our days. Disability communities have a name for this idea: crip time — time that runs by the body's own pace rather than the factory's. The endoliths keep crip time at a planetary scale. And it matters far beyond Earth: this quiet, sheltered, ultra-slow way of living is one of the best templates we have for where life could be waiting under the surface of Mars. A pace we'd dismiss as barely alive may be exactly the pace that survives where nothing fast could. i · the whole of it Here is the whole of it, before anything else: your place among us is not a prize you win. It is yours because you are here. "Inclusion safety is not earned but owed. Giving inclusion safety is a moral imperative." Timothy R. Clark, The 4 Stages of Psychological Safety

ii · worth before worthiness We will not audition you. Inclusion is a judgment about your worth — which you have, entire, already — not a verdict on your worthiness, which is no one's to weigh at the door. "Including another human being should be an act of prejudgment based on that person's worth, not an act of judgment based on that person's worthiness." Timothy R. Clark, The 4 Stages of Psychological Safety There is no litmus test at this threshold — not your diagnosis, your speech, your output, your history, or how easily others can make sense of you. Worth comes first. Worthiness, if it is ever anyone's business at all, comes long after, and not here.

iii · be human, be harmless What does it take to qualify? Two things. Be human. Be harmless. Meet both and you are in. There is exactly one disqualifier at this door, and it is not difference — it is harm. We say the second part out loud, because a welcome that tolerated harm would betray the very people it exists to keep safe. The one bar Acceptance is owed to everyone. Safety from harm is owed to everyone, too — and it is the single thing that can cost you your place here. Not your way of being. Only harm.

iv · the binding thing Frederick Douglass drew the line for good: "I know of no rights of race superior to the rights of humanity." Frederick Douglass Read it for every characteristic, not race alone. When we include one another, we set our differences beneath a deeper, common thing — and agree that the common thing matters more.

v · older than humanity And here we go one floor deeper than the textbook. The common thing beneath our differences is older than humanity. You, and we, and everyone at this door were made in the same stars — the same hydrogen from the same beginning, the same calcium and iron from the same dying giants. Kinship is not a courtesy we extend to you. It is the material you are made of. You do not have to earn your way in. You were ★stuff all along. Belonging here is not conferred; it is constitutive — true of you before you arrived, true whether or not anyone ever tells you so. We are only saying out loud what the atoms settled long ago.

vi · come in So: if you have flesh and blood, we accept you. If you are made of stars — and you are — you are already one of us. Come in. Rest. You are owed this. Inclusion is the first of four doors — beyond it lie the freedom to learn, to contribute, and to challenge. But none of them open until this one does. So we hold this one open first, and for everyone.

Owed, not earned. Inclusion safety — the first stage of psychological safety — is not a reward for the worthy. It is the baseline we owe one another simply for being here. This is our creed for it. L★S A Star Stuff creed on inclusion safety — the first of Timothy R. Clark's four stages of psychological safety. The definitions and the quoted lines are Clark's, from The 4 Stages of Psychological Safety (worth before worthiness; be human and be harmless; the only disqualifier is the threat of harm). Frederick Douglass's line is his own. For the fuller treatment, and how it meets neurodiversity, see Stimpunks' Psychological Safety. The move past "common humanity" to common origin — that belonging is constitutive because we are made of the same star stuff — is ours. This page rests here. You made it to the bottom. You were ★stuff all along — and you were owed a place the whole time. We love you down to it. The cosmic turn: a knowledge garden is how star stuff comes to know itself — a supernova scatters its forged elements like a seed-head (SN 1006, liberating iron), and the universe knows itself not as a vault but as a garden, by growing and seeding. Held in common, not enclosed: CC BY-SA, print free, share freely — the licence line is the seed dispersal. Grounded in Caulfield, Appleton, Bush, Deleuze & Guattari, Ostrom, and Sagan, and rooted in Stimpunks' own garden and commons. Eight spreads, six diagrams, a cover bed of blooms keyed to the prior zines' colours, a “Not:” refusals set. 8 spreads→

Zine No. 1 Bone Song Stimpunks Zines On piezoelectric matter, star-forged calcium, and the universe that doesn't pathologize its own variation. Six spreads including the full prose poem, diagrams, and the neurodiversity reframe. 6 spreads→
Love You Down To Your Star Stuff

Zine No. 2 Love You Down To Your Star Stuff Stimpunks Zines The full phrase as a zine — the cosmology of care. What Sagan said, what the elements are, what "down to" means as a direction, and six affirmations across every register. 6 spreads→

Zine No. 6 Eternal Sunshine Stimpunks Zines The Sun is the nearest star, so every warm morning is starlight — and the light was always in you. A golden-hour zine on warmth, authenticity, and the counter-deficit turn: the light was always yours, the sky was in the way. Six spreads with diagrams, affirmations, and a "Not:" refusals set. 6 spreads→

Zine No. 7 You Were Never One Thing Stimpunks Zines You are a collective. Mitochondria were once free-living bacteria that never left — every cell you have is a truce between former strangers. A companion to Bone Song, grounding interdependence over independence in verified cell biology, with diagrams, a prose poem, and a "Not:" refusals set. 6 spreads→

Zine No. 8 The Universe Runs on Difference Stimpunks Zines Variety is resilience; monoculture is the fragile, engineered thing — one blight from collapse. The Cavendish argument across scales: the near-uniform early universe that needed tiny differences to make any structure at all, the Cavendish banana, neurodiversity via the spiky profile and the competency network, and ethodiversity — the more-than-human variety of ways of being. Sameness is a single point of failure; difference is the default state of matter. Seven spreads, five diagrams, a "Not:" refusals set. 7 spreads→

Zine No. 9 The Lines We Drew Stimpunks Zines Constellations are lines we impose from one vantage point — Orion's stars sit light-years apart at wildly different depths, and the belt only lines up from here. So is the bell curve; so is the border between "disorder" and "difference." The companion argument to the Constellation Field Guide: the error curve borrowed from astronomy and turned into "the average man," the DSM's moving border, epistemic injustice and the words to name ourselves, and why a human-made line is ours to redraw. Eight spreads, five diagrams, a "Not:" refusals set. 8 spreads→
The Dead Stars Still Reach Us

Zine No. 10 The Dead Stars Still Reach Us Stimpunks Zines The time-delay of starlight as inheritance and accountability. We see stars as they were; some still shining have already gone dark — and their scattered elements become us. A memorial register read as ancestry: Highlander and our own elders, the ones the Cult of Compliance took, and why memory is labor owed forward. Carries Ira Socol and Page & Woodland in full, closing on “forgetting is a tool of white supremacy — memory is the work.” Eight spreads, five diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set. 8 spreads→

Zine No. 17 The Nearest Body Stimpunks Zines Tides and co-regulation as star stuff. The Sun out-masses the Moon 27 million times, yet the Moon runs the tide — because tidal force falls off with the cube of distance, and nearness beats mass. So co-regulation is gravity: a safe-enough nervous system nearby pulls yours into rhythm, at a distance, without touching. Spring and neap tides as aligned or crossed pulls, parallel presence as tidal locking, meerkat mode as a sea that lost its moon, and the ecosystemic turn — the storm is in the weather, not the water. Grounded in the Stimpunks glossary (co-regulation, polyvagal theory, meerkat mode, ARLES, regulation-first), with a hydrofeminist thread carried inward from No. 14. Eight spreads, six diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set. 8 spreads→

Zine No. 19 No Universal Now Stimpunks Zines Crip time, read through relativity — with a guest coda by Helen Edgar. Physics says there is no universal “now”: simultaneity is relative and clocks run at different rates by speed and gravity (your phone's GPS corrects for it). So the one true clock is a human invention — railway-and-factory standard time, a convention we mistook for a law and then began grading bodies and minds against. Crip time (Zola & Gill, Kafer, Samuels, Price) bends the clock back to fit us instead of bending us to it — the same move as Minor Worlds, now applied to time. Monotropic spiral time and felt time (Helen Edgar, Bergson, Deleuze) are their own real clock, measured in intensity, not minutes; Samuels' time travel, grief time, and broken time hold the hard edges too. The reading: no clock is master, and being “off the clock” is closer to the truth than fitting it. Nine spreads, seven diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set, and a closing coda by Helen Edgar on spiral time. 9 spreads→

Zine No. 20 The Same Water Stimpunks Zines Fluctuating capacity, read through the physics of phase transitions. Water doesn't get gradually stiffer as it cools — it holds, then flips to ice all at once at a threshold. Same H₂O, different state, and the conditions (not the substance) decide which. So the exhausting question — why could you do it yesterday and not today? — has a clean answer: capacity is a state, not a trait, and you were near a boundary. The hardest part is the crossing itself (threshold anxiety is sensitivity to a real edge — broken thresholds, not broken people); you can be supercooled, held past your limit until one small thing tips everything at once; and recovery slows near the edge, because that's how systems behave. Nothing is fixed or broken — fluid adaptation and weather-bodies, re-adapting to a changed climate. Extends Minor Worlds: change the conditions, not the substance. Grounded in phase-transition physics, Cynthia Kim, Helen Edgar, and Stimpunks' own threshold anxiety. Eight spreads, six diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set. 8 spreads→

Zine No. 21 Not a Line Stimpunks Zines The spectrum was never a severity scale — after Helen Edgar & Patrick Dwyer. “Spectrum” is the most misread word in our vocabulary: people hear a line from mild to severe. But a real spectrum isn't a ladder — split a star's light and every element signs its own pattern of lines, a fingerprint, which is the only way we know what stars are made of. And the sky's figure was never a line: it's a constellation. The zine follows the escalation from Helen Edgar's brand-new essay — the line of neuronormativity, to the spiky profile (better, but still a grid measured from a baseline), to a constellation of intensities: no rank, no norm, no line. Patrick Dwyer's autism constellation anchors it; the functioning-labels critique shows how the line gatekeeps support (“not disabled enough” vs “too disabled”). Held with care: refusing the line doesn't erase that some of us need far more support — need is not a rank; name it instead. Cashes in the rainbow motif on every page and hands off to the Constellation Field Guide. Eight spreads, spectrum-forward diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set. 8 spreads→

Zine No. 23 Bodies of Water Stimpunks Zines Hydrofeminism as belonging, read through star stuff — after Astrida Neimanis. You are not a container of water; you are water, roughly 60% of you, briefly gathered into a shape. And none of it is only yours: it was rain, river, cloud, and the inside of other creatures first. Neimanis's gestationality (we each began inside another body's water) and Stacy Alaimo's transcorporeality dissolve the clean edge — we are all downstream of one another, permeable and borrowed. The crucial move, held with care: watery belonging is not dissolution into sameness. Where two rivers meet, the confluence runs braided for miles — one channel, two waters, still distinct. That's the neurodiversity paradigm in an image: the spiky profile survives the merge. A dedicated spread carries shared/collective flow — monotropism's deep channels can align into shared flow (Autistic Realms, Helen Edgar); a watering hole is where currents pool. So belonging is a current, not a border — build watering holes, keep the water moving. Much of Earth's water is older than the Sun. Eight spreads, six diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set. 8 spreads→

Zine No. 24 Shared Air Stimpunks Zines The air we share, read through star stuff and solarpunk — a companion to Bodies of Water. There is only one air: a single, well-mixed body with no walls in it, so thoroughly circulated that your next breath very likely holds atoms once breathed by strangers and by trees across the world. It's a reciprocal breath — we exhale what plants inhale, and our oxygen is the exhaust of ancient cyanobacteria (the Great Oxidation Event, ~2.4 billion years ago), forged first in stars. Every room we share is a shared-air space (a term coined by Helen Edgar & Ryan Boren): in it we trade breath and co-regulate, nervous systems settling into a shared rhythm. The neurodiversity turn: many of us are the canaries of that room. Miners carried canaries because the birds felt the bad air first — not because they were weak, but because they were sensitive, and their alarm was information. Our sensitivity to fragrance, stale air, and fluorescent hum is an early-warning system, not a flaw: don't blame the bird, change the air — build it breathable for the canaries and it's breathable for all. Which raises the harder question: habitable, and for whom? The burden of shared air falls unevenly, so breathable air is a commons, not a private accommodation one person quietly manages. The response is solarpunk: clean air as infrastructure as resistance — open windows, plants, masks, DIY Corsi–Rosenthal boxes — mutual aid you can build in an afternoon. Move quietly and plant things. Nine spreads, seven diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set. 9 spreads→

Zine No. 25 Shared Signal Stimpunks Zines Connection carried across distance, read through star stuff — a companion to Shared Air. The electromagnetic spectrum is one continuous field: radio waves and starlight are the same phenomenon at different wavelengths, and the same physics that carries a voice call carries a star's light. Shared-signal space — a term coined by Helen Edgar — is the counterpart to shared-air space: a call, a message, a voice note, a synthesised voice, carrying the rhythm on a signal instead of the air of a room. A voice note is breath, timestamped and sent; co-regulation crosses a screen too — thinner, but real (Porges; Streuber et al.). For many of us, text and AAC aren't a fallback from speech but the clearer channel — thinking time, structure, fewer sensory demands, a record to return to (Howard & Sedgewick) — and AAC is the real communication, not a workaround. Aversion to the phone is information, not fragility. Reachable, and for whom? Communication access is a commons; we build our own watering holes — the Autistic Rhizome (Edgar), Discords, AAC — sideways and underground, where lurking counts. The oldest signal of all is a dead star's light still reaching your eye: signal lets connection cross a gap touch can't, so no channel is the master channel (Milton). Nine spreads, seven diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set. 9 spreads→

Zine No. 11 · Guest Why Difference Comes First Guest zine · Helen Edgar A guest zine by Helen Edgar (Autistic Realms), in her own voice. One thread followed down three scales — relational quantum mechanics, the cosmic microwave background, and Deleuze — to the same shape: difference comes first, and the baseline is the thing that got built. It ends where the flat line, and even the spiky profile, give way to a constellation of intensities: a self that is dynamic, relational, and never finished. Ten spreads. 10 spreads · guest→

Zine No. 22 No One Is the Leader Stimpunks Zines Emergence and the murmuration — a flock has no captain, and neither does a self. Hundreds of thousands of starlings make vast rolling shapes with no leader and no plan: each bird tracks only its six or seven nearest neighbours (Ballerini & the STARFLAG project), and the whole emerges from that one local rule. Philip Anderson's “More Is Different” (1972) is the spine — the founding statement of anti-reductionism: at each level of scale new laws appear that the parts don't contain, so knowing the parts never rebuilds the whole. The early universe did the same, self-organising faint density ripples into the cosmic web with no architect. Two payoffs land it home: the whole person is realer than any diagnostic checklist of parts (you are not a list of deficits — you are the murmuration), and our best neurodivergent collectives — NeurodiVentures — are leaderless murmurations, not org charts (competency networks and catalysts rather than leaders; decisions where the knowledge lives). A “the whole exceeds the parts” zine. Held with care: leaderless is not structureless. Eight spreads, flock-and-web diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set. 8 spreads→

Zine No. 26 A Mycelium and a Rhizome Stimpunks Zines How neurodivergent knowledge and community grow, read through star stuff — no trunk, no center, many doors. A tree has one trunk and a chain of command; you climb it or you're lost. A rhizome (Deleuze & Guattari) has no root to ask permission of, so you can enter anywhere — Spiky Profiles → Monotropism → Deep Attention, or in from burnout, or a word that finally fit. No prerequisite, no gatekeeper. And a mycelium is the life in that shape: fungal threads carry nutrients and signals between trees that never touch (the “wood wide web,” Simard), thickening the paths that help and letting the rest fade; a brainless slime mold rebuilds the Tokyo rail network (Tero et al.). Zoom all the way out and the shape returns — the cosmic web of dark-matter filaments, the universe's largest structure, looks like a mycelium, like a neuron: not a pyramid, a web. We're already building it. Gray-Hammond and Munday name it neuro-anarchy; the Autistic Rhizome is “a network with no single point of origin,” members as equals held by a do-no-harm ethic, resilient because nothing depends on a center (with Helen Edgar's watering holes). Where the map meets soil is Cavendish Space. Decentralization isn't disorder — it's the oldest structure there is. Eight spreads, six diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set. 8 spreads→

Zine No. 28 · Guest Wyrd & Weird Stimpunks Zines · Helen Edgar On the old word for fate, and the newer word we made of it — a guest zine by Helen Edgar (Autistic Realms), rehoused in the Star Stuff style. Long before “weird” meant strange, wyrd meant becoming: Old English wyrd comes from weorþan, “to become,” and is twined with the root of “worth.” Fate was never drawn as a straight line from birth to death but as cloth — the Norns' weaving at the well beneath Yggdrasill, the “web of man” — many threads crossing, none load-bearing alone. The Weird Sisters carried the word down through Holinshed to Shakespeare's Macbeth; over centuries “weird” drifted into an insult, and Autistic and disabled communities have run that drift backward, taking it up again as a name, not a verdict — which is etymologically honest, not just cheek. Held with care: wyrd is not a script, not doom, not a synonym for wrong, not something done to you alone. Under the root, weorþan meant “to become,” never “to be”: nobody is finished, and becoming was never the flaw — it was the design. You were never written; you are still being woven. Nine spreads, six diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set, a “threads already running” map of its kin in the collection, and Helen's own sources & notes. 9 spreads→

Zine No. 29 · Guest Only in Relation Stimpunks Zines · after Helen Edgar Relational quantum physics, and what it means to be Autistic — a guest zine developed after Helen Edgar (Autistic Realms) from her essay “We Are Made of Relations.” In Carlo Rovelli's relational quantum mechanics a particle has no standalone properties; what it is becomes definite only in relation to another system (Rovelli, 1996). The count gives it away: two distinct coins make four outcomes, but two identical bosons make only three — what's fundamental isn't the standalone particle but the symmetry, the relation (Webster, 2026). Karen Barad calls the relation-before-parts intra-action; the human version, intradependence — made of each other, deeper than interdependence — Helen draws from Barad too. Read through Deleuze, “objects emerge out of more fundamental processes of differentiation”: difference first, then relation, and the tidy standalone object is the thing that got built. The payoff lands on our own work — the double empathy problem (Milton, 2012) lives in the relation, not one mind, and Helen widens it into DEEP; and in the ARLES ladder Relational sits near the base with Regulation inside it, because regulation is relational, so you change the field, not the person. Held with care: not quantum mysticism, not “everything is connected” as a vibe, not dissolution into sameness — the spiky profile survives the merge. A rhyme, not a proof. Nine spreads, seven diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set. 9 spreads→

Zine No. 30 · Guest Always Migrating Stimpunks Zines · Helen Edgar Migration, monotropism, and the galaxy you're already made of — a guest zine by Helen Edgar (Autistic Realms), written after Brigit Anna McNeill's The Living Page migration workshop and rehoused here in the Star Stuff style. Every migrating body is made of matter that already migrated once, so migration was never a metaphor borrowed from animals: it's one of the oldest facts about star stuff. A bird crosses an ocean on a compass sense we still can't fully explain — light striking cryptochrome in the eye makes a pair of electrons whose spins stay linked, and that linked pair is thought to be part of how it reads the Earth's faint field (Hore & Mouritsen; Mouritsen). Entanglement's lesson: once two things have been in relation, they stay in relation — separateness was always the less accurate story, which is Rovelli's relational quantum mechanics in a wingbeat. Zoom out and the pattern holds: the Sagittarius dwarf is still arriving in our halo, and the Milky Way–Andromeda collision everyone called settled is now closer to a coin-flip (Sawala et al., 2025) — a tug, not a destination. Then the turn inward: the bodily restlessness that builds before anything is decided is monotropism's gravity, attention gathered into a few bright points rather than spread as an even glow — and masking teaches us to quieten it until we lose our own north. Neuroqueering is the refusal; Pernille Fraser's “Can we trust the space you offer?” asks it from the other side. Widened by ethodiversity and the double empathy problem, and by Barad's intra-action — the liminal crossing isn't empty transit, it's where the shaping happens. Closes past the spiky profile: not a chart, a constellation of intensities. Eleven spreads, eight diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set, and a threads-already-running map of its kin. 11 spreads · guest→

Zine No. 5 Underground Stimpunks Zines The below to Bone Song's above — the mycelial worldview as an act of love. Networks with no center, decomposition as renewal, and the quiet dark where the realest work gets done. Six spreads with a prose poem, diagrams, a "Not:" refusals set, and reflection questions. 6 spreads→

Zine No. 14 The Council of All Beings Stimpunks Zines Multispecies justice and more-than-human governance, read as star stuff. Every being at the table — soil, river, beaver, cuckoo, meadow — is forged from the same stellar matter, so the Council of All Beings is the universe convening with itself, and you cannot rank what you are made of. Carries the ethodiversity thread from No. 8 outward: the cosmos varies not only in what it makes but in how its creatures live. Six spreads of argument, then a hydrofeminist coda — the “service provider” critique and the four dimensions of justice, ethodiversity and ethonormativity after Tarragnat, the role-play method (speaking as the soil and the river), the proxy problem and the Umwelt, and Rights of Nature meeting hydrofeminism at Te Awa Tupua, closing on a coda where the council dissolves into flow. Nine spreads, six diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set. 9 spreads→

Zine No. 15 Every Creature's Own Sky Stimpunks Zines Umwelt as star stuff. Every creature is sealed in its own complete perceptual world — the tick's three signals, the bat's echo, the mantis shrimp's light, the dog's scent-time — and each world is whole, not a partial view of one real world underneath. There is no neutral, default way to sense. The animals do the arguing, so that when minds enter, the point lands as recognition: monotropism is an attention-world, Autistic perception a different and complete sky, not a broken copy of a standard one. And when two worlds meet — human and bat, one mind and another — the gap is mutual: the double empathy problem, arrived at without lecturing. Not one correct channel, but mutual translation. Carries the Umwelt thread from No. 14 inward, from von Uexküll through Tarragnat, Manning, Milton, and Despret. Eight spreads, six diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set. 8 spreads→

Zine No. 16 Minor Worlds Stimpunks Zines Niche construction as star stuff, and the third of a loose trilogy — how we treat other worlds (No. 14), how we sense them (No. 15), and here, how we build them. Organisms don't just adapt to a fixed environment; they remake it — the beaver's dam, the spider's web — and pass the built world on as ecological inheritance. So the neurodiversity turn is plain: don't fix the mind, change the environment (positive niche construction — there is no “normal” brain in a vat). Stimming is worldmaking; minor worlds and niche communities are real, not lesser; and no niche is neutral — the “default” room was built for one kind of mind, so the fix is reconstruction, not accommodation. Grounded in Odling-Smee & Laland, Armstrong, Tarragnat, Manning, Kadodia & Krueger, and Haraway, and rooted in Stimpunks' own glossary. Eight spreads, six diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set. 8 spreads→

Zine No. 27 Every Nervous System Stimpunks Zines More-than-human neurodiversity, read through star stuff. There is no standard nervous system — not across species, and not within one: the octopus's mind distributed down its arms, the jellyfish's centreless nerve net, the worm's fully mapped 302 neurons. Read neurodiversity literally and it never stopped at the human. Following Ombre Tarragnat's antispeciesist–posthumanist philosophy: there's “no valid reason to be anthropocentric when you talk about neurodiversity,” and ethodiversity — behaviour reclaimed as “a subjective response to a bodymind's situation” — is a fundamentally animal phenomenon. Ethonormativity punishes the ethodivergent (the horse who refuses the rider, the cat who resists petting — abandoned or euthanised). And the core move: neurodivergent people are pathologised by being animalised, so the liberation is to reclaim animality — not bestialisation (the speciesist, neuronormative “less-than-human” split, after Butler 2020) but (hum)animality, kin. Distance is not disconnection: shutting down can be how we keep relation. Every nervous system is the universe wired up to feel itself, no two ever the same. “I would rather be a divergent animal than a typical human.” Eight spreads, six diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set. 8 spreads→
Five Times a Crab, Seven Times Not

Zine No. 31 Five Times a Crab, Seven Times Not Stimpunks Zines Convergent evolution and “attractors,” read against the primary literature — written after Brett D. Wick's essay When Everything Becomes a Crab. The crab-like body plan really did evolve at least five times in decapod crustaceans, which is the part everyone quotes. It was also lost at least seven times — decarcinization, the commoner event — and Wolfe, Luque & Bracken-Grissom (BioEssays, 2021) report that the reasons for the recurrence remain a mystery, with carcinized lineages running from millimetres to metres across nearly every habitat on Earth. So convergence produced no sameness, and the basin is not a destiny. Our eye and the octopus's converged on the same camera and were built backwards from each other, which is why a system that grades the route instead of the outcome will fail an eye. Waddington's canalized landscape gives the picture; “attractor” is named as a metaphor borrowed from dynamical systems. Then the turn: nature's basin permits the millions who never roll in, while engineered systems write the attractor into the rules — engagement chosen as the objective and everything downhill of it becoming vertical video, one route to the answer and a diagnosis for the others. Cavendish monoculture against Cavendish Space, on the ARLES Environment and Systems rungs. Ideas ripen the same way: Ogburn & Thomas's 148 multiples, Merton's singletons-are-the-exception, Tao's “maths at internet speed,” and Brian Eno's scenius quoted from the 1996 primary rather than the altered version in circulation. Closes on our own history — neurodiversity was itself developed collectively. Gould and Conway Morris are left unresolved on purpose. A rhyme, not a proof. 12 spreads→

Zine No. 32 The Skeleton That Skipped Bone Stimpunks Zines A companion and a counter-song to Bone Song, written for a young person in our community whose special interest is sharks. This collection opens on a skeleton that is piezoelectric — press it and it makes voltage. Sharks, rays and chimaeras are vertebrates with no true bone at all: a cartilage skeleton stiffened by thousands of mineral tiles called tesserae, which Dean & Summers (Zoology, 2006) describe as tuned species by species and even to how the animal feeds. Then the finding that changes the story. Sharks were taught for a century as the before picture — cartilage first, bone later, primitive, not there yet. But Brazeau and colleagues (Nature Ecology & Evolution, 2020) describe endochondral bone in Minjinia turgenensis, an Early Devonian fish near the common ancestry of jawed vertebrates. If the shared ancestor had bone, the shark's bonelessness is not a failure to arrive — it is a loss, derived rather than primitive, and the same shape of fact as the crab body plan being lost more often than gained. Which exposes the verdict buried in the word primitive, the same one hiding in low-functioning and delayed. Then the other half: because sharks were said not to get cancer, their cartilage was ground into pills. Ostrander et al. (Cancer Research, 2004) documented 42 chondrichthyan tumours across at least 21 species, at least 15 malignant; Loprinzi et al. (Cancer, 2005) ran the trial and found no benefit to survival or quality of life. A body read as a cure gets harvested — and extraction always starts as appreciation. The skeleton is for the animal. A rhyme, not a proof. 12 spreads→

Zine No. 33 The Ick Is a Border Stimpunks Zines Disgust feels like a fact about the animal. It is a fact about the frame. Rozin & Fallon (Psychological Review, 1987) treat disgust as a food emotion at root, whose objects are largely learned — arriving across a child's first eight years and running on the magical law of contagion, where one touch renders a whole plate inedible forever. A reaction that far out of proportion to any physical fact is a rule about categories, and rules about categories are taught. Then three arrangements that read as gross and are, in frame, simply competent. Osedax, the bone-eating worm (Rouse, Goffredi & Vrijenhoek, Science, 2004): no mouth, no gut, a vascularised root system dissolving whale bone, dozens of dwarf males inside the female's tube. The deep-sea anglerfishes, whose fused males cost them their immunity — Swann, Holland, Petersen, Pietsch & Boehm (Science, 2020) found loss of functional aicda, and in permanent attachment loss of rag, abolishing the hallmark of adaptive immunity. To stay joined to another body they gave up the machinery that tells self from not-self. And the whale fall (Smith & Baco, 2003): a pulse of food worth roughly 2,000 years of background supply, a sulphophilic stage lasting decades, a mean of 185 macrofaunal species — richer than any other hard surface down there. Then the turn. The same reflex fires at feeding tubes, drooling, stimming, incontinence and AAC; Nussbaum calls it projective disgust, where a group of people becomes a buffer against the animal nature we would rather deny. Two frames to widen past — the neuronormative and the anthronormative. A house companion to Helen Edgar's Wyrd & Weird: weird was reclaimed, gross gets disarmed. Nobody is guilty of a flinch; everyone is answerable for the two seconds after. 13 spreads→
Two Hundred Years Before You're Grown

Zine No. 34 Two Hundred Years Before You're Grown Stimpunks Zines The Greenland shark is the longest-lived vertebrate known, and it does not reach maturity until it is about 156 years old. Nielsen et al. (Science, 2016) radiocarbon-dated the eye lenses of 28 females — the lens core is laid down before birth and never replaced, so they read each animal's age against the atmospheric bomb pulse from 1950s nuclear testing — and found a life span of at least 272 years, the largest animal at 392 ± 120. It is also the slowest fish for its size: 0.34 m/s, one tail-beat every seven seconds (Watanabe et al., 2012), and it eats seals anyway, apparently by arriving quietly while they sleep — the strategy needs the trait. Nearly all of them carry a copepod clamped to the cornea, and it costs them almost nothing, because vision is not what the Arctic deep asks for. So late turns out to be a comparison, not a measurement; the ruler was always the variable. But this is not a zine about slow being beautiful: Nielsen's own paper raises the conservation alarm, because an animal needing a century and a half to reproduce cannot recover from pressure arriving in decades, and the species is IUCN Vulnerable. Slow is survivable or it isn't, and the environment decides — which is the social model of disability, stated in fish. Names the standard defence of the clock too: Alfie Kohn's BGUTI, "Better Get Used To It," which almost by definition ignores developmental differences — and cannot survive noticing them. A rhyme, not a proof. 13 spreads→

Zine No. 35 Everywhere That Turtles Go Stimpunks Zines Tyson Yunkaporta writes in Sand Talk that a Star Dreaming Oldman Juma Fejo of the Larrakia People wants to share with all peoples "goes everywhere that turtles go — and there are turtles all over the world, even in desert country, so it connects everybody." That reads like a figure of speech and is actually a range map, so we checked it: roughly 357 species on every continent but Antarctica, in every warm ocean, and in the arid interior, where Chelodina steindachneri buries itself in a dry Pilbara riverbed and waits out a year without water. The primary literature then reverses the obvious reading twice. Lyson et al. (Current Biology, 2016) find the shell began as an adaptation for burrowing, not armour — broadened ribs "provide little protection" and cost you speed and breath; protection is a later exaptation. And Lyson et al. (Nature Communications, 2014) find the price: lock your ribs into a shell and you lose the ordinary way of breathing, so turtles run their lungs off a sling of abdominal muscle instead. Side-necks and hidden-necks answered one problem two ways. Sex is set by the temperature of the sand, not by chromosomes — which makes the Discworld philosophers' failed expedition to determine Great A'Tuin's sex a better joke than they knew. A hatchling learns the magnetic field of one beach and finds it again decades later. And every people had to think with this animal: Turtle Island, ao in the Huainanzi, Kurma — who is a pivot for churning and not a world-bearer — and Great A'Tuin. They are not the same turtle, and that is the connection. Carries the Fibonacci passage and says plainly where it stops being biology. ~48% of turtle species are threatened. A rhyme, not a proof. 13 spreads→

Zine No. 36 The Layer We Call Essential Stimpunks Zines Mortensen et al. (Frontiers in Neuroanatomy, 2014) counted the long-finned pilot whale's neocortex and found roughly 37.2 billion neurons — "almost twice as many neocortical neurons as humans," the first animal ever counted above us. Then, in the same paper, they conclude that absolute neuron number is "not correlated with the superior cognitive abilities of humans." The yardstick came back against us and the ranking survived, because it was never resting on the count. Underneath sits the architecture: the cetacean neocortex is agranular, with layer IV — the input layer our textbooks call canonical — absent or underdeveloped, and layer I apparently taking the job instead, giving "a very different connectivity scheme compared to more commonly studied species, like rats and macaque monkeys." Manger (2006) read that missing layer as evidence there is no neural basis for complex cognition in cetaceans; sixteen authors replied in Biological Reviews that these features are "a non-primate route to neuroanatomical (and cognitive) complexity." Difference read as deficit, conducted by neuroscientists, about whales. Held with care: thermogenesis is a serious hypothesis and a brain can do heat work and thought work at once — the claim here is only about which reading you get for free. On neurodiversity, the honest answer: there is no cetacean diagnostic literature and this zine does not invent one. What exists is variation inside single populations — sponging in 15 of 141 known Shark Bay mothers, down one matriline (Krützen et al., 2005), spongers more solitary and foraging longer (Mann et al., 2008) — read through ethodiversity (Ombre Tarragnat), which needs no clinic. Plus 8,719 sperm whale codas resolving into ~143 combinations where 21 had been described, because someone borrowed rubato from music. And eight days off Pico with an S-spined bottlenose dolphin among sperm whales, the rubs returned — a paper titled "Repeated Non-Agonistic Interactions," because "adopted" was the press's word. Douglas Adams got the joke in 1979, ranking us third behind the mice. Then he went to see the baiji. A rhyme, not a proof. 13 spreads→

Unmasking as authorship rather than exposure, the freedom of many selves, bringing the hidden to the front, and authenticity as our purest freedom. From “Changes” and Space Oddity to Blackstar, difference read as direction, not deficit. Eight spreads, each with an embedded Bowie performance, plus a “Not:” refusals set. 8 spreads→

Feeling alien, the mothership's invitation, naming your people, refusing the cure, stimming in the open, and the way back to Earth. Eight spreads, each with an embedded AURORA performance, plus a “Not:” refusals set. 8 spreads→

Field Guide No. 5 A Field Guide to the Ways of Being a Star Star Stuff Field Guides Eight ways to be a star — the long slow burn of a red dwarf, the so-called “failed” brown dwarf, energy pulsing on its own rhythm, a pulsar’s millisecond precision, stars bound in pairs, the red giant’s later phase, the white dwarf’s long afterward, and the brief brilliance of a blue giant. Astronomy’s own names hide verdicts; the sky doesn’t grade. Each entry maps its place on the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram, with a “sounds like / actually” table and full field notes. 8 stars→

Field Guide No. 6 A Field Guide to Symbioses Star Stuff Field Guides Mutual aid, written into biology — twelve partnerships across the tree of life, read as mutual aid. Fungi and roots trading underground, bacteria making soil, a cleaner fish trusted by predators who could swallow it, algae building reefs that shelter a quarter of ocean life, the fig and its wasp that cannot live without each other. Interdependence is the rule, not the exception: Kropotkin showed mutual aid is a factor of evolution; Margulis, that life “took over the globe not by combat, but by networking.” This isn't “nature is nice” — parasites are real too, and the ghost pipe (Monotropa uniflora) is the honest one-way case, a myco-heterotroph that only takes, modelling receiving without reciprocating — and a bridge to monotropism (with Helen Edgar's tribute to Dinah Murray). It's that nothing living stands alone. What biology has always done, disability-justice communities name and practice: the human specimen is our own care webs and spoon shares (Spade, Mingus, Piepzna-Samarasinha, Kafai, Lewis), and a closing coda swaps the language of management for the language of living systems — symbiosis over competition, competency networks over leadership, coordination over management. Each entry maps who gives what and gets what, with full field notes. Solidarity, not charity; interdependence, not independence. 12 symbioses→
A Field Guide to Nervous Systems

Field Guide No. 7 A Field Guide to Nervous Systems Star Stuff Field Guides Eleven ways to have a nervous system — the companion catalogue to Every Nervous System (Zine No. 27). The jellyfish's centreless net, older than brains; the octopus's mind spread through its arms (two-thirds of its neurons outside the brain); the worm's fully mapped 302 neurons; the honeybee's million-neuron cognition and swarm mind; a jumping spider planning routes with a brain smaller than a pinhead; an electric fish reading a sense we lack; the star-nosed mole's 22-ray touch-world; the corvid's forebrain packed denser than a primate's (Olkowicz 2016); the elephant's 257 billion neurons, almost all cerebellar; a slime mold solving mazes with no neurons at all; and us — about 86 billion neurons, one arrangement among many, not the top of any ladder. Neuroscience hides verdicts in its words — “primitive,” “simple,” “lower” — but the animal kingdom keeps no standard nervous system. Each entry maps its architecture, reframes the deficit reading (“sounds like / actually”), and carries full field notes. There is no standard nervous system. 11 systems→
A Field Guide to the Ways of Migrating

Field Guide No. 8 A Field Guide to the Ways of Migrating Star Stuff Field Guides Fifteen ways of migrating — the companion catalogue to Always Migrating (Zine No. 30). Say “migration” and most of us picture one shape: a long line, north in spring, back in autumn. Almost nothing does that. The Arctic tern flies ~71,000 km a year and refuses the straight line, riding wind in vast S-shaped detours because the long way is the cheap way. A juvenile godwit crossed 13,560 km in 11 days without landing — held with care, since it shrinks its own organs to do it and a migrant who rests is not a lesser migrant. No monarch finishes the round trip: several short-lived generations work north and one “super” generation, living 8–9 months instead of weeks, flies the whole way back. Salmon find one stream by the magnetic field they imprinted on, then die and carry the ocean up into the forest. The largest migration on Earth is a few hundred metres straight up, every night, in the dark — distance was never the measure. Spiderlings rig silk and let atmospheric electricity carry them; trees migrate at metres a year, seed by seed; the Sahara crosses an ocean as dust and fertilises the Amazon; a star gets handed to a wider orbit and the Sun is probably not from here. The centre of the guide is partial migration — populations holding both migrants and residents, described in the literature as the commonest form, the one all others derive from. Variation within a population isn't the anomaly; it's the mechanism. Closes on us: the crossing made in place, when the word arrives and every year behind you rearranges. Held with care throughout — this reads migration as a way of being, never as a frame for forced human displacement. Fifteen entries, route-shape diagrams, a “Not:” refusals set. 15 ways→
A Field Guide to Being a Shark

Field Guide No. 9 A Field Guide to Being a Shark Star Stuff Field Guides Twelve ways to be a shark — the companion catalogue to the shark set (Zines 32, 33 and 34), written for a young person in our community whose special interest is sharks. These are not distant relatives: one clade, one body plan, four hundred million years. And inside it, almost nothing holds still. The whale shark reaches ~18.8 m and lives on plankton; the dwarf lanternshark tops out near 20 cm and erases its own silhouette by lighting its belly to match the light coming down. The goblin shark cannot give chase in the dark, so it doesn't — the jaws fire forward at up to 3.1 m/s, the fastest protrusion known in any shark. The thresher hunts with the far end of itself, whipping its tail overhead to stun several fish at once. The epaulette shark walks between tide pools on its fins and rides out near-anoxia by suppressing its own metabolism. The cookiecutter, at fifty centimetres, takes a neat plug out of animals hundreds of times its size and everything swims off alive. The bonnethead eats seagrass and — tested in 2018 — digests it, which made "sharks are carnivores" a category nobody had checked rather than a finding. Two entries are here because of a phrase rather than an animal: the great hammerhead's head does not sharpen its electrosense (tested directly, it widens the search area instead), and the frilled shark is not a living fossil, because nothing alive is. One points up, one points down, and both skip what the animal is doing. Twelve entries, schematic diagrams, a "Not:" refusals set. There is no standard shark. 12 ways→
A Field Guide to Being a Turtle

Field Guide No. 10 A Field Guide to Being a Turtle Star Stuff Field Guides Twelve ways to be a turtle, and five turtles people made — the companion catalogue to Everywhere That Turtles Go (No. 35). Almost every entry is a thing a turtle is supposed to have and doesn't. The leatherback has no bony carapace at all, just hundreds of interlocking ossicles in oily skin — and it dives to 1,280 m and holds its body up to 18 °C above the sea around it, which gives it the largest range of any reptile alive. The mata mata has weak jaw muscles and almost no tongue and is a superb predator, because it never bites: the mouth is a pump, and every "weakness" on the list is a component of it. The Fitzroy River turtle takes about 70% of its oxygen in through two enlarged sacs at the far end of itself. The Chinese softshell excretes urea through the lining of its mouth rather than its kidneys — the head-dipping that looks like drinking is the opposite of drinking. Painted turtle hatchlings spend their first winter in a nest below −10 °C by supercooling, and what decides whether they live is not how tough they are but what touches them. And the Arrau was filed as a silent animal until somebody brought a hydrophone: 2,122 recorded sounds in eleven types, hatchlings calling from inside the egg, and females coming and answering — the first evidence of post-hatching parental care in any turtle. The silence was ours. The last entry is the bill: Rafetus swinhoei, two or three animals left, the last known female dead in April 2023. The five turtles people made — Turtle Island, ao, Kurma (a pivot for churning, not a world-bearer), Great A'Tuin, and a Larrakia Star Dreaming we cite rather than retell — get a separate section and a deliberately different card, because they are not five drafts of one story. There is no standard turtle. 12 + 5→
A Field Guide to Being a Tortoise

Field Guide No. 11 A Field Guide to Being a Tortoise Star Stuff Field Guides Twelve land tortoises — Testudinidae — and an arc that runs from the Moon to a graveyard to a beginning. It opens where this collection has to open: on 15 September 1968, Zond 5 carried two Soviet steppe tortoises around the far side of the Moon and brought them back alive, two months before Apollo 8 carried any human. They lost about a tenth of their body weight and were otherwise fine. Then the ordinary astonishments of a slow land animal: the gopher tortoise digs burrows over fourteen metres long that more than 350 other species live in, which is the argument for building rooms that fit whoever needs them most, stated in reptile. The pancake tortoise has a shell whose bone is full of holes and is the fastest and best-climbing tortoise there is — and the beloved story that it inflates itself inside a rock crevice is now believed to be wrong, so the guide says so instead of repeating it. In July 2020 an Aldabra giant tortoise was filmed hunting and swallowing a tern chick, the first deliberate hunt ever recorded in a wild tortoise, which turned "tortoises are herbivores" from a law back into a summary of what we had happened to watch. Jonathan hatched around 1832 and is still on the lawn. The speckled padloper is six centimetres and complete. And then four entries marked as unfinished, because their endings are decisions rather than facts: the star tortoise, most trafficked tortoise on Earth and trafficked because it is beautiful; the ploughshare, whose shell conservationists engrave to spoil it for the market, and it may not be working; Lonesome George, who died in 2012 and took Pinta with him; and Fernanda, found alive in 2019 after 113 years of "extinct." It ends on Île aux Aigrettes, where an Aldabra tortoise is doing an extinct Mauritian tortoise's job — 529 hatchlings in eleven years. Not restoring what was lost. Finding another way for the function to happen. 12 tortoises→

The Shorthands LYDTYSS is the full phrase — Love You Down To Your Star Stuff — and it carries everything. But it's a mouthful, and language that lives in community needs forms that fit in a text message, a sticker, a caption, a moment. These are the shorthands we use and what each one carries. LYDTYSS Love You Down To Your Star Stuff The source. Use it when you want the full weight of the phrase — in writing, in titles, in contexts where the whole arc matters. It's cumbersome on purpose in the same way a full name is: it holds the complete thing. LYSS Love You, Star Stuff The warmest shorthand. Pronounceable — it sounds like a name, like a term of endearment, which is exactly what it is. Use it the way you'd use love you — quick, direct, meant. The comma does quiet work: it addresses you as star stuff directly, not just describes you as containing it. LUSS Love U Star Stuff The punk version. The dropped vowel is deliberate — it leans into informal, texty, a little defiant. Where LYSS is tender, LUSS has an edge. Both are correct. Both are true. L★S Love ★ Star Stuff The most visual shorthand. The star does double duty — it is both the symbol of what we're made of and the punctuation that holds love and star stuff together. Works in print, on stickers, as a hashtag, as a signature. The star is load-bearing. ★stuff Star Stuff The noun on its own. Use it as an identity, a descriptor, a reclamation. We are ★stuff. It carries the Sagan lineage — the specific weight of that phrase — while making it communal and punk. When you see ★stuff, you are seeing the raw material named directly, without the love clause, because sometimes you just need to name what you are. Which register you reach for depends on the moment. LYSS for tenderness. LUSS for solidarity with an edge. L★S when the visual matters. ★stuff when you're naming the thing itself. LYDTYSS when you need the whole phrase to do its full work.
