a few neighbours · no captain 22 Emergence No One Is the Leader on murmurations, emergence, and the whole that exceeds its parts — a flock has no captain, and neither does a self L★S Love You Down To Your Star Stuff · open edition ·

The murmuration No one is the leader At dusk, hundreds of thousands of starlings pour across the sky in one rolling, folding shape — splitting, pooling, turning inside out, all as if breathed by a single lung. Watch for an hour and you will never find the bird in charge, because there isn't one. The physics is almost unbearably simple. Each starling attends to only its six or seven nearest neighbours — not a fixed distance but a fixed few companions (Ballerini and the STARFLAG project, 2008). Match their heading, hold your spacing, turn when they turn. That local rule, run by every bird at once, is the entire program. From it: a whole that no bird intends, no bird can see, and no bird commands. Order without a ruler. This has a name — emergence — and once you have seen it, you start seeing it everywhere. Look for the bird giving orders. There is none. That absence is the miracle. one bird tracks seven — the sky moves as one seven neighbours, no captain local rules, global shape No One Is the Leader · Stimpunks

the parts every rule, listed more something new knowing the parts does not rebuild the whole more is different the whole is not the sum reduction doesn't run backwards Anti-reductionism More is different In 1972 the physicist Philip Anderson gave this its clearest statement, in an essay called More Is Different. Take reality apart and you find simpler laws — atoms, then particles, all the way down. But the reverse fails: knowing every rule the parts obey does not let you predict, or rebuild, the whole they make. At each new level of scale, entirely new properties, patterns, and laws appear that simply aren't present in the parts. Wetness isn't in one water molecule. Life isn't in one atom. The murmuration isn't in one starling. You don't get them by adding; you get them by relating. Reductionism took the world apart to name it — and then handed us the pieces as if they were the thing. But the whole was never more of the parts. It was something different. The whole isn't more of the parts. It's different from them. — after P. W. Anderson, "More Is Different," 1972 No One Is the Leader · Stimpunks

Structure formation The universe self-organised The largest structures there are did exactly the same thing. The infant universe was almost perfectly smooth — but not quite. Faint ripples of denser and emptier, printed into the cosmic microwave background, were the whole seed. Gravity did the rest. Denser patches pulled a little harder, drew in a little more, pulled harder still. Over billions of years matter drained out of the voids and strung itself along threads, until the whole cosmos had woven the cosmic web — galaxies beaded along filaments around enormous bubbles of empty space. No architect drew it. No first galaxy gave the order. Gravity plus a whisper of unevenness, run everywhere at once, was enough. The cosmic web is a murmuration written in gravity — turning so slowly we mistake it for a plan. No blueprint. No architect. Just gravity, a little unevenness, and time. void galaxies on filaments · voids between the cosmic web a flock frozen in gravity No One Is the Leader · Stimpunks

the checklist deficits counted the whole the parts don't add up to you you exceed them a person is an emergence realer than the list The whole person You are not a checklist Here is the first thing the flock teaches. A diagnosis is a list of parts: traits itemised, deficits counted, boxes ticked against a baseline. Useful, sometimes. But you can no more rebuild a person from that list than rebuild a murmuration from one bird's rules. A person is what emerges — a whole that is different from, and realer than, the sum of the criteria. The checklist is the parts. You are the murmuration. This is difference first in a new key: not a defective version of a standard human, but a whole that no inventory of missing pieces could ever contain. When a system reduces you to a score, it has confused the feathers for the flight. More is different — and you are the more. A checklist of deficits is a pile of feathers. You are the flock in flight. No One Is the Leader · Stimpunks
A murmuration, not an org chart

org chart orders down a chain competency network eye-level · trust · gifts decisions where the knowledge already lives flock, not hierarchy nobody at the top NeurodiVentures A murmuration, not an org chart The second thing the flock teaches is how we gather. Our healthiest collectives — NeurodiVentures — run like murmurations, not org charts: no boss at the top passing orders down a chain, but competency networks and catalysts rather than leadership and leaders. The local rules are few — everyone teaches and learns, trust extended first, decisions made where the knowledge already lives. From them, a collective intelligence emerges that no single mind could hold. Hierarchy hoards the privilege of not needing to learn; a flock keeps everyone attending to their neighbours. Nota leader to find — no bird carries the plan. Notan org chart — a competency network, a map of gifts. Notorders from the top — decisions where the knowledge lives. Nota hero or a lone genius — a whole no single part contains. No One Is the Leader · Stimpunks

many birds · one figure no one drew it · all of them made it the whole, arriving star stuff, self-assembling The whole The whole is the miracle Bring it together. Starlings, the cosmic web, a mind, a movement — one pattern runs through all of them: put enough parts into relation and something arrives that no part contains and no ruler commands. That something new is not noise to be reduced away. It is the whole point. You are not a set of deficits managed by a captain in your head — you are an emergence, whole and in motion. And we, together, are not an org chart waiting on a leader — we are a murmuration, turning as one because we tend to the few beside us. No one is the leader. That was never a lack. It's how star stuff has made every ordered thing it has ever made — including you, including us. More is different. You are the more. We are the more. No One Is the Leader · Stimpunks

What are the few local rules — the neighbours you attend to — that let your people move as one? Where are you waiting for a leader, when what you need is a murmuration? No One Is the Leader is the twenty-second zine in the Stimpunks series, and it names the principle that quietly runs under the whole collection: order without a ruler. Its spine is emergence — Philip W. Anderson's "More Is Different" (Science, 1972), the founding statement of anti-reductionism: at each level of scale, new laws appear that the parts don't contain, so knowing the parts never rebuilds the whole. The science: starling murmurations and the finding that each bird tracks a fixed number of nearest neighbours — roughly six or seven — rather than a fixed distance (Ballerini et al., the STARFLAG project, PNAS 2008), the topological rule from which flocking self-organises (with an early nod to Craig Reynolds' 1986 "boids"); and cosmic structure formation — primordial density fluctuations imprinted in the cosmic microwave background, amplified by gravitational instability into the cosmic web of filaments and voids. Two murmurations, one made of birds and one made of galaxies, neither with an architect. The lived knowledge: non-hierarchical, self-organising neurodivergent collectives — NeurodiVentures (Jorn Bettin; Autistic Collaboration, autcollab.org), built with competency networks in place of leadership and hierarchy (Laloux 2014; Bettin & Elliffe 2016), where power is understood as "the privilege of not needing to learn" and omni-directional learning keeps everyone both teaching and learning. adrienne maree brown's Emergent Strategy (2017) reads the murmuration as organising wisdom, and we follow her lead. The whole-person reading rests on the neurodiversity paradigm (Nick Walker) and our own Why Difference Comes First (No. 11). Held with care: leaderless is not structureless — a murmuration is intensely organised, it simply has no ruler; self-organising is not chaos, and distributing decisions is not abandoning support or accountability. The star stuff is Carl Sagan's, and the SN 1006 remnant on every Stimpunks page. The reading — that no one is the leader, and that this was never a lack — is ours. You were an emergence, whole and in motion, all along. no clock the universe keeps 19 Time No Universal Now on relativity, crip time, and the clock that was never the universe's — with a coda by Helen Edgar L★S Love You Down To Your Star Stuff · open edition ·

Relativity No master clock Newton assumed one universal time, ticking the same everywhere — a single clock the whole cosmos runs by. For two centuries it seemed obvious. It's also wrong. Einstein showed that simultaneity is relative: two events that happen "at the same time" for me can happen at different times for you, if we're moving differently. Worse for the master clock — time itself runs slower the faster you travel, and slower again the deeper you sit in gravity. This isn't a thought experiment: the GPS in your phone only works because engineers correct for the satellites' clocks ticking faster than clocks on the ground. There is no clock the universe checks against. Every clock keeps its own honest time. The universe keeps no master clock. Why should you? an event A · now B · now time ↑ two observers, two "nows" simultaneity is relative No Universal Now · Stimpunks
The clock is a human invention

9 · 10 · 11 · 12 stamped onto bodies & minds railway time · factory time a convention, not a law Standard time The clock is a human invention So if nature keeps no universal now, where did the one true clock come from? We built it. Synchronized clock time — the shared minute, the timetable, the standardized zones — is barely a century and a half old, an agreement stitched together for railways and factories so trains would not collide and shifts would start together. It is genuinely useful. But it is a convention, not a law of physics — and somewhere along the way we forgot we invented it and began treating it as reality itself, then measuring bodies and minds against it. Be productive on its schedule; wake, work, and rest on its count. The clock stopped being a tool and became a judge. You can't fail a law of nature. You can only fail to fit a rule someone wrote. We built the clock, then mistook it for the sky. No Universal Now · Stimpunks

Crip time Crip time bends the clock Disabled people have a name for living off that clock: crip time. Irving Zola and Carol Gill were among the first to write it into disability studies — a term already alive in the community; it means the extra time and the flexible time — arriving at various intervals, processing at various rates, needing more hours or fewer or simply other ones. The usual reading is that we are failing to keep up. Crip time says the opposite: the schedule was built narrow, and a body meeting it late is information about the schedule. As Alison Kafer puts it, rather than bend disabled minds and bodies to the clock, crip time bends the clock to meet disabled minds and bodies. Which is exactly the move of Minor Worlds: don't fix the person — change the thing around them. Here the thing is time itself. Rather than bend the body to the clock, bend the clock to the body. — after Alison Kafer bend the body to the clock bend the clock to the body room to move same body, two clocks flex time, exploded No Universal Now · Stimpunks

clock time spiral time a smell pulls a thread across decades not a line — a spiral time folds back on itself Monotropic time Spiral time, felt time For many neurodivergent people, time was never a line to begin with. In a monotropic attention tunnel it stretches and folds — an hour of flow vanishes; a bad ten minutes lasts a week. Memory works the same way: not a shelf of dated files but a spiral you re-navigate, where a smell tugs a thread across decades and yesterday can feel further off than childhood. Marta Rose named this spiral time; Helen Edgar, writing of felt time, describes how a moment from years ago might feel like now, while a conversation from yesterday feels distant. It's why "what did you do last weekend?" can land as a demand rather than a question. Not broken clock-reading — a different clock, measured in intensity, not minutes. Bergson called this lived duration; physics, in its own tongue, already agreed that duration bends. Remembering isn't recall. It's re-navigation. — Helen Edgar, More Realms No Universal Now · Stimpunks

Six ways of looking Time travel, broken time None of this is only lovely. Ellen Samuels, in Six Ways of Looking at Crip Time, holds the hard edges too. Crip time is time travel — a wormhole of jerky stops and starts that pulls you out of the tidy line of life-stages, so you meet the frailties of old age while young, or get treated as a child at any age. It is grief time and sick time: the days that swell around a loss, the strange arithmetic where you must earn the very hours in which to be ill. Capacity arrives and departs on its own schedule, and the clock offers no credit for it. So we hold both at once — the flexibility is a gift, and the brokenness is real. Naming it plainly is how we stop grading ourselves against a straight line we were never on. Notlate — keeping a different, honest time. Notbehind — we were never on your line. Notlazy or slow — running a clock the wall can't read. Nota schedule to be fixed to — a schedule that should bend to us. the expected line crip time stops · starts · loops · gaps a wormhole, not a timeline held: gift and grief at once No Universal Now · Stimpunks
Star stuff keeps its own time

many clocks · no master each keeps its own time and none is late Arrive where we started Star stuff keeps its own time So here is the whole of it. The cosmos runs on countless clocks and no master; so do we. The wall clock is a fine tool and a terrible judge, and it never was the sky. T.S. Eliot wrote of arriving where we started and knowing the place for the first time — the shape of spiral time, and of star stuff, which is forged, scattered, and gathered back into new forms that remember. You are made of atoms billions of years old, keeping time no watch can hold. You were never late. There is no schedule to be late to — only your own true time, which the universe has kept, patiently, since the first star. Made of star stuff, you keep the oldest time there is — your own. No Universal Now · Stimpunks

Coda a guest passage by Helen Edgar · Autistic Realms / More Realms Memories scatter like shards of seaglass along a fractured spiral, the centre always slipping just beyond my grasp. Remembering isn't straightforward for me; it's less recall and more a process of re-navigation. Time folds back in on itself. A moment from years ago might feel like now, while a conversation from yesterday feels distant or unretrievable — unless something hooks me in and brings it back into focus. My memories don't line up neatly. They tangle, twist, merge, and drift like mist through a forest. Sometimes I'm not remembering in the traditional sense at all, but kind of re-sensing — a texture, a tone of voice, the way the light fell. It can be disorienting, in a world that expects time and memory to be neat and logical. But it is also a kind of richness, a depth of connection that linear systems miss. We shall not cease from exploration — and arrive where we started, and know the place for the first time. — Helen Edgar · on felt time & monotropic memory · morerealms.com closing line after T.S. Eliot, Four Quartets No Universal Now · Stimpunks

a fingerprint, not a ladder 21 Spectrum Not a Line on spectra, constellations, and why "mild to severe" was always the wrong picture — after Helen Edgar & Patrick Dwyer L★S Love You Down To Your Star Stuff · open edition ·
A spectrum is not a line

Spectroscopy A spectrum is not a line Split white light through a prism and you don't get a ranking from a bad end to a good end. You get a fan of every wavelength at once — red through violet, none higher or lower, just light spread out by colour. Now split the light of a star. Threaded through its spectrum are fine dark and bright lines — and here's the wonder: every element leaves its own exact pattern of them, a fingerprint. Hydrogen signs one way, helium another, iron another still. Reading those lines is the only way we know what the stars are made of. So a spectrum was never a scale of more-or-less. It is a signature of what something is made of. A spectrum doesn't rank a star. It tells you what the star is made of. every wavelength hydrogen iron each element, its own fingerprint a fan, then a signature this is how we read the stars Not a Line · Stimpunks

mild severe where are you? the line of neuronormativity one axis · one ranking the picture we were handed a ladder, not a fingerprint The severity scale But we heard a line Then the word crossed into talk about autism, and something was lost in translation. Spectrum got heard as a line: mild at one end, severe at the other, everyone slotted somewhere between. High-functioning here, low-functioning there. "A little bit Autistic." "We're all somewhere on it." Patrick Dwyer names the problem plainly: a single line from "highest" to "lowest functioning" erases how the same person struggles more or less in different domains, on different days, in different rooms. And functioning labels don't just mislead — they gatekeep, sorting us into "not disabled enough" to deserve support or "too disabled" to be trusted with our own choices. The word meant fingerprint. We heard ladder. "Mild to severe" measures how much you inconvenience us — not who you are. Not a Line · Stimpunks

The spiky profile Better — but still a grid Many of us met a better picture: the spiky profile. Not uniformly mild or severe but jagged — high in some domains, low in others, peaks and troughs across social, sensory, cognitive, and motor. It kills the single dial, and that matters. But as Helen Edgar points out, the spiky profile still plots us on a grid. It reads our peaks and dips as distances from a flat, expected baseline — the line of neuronormativity — frozen at one moment of assessment. A better chart is still a chart of how far we fall from normal. It traded one line for a row of them. Progress — but still a grid, and still a baseline we're measured against. The spiky profile stopped ranking us on one line — and started ranking us on many. baseline peaks & troughs — measured from the line jagged, but still plotted a better chart is still a chart Not a Line · Stimpunks

no axis · no baseline · no rank a figure, not a score read from where you stand The constellation A constellation, not a chart So drop the grid entirely. Patrick Dwyer offers a different figure: an autism constellation — not a point on a scale but many stars in many positions, each Autistic person a different arrangement of them. Helen Edgar carries it further: a constellation of intensities. Not points plotted on a chart but an interdependent, monotropic galaxy — sensory, cognitive, and relational ways of being in ever-shifting relation. A constellation has no baseline and no rank; its stars sit at wildly different distances and cohere into a figure only from where you happen to stand. Relational, contextual, alive. That is us: not a measurement, but a pattern of light. always in motion, always connecting, always becoming — never fixed, never finished. — Helen Edgar Not a Line · Stimpunks
No line, no centre, no norm

no baseline to measure from free of the ruler no norm star Difference first No line, no centre, no norm Here is what a constellation quietly refuses. With no line, there's no top to reach and no bottom to fall to — and no centre either. The whole machinery of functioning levels assumed a norm to measure our distance from. A constellation has no norm star. This is the frame we keep returning to: difference comes first. Difference isn't deviation from a standard human; the standard was a story we told — and then used to decide who got believed, supported, or dismissed. And — this matters — refusing the line is not refusing that some of us need far more support. It refuses that support needs rank us. The honest replacement for a label was never a better label; it's naming the specific support each of us actually needs. No line. And still, all the care. Nothigh- or low-functioning — labels that gatekeep support, not descriptions of us. Notmild or severe — a fingerprint has no volume knob. Not"a little bit on the spectrum" — the spectrum was never a little-to-a-lot. Nota dial to be set — a constellation to be read. Not a Line · Stimpunks

each a fingerprint · together a constellation the two skies, at once signature and figure The whole light Every star its own spectrum Bring the two skies together. Read any star's light and you get not a rank but a fingerprint — this one rich in iron, that one in helium, each unmistakably itself. And no star sits on a line; they hang at every distance, making figures only a living eye can join. We are both at once: each of us a whole spectrum, a signature no one else carries — and together a constellation, a pattern that shifts with where we stand and who we stand among. The rainbow on every page of this site was never a ladder from red to violet. It's the whole light, arriving at once. This is what the creed meant all along: every colour, key, and frequency of neurodiversity. You are not high or low on anything. You are star stuff, reading itself. You are not a point on a line. You are a whole spectrum — a constellation no one has ever seen before. Not a Line · Stimpunks

L★S The spectrum was never a line from mild to severe. A spectrum is a fingerprint; the sky's figure is a constellation. You are not ranked — you are read. If you drew yourself as a constellation instead of a score, what would be in it? What specific support do you actually need — named, not ranked? Not a Line is the twenty-first zine in the Stimpunks series, and it argues for the metaphor Star Stuff already runs on: the sky is organised by constellations, not lines. It is built, with gratitude, on two pieces — Patrick Dwyer's "The Autism Constellation" (Autistic Scholar, 2020) and Helen Edgar's "The Constellation of Intensities: Neuroqueering the Spiky Profile" (Autistic Realms, 2026), whose line → spiky profile → constellation is this zine's spine. The metaphor is older than any one essay, and belongs to the Autistic community. Dwyer notes in a 2021 update that he did not coin it: Caroline Hearst had built a physical autism-constellation model and shown it at events, and the idea was already moving by word of mouth before that — with Larry Arnold an early proponent and Damian Milton and the late Dinah Murray discussing similar concepts. In correspondence with Helen Edgar, Milton credits Larry Arnold as the first he knows of to use "constellation" in place of "spectrum." We name them here because a zine against ranking people should not erase the people whose idea this is. The science: dispersion and the prism (Newton); the electromagnetic spectrum; spectroscopy and spectral lines (Fraunhofer; Kirchhoff & Bunsen), by which each element's fingerprint reveals what stars are made of; and the constellation as a relational, perspective-made figure. The lived knowledge: the critique of functioning labels as gatekeeping (Ollibean; the Autistic Self Advocacy Network; "Words That Wound," NeuroHub Community); the spiky profile; monotropism; and the difference-first frame of Helen Edgar's Why Difference Comes First (No. 11). Held with care: refusing the severity line does not deny that some of us need far more support — functioning labels harm precisely because they gatekeep it. The just alternative is naming specific support needs: no rank, and all the care. The star stuff is Carl Sagan's, and the SN 1006 remnant on every Stimpunks page. The reading — that you are a fingerprint and a constellation, never a point on a line — is ours. You were ★stuff, and a whole spectrum, all along. ↑ ↓ the relation comes first 29 Relation Only in Relation relational quantum physics, and what it means to be Autistic after Helen Edgar · Autistic Realms · a relation, still becoming L★S Love You Down To Your Star Stuff · open edition ·

The physics Only in relation A particle, on its own, doesn't quietly hoard its properties in private. In Carlo Rovelli's relational quantum mechanics, a system's properties become definite only relative to another system it interacts with (Rovelli, 1996). There's no view from nowhere in which an electron already "has" its values, waiting to be read. What is real is what happens between systems. An honest caution before we go further: RQM is one interpretation of quantum theory among several, and physicists still argue it. We're not smuggling physics in to prove anything about people. We are noticing a rhyme, not collecting a proof. "There is no absolute, observer-independent description of a person that tells the whole truth about themselves." — Helen Edgar, We Are Made of Relations (2026) the same particle, two situations in isolation ? no fact of the matter in relation ↑ definite — for that system a value is something two systems have between them not something one holds alone Only in Relation · after Helen Edgar

count the outcomes two coins — distinct H H H T T H T T 4 two bosons — identical H H H T T T (H T = T H) 3 the missing 4th is the tell nature can't tell the two apart so it doesn't count them apart What is actually real Count the bosons Flip two coins and you get four outcomes — HH, HT, TH, TT — because the coins are distinct objects, so "heads-then-tails" and "tails-then-heads" are two different things. Do the same with two identical quantum particles — two bosons — and nature counts only three. The two mixed cases collapse into one, because there is no fact about which particle is which (Webster, 2026). That vanished fourth outcome is measurable, and it is the tell: what's fundamental isn't the standalone particle. It's the symmetry — the relation — that says these two can't be told apart. "What is fundamentally real are not particles as such, but rather the laws and symmetries … that govern their behaviour." — George Webster, IAI (2026) Only in Relation · after Helen Edgar

Relation before relata Made of each other Entangled particles can't be described one at a time. The pair carries correlations the parts simply don't have on their own — measure one and you've said something about the other, however far apart they've drifted. The physicist-philosopher Karen Barad calls this intra-action: not the meeting of two things that already exist separately, but a relation out of which the parts come to be distinct at all (Barad, 2007). The relation is first. The "things" are what it leaves behind. There's a word for the human version, one Helen draws from Barad: intradependence — not two finished people who later depend on each other, but selves made of each other from the start. Deeper than interdependence. We don't arrive as sealed units who only later reach out. We are, from the start, relations wearing the shape of a person. inter- vs intra- inter-action two wholes, then a link intra-action one relation, then parts the bond is the origin, not the bridge the parts are what the relation leaves behind made of each other Only in Relation · after Helen Edgar

what comes first difference · relation objects (late arrivals) first the differentiating, then the things the object is what got built The order of things Difference, then relation Reading the physics through Deleuze, George Webster puts the metaphysics plainly: "Objects do not come first and then differ; rather, objects emerge out of more fundamental processes of differentiation." — George Webster, reading Deleuze (2026) First there is difference and relation; the tidy, standalone object is the late arrival — the thing that gets built. It's the same move Star Stuff has made from the start in Why Difference Comes First: the measured, average "normal person" was never the ground floor. Difference is. Turn it one notch further and relation is. Only in Relation · after Helen Edgar

What it means for us The gap is two-way When an Autistic person and a non-Autistic person misunderstand each other, the old story put the deficit in one of them — the Autistic one. Damian Milton named the truer picture: the double empathy problem. The misunderstanding runs both ways — a mismatch between two differently-built minds, not a fault inside one (Milton, 2012). Relational physics says: of course it does. The trouble was never sitting inside a single object. It lives in the relation. Helen widens double empathy into DEEP — Dynamic, Embodied, Ecological, Political — because the mismatch isn't a static glitch between two heads. It's alive, bodily, environmental, and shaped by power. Change the lighting, the pace, the assumptions, the room — and the "deficit" you were measuring moves. It was in the relation all along. where the gap lives one mind another mind not one side — the space between double empathy, made DEEP a mismatch is a property of the pair it has no single owner Only in Relation · after Helen Edgar

the ARLES ladder Systems Environment Lived exp. Relational + Regulation Attention near the base — on purpose regulation lives inside the relational rung not a private skill Up the ladder Regulation is relational This is why, in Stimpunks' ARLES ladder, Relational sits near the base — and why Regulation lives inside it. Regulation isn't a skill you own privately and keep failing to deploy. We co-regulate: nervous systems settle, or don't, in relation to other bodies, other pacing, a room that holds us or doesn't. So the support that actually works doesn't try to repair an isolated person. It changes the relational field — the sensory environment, the pacing, the temporal texture, a community's capacity to hold different ways of being. If it's not working, it's not the person. It's the environment, the relationships, or the system. — Stimpunks · ARLES "We are not broken objects. We are relations, all of us still becoming." — Helen Edgar (2026) Only in Relation · after Helen Edgar

Held with care What we are not saying Relational physics rhymes with how we already know support works. It is not a licence for the traps that show up whenever "quantum" meets "people." Notquantum mysticism. No "quantum consciousness," no mind magically collapsing reality. In physics the "observer" is any system at all — a speck of dust will do. Not"everything is connected" as a vibe. This is a specific claim about how properties come to be, not a warm fog. Notdissolution into sameness. Being a relation doesn't melt you. Where two rivers meet they run braided for miles — one current, still distinct. The spiky profile survives the merge. Notphysics proving a politics. A rhyme, not a proof. Our belonging stands on its own; the physics only rhymes with it. Nota duty to stay connected. Relational doesn't mean always available. Some of us need less contact, not more — and need is not a rank. the confluence, not the blur one channel · two waters · still distinct relation is not erasure difference survives belonging Only in Relation · after Helen Edgar

we all share air 24 Air Shared Air on breath, co-regulation, and the air we hold in common L★S Love You Down To Your Star Stuff · open edition ·

The atmosphere One ocean of air There is only one air. The atmosphere is a single, restless, well-mixed body — no walls inside it, no separate airs for separate people. What you breathe out drifts and spreads, and within a year or two it has circled the whole planet. A breath here becomes a breath everywhere. It mixes so completely that the numbers turn tender. One breath holds something like ten thousand billion billion molecules — so many that, once an old breath has scattered through the sky, your next lungful very likely carries a few atoms once breathed by people long gone, and by strangers on the far side of the Earth right now. We are not sipping from separate cups. We are all drinking from the same sky. We are all drinking from the same sky. one thin shell of air a breath here becomes a breath everywhere one connected body of air no separate skies Shared Air · Stimpunks

you tree O₂ → ← CO₂ each breathes what the other breathes out respiration ↔ photosynthesis breathing on opposite beats The reciprocal breath What the trees exhale Your breath is a conversation with the green world. You breathe in oxygen and breathe out carbon; leaves do the mirror image — taking in your carbon, handing back oxygen. Inhale, exhale, inhale: the forest is breathing with you, on the opposite beat. And the oxygen itself is a gift older than animals. For most of Earth's history there was almost none to breathe — until cyanobacteria invented photosynthesis and, across the Great Oxidation Event some 2.4 billion years ago, slowly exhaled an entire breathable sky. Every lungful you take is the exhaust of ancient microbes, kept fresh by every plant since. Follow the atoms back further and they leave the planet: the oxygen and nitrogen in the air were forged in the hearts of stars. You breathe star stuff that life remade for life. Every breath is the exhaust of ancient life — forged first in stars. Shared Air · Stimpunks

Shared-air space The room we breathe together When we share a room, we don't just stand near each other — we breathe the same air, in and out, trading it between our bodies breath by breath. This is shared-air space: the literal, physical air we hold in common every time we're together in a room. And our bodies know it. Nervous systems in the same space read one another without being told — the pace of a breath, the set of a shoulder, the tone of a voice — and start to settle into a shared rhythm. A calm body near you slows your breathing; a braced one quickens it. We co-regulate through the air, mostly below noticing. A steady nervous system nearby can pull yours into rhythm. So shared-air space is never only chemistry. It is nervous-system space too. Whether the air feels safe — how loud, how bright, how crowded, whether you can breathe easy — decides whether the bodies in it can settle, or must stay on guard. Good air makes room to regulate; hostile air leaves everyone bracing alone. To share a room is to trade breath — and to tune our nervous systems to each other. two bodies · one air breathing into the same rhythm breath traded · rhythms settling co-regulation through the air Shared Air · Stimpunks

who senses the bad air first? clean dangerous → canary most people the alarm is information sensitive first · a signal, not a flaw read it, don't blame it Sensory sensitivity Listen to the canaries Miners once carried canaries underground. The little birds felt the bad air — the odourless gas, the thinning oxygen — long before any person could. Not because they were weak, but because they were sensitive: their alarm was information, and it saved lives. Many of us are the canaries of the shared room. We catch the perfume three desks away, the stale unmoved air, the cleaning-chemical sting, the fluorescent hum pressing on the skull. Our discomfort isn't fussiness or fragility — it's an early-warning system telling everyone the air has gone bad. The old mistake is to blame the bird: you're too sensitive. The wiser move is to read the signal and change the air. The habitability question Habitable — and for whom? Shared air is only shared if everyone in it can breathe. So the phrase carries a harder question: habitable, and for whom? One person's ordinary afternoon is another's asthma attack, migraine, or infection. Too often the fix gets dumped on whoever is harmed: mask alone, sit by the door, send the email that starts "so sorry to be difficult." That's backwards. Breathable air is a commons — a collective responsibility, not a private accommodation one person has to quietly manage. The spectrum One field of signal Tune a radio, warm your hands at a fire, catch a sunburn, sit for an X-ray — every time, you are using the same single thing. Radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays are not different substances. They are one electromagnetic field, vibrating at different speeds. Radio is only light too slow and long for our eyes; colour is just the signal our eyes happen to catch. So there is no ladder of realness running from "in person" at the top down to "mere signal." There is one continuous spectrum, and we live our whole lives inside it. The voice on a call and the light off a face across a table are the same phenomenon, cut at different wavelengths. One field. No separate signals — no more than there are separate airs. Radio and starlight are the same thing, cut at different wavelengths. one continuous field long / slow short / fast radio· your call infrared· fire visible· a face X / γ· a scan same wave · different wavelength radio · fire · colour · a scan one spectrum, end to end Shared Signal · Stimpunks

encode → send → decode encode decode a voice, folded onto a wave the mirror of exhale & inhale transmit · receive breath, timestamped and sent Transmit · receive The reciprocal signal Every signal is a two-sided act, the way every breath is. One body encodes — folds a voice, a word, a feeling onto a wave — and another decodes it back into meaning. Transmit and receive: the mirror of exhale and inhale. And what rides the wave is more than information. Voice carries breath — the pace of a sentence, the pause before a hard word, the exhale under a laugh, sent unedited. A voice note is breath, timestamped and sent. You aren't only receiving data; you're receiving someone's nervous system, encoded in sound. The physics doesn't care how far. The same law that carries your voice to a friend across the country carries a star's light across the galaxy. Encode, send, decode — it is how the universe has always passed itself along. A term Helen coined Shared-signal space Shared-air space is the room — proximity, breath, nervous systems settling into one another's rhythm. It needed a counterpart. Not a lesser one. Helen Edgar named it: shared-signal space — connection carried on a signal instead of on the air of a room. A call, a message, a voice note, a synthesised voice: the rhythm still crosses, only now over distance. Does it really carry? Measurably, yes. The tone and pace of a voice cue safety below awareness (Porges, 2011), and that cueing doesn't stop at the edge of a screen: two people's heart-rhythms fall into sync even when they meet remotely — in shared virtual space, at levels comparable to being in the same room (Streuber et al., 2026). Some channels are thinner than that — a laggy call, a dropped word, text with no voice at all — and still the rhythm crosses. Distance can thin the channel. It does not empty it. And for many of us the signal-carried channel is where regulation and honest connection come easiest. Distance thins the channel. It does not empty it. co-regulation, carried in the room over signal thinner amplitude · same rhythm the rhythm still crosses thinner, but real Shared Signal · Stimpunks

live speech reply now tone, live no record all at once text · AAC … thinking time a saved record reread · revise thinking time · a record · fewer demands the thought, let through Text & AAC The clearer channel For many Autistic people, the written word isn't a downgrade from speech — it's the channel that finally lets the thought through. Text takes away the real-time crush: no instant reply owed, no tone to decode on the fly, no face to read while hunting for words. A message can be drafted, reread, and fixed before it's sent, so what lands is closer to what was meant. The largest survey of Autistic adults' own preferences found phone calls ranked last, again and again, and written channels near the top — for four steady reasons: thinking time, structure, fewer sensory demands, and a record to return to (Howard & Sedgewick, 2021). The same is true, and truer, of AAC. Symbol boards, letterboards, text-to-speech run through the written channel, not the spoken one. For non-speaking and minimally speaking people, AAC isn't a workaround bolted onto "real" communication. It is the real communication. Not a fallback from speech. For many of us, the version that finally lets the thought through. Shared Signal · Stimpunks

Anything but the phone Listen to the phone-averse "Anything but the phone!" is such a common Autistic refrain that researchers made it their title (Howard & Sedgewick, 2021). The live call asks for everything at once — instant response, tone read in real time, no record, no pause — and gives the least room to think. Dread of that channel isn't rudeness or fragility, any more than the canary's alarm was weakness. It's information: a signal that this channel is costly, and that a better one exists. Offer the text option and watch who suddenly comes through clearly. The fix isn't to toughen people up for phone calls. It's to stop treating one demanding channel as the toll for being reachable at all. Ask how someone would rather be reached — then reach them there. Build your own watering hole First the justice question, the twin of Shared Air's: reachable, and for whom? A signal life runs on data plans, devices, batteries, and platforms built by other people. When those cost too much or lock us out, "just message me" quietly excludes. Communication access is a commons, not a favour. So we build. The Autistic Rhizome (Edgar, 2026) spreads sideways and underground — no ladder, no single correct path: a Discord alive at 2am, a thread reopened after three years as if no time had passed, a reply to a stranger that becomes a friendship. Online spaces work as watering holes — loosely held, come-and-go, where presence alone can sustain connection. Lurking counts. One reply after months counts. Nobody handed us these rooms. Every star you see is a signal that outran its source — light that left so long ago that some of those stars are already gone. We wrote a whole zine about it: the dead stars still reach us. The reaching is real even when the one who sent it is out of reach. That is the deepest thing a signal does: it lets connection cross a gap that touch cannot. Six Ways a Fact Goes Wrong

Six Ways a Fact Goes Wrong A story that fits gets less scrutiny, which is exactly when it needs more. These are the six shapes the failure takes, and the tell that gives each one away. 01 The quote nobody said The most quotable version of a thought is rarely the one a person produced. What circulates is a compression — true in spirit, absent from the text. Tell More quotable than anything anyone says out loud. Do Search the actual book. 02 The number that went stale Measurements get superseded. The old value keeps circulating in museum copy and popular science for decades with nothing marking it expired. Tell Repeated everywhere, dated nowhere. Do Check the source you cited gives your number. 03 The story told backwards The facts survive the retelling and the emphasis doesn't, so the meaning inverts while every single sentence stays defensible. Tell The paper's own hedge is missing. Do Read what the authors said they don't know. 04 The credit that drifted Attribution decays toward tidiness. A collective becomes a founder, a documenter becomes a coiner, and the citable name absorbs everyone around it. Tell One name where a community was. Do Find the first printed instance, not the famous one. 05 The press release, not the paper Between the finding and the public sits a layer whose job is to make it interesting. Its output isn't a lie. It's a livelier verb. Tell The vivid verb is doing the work. Do Open the abstract. See which word the authors chose. 06 The finding that flatters you The other five are accidents. This one is an appetite — and it is the only one that will find you rather than the other way round. Tell You wanted it true before you read it. Do Slow down here. Don't speed up. the argument, seventeen worked corrections and every source: starstuff.earth/too-good-to-check print freely · share freely · CC BY-SA 4.0 See reverse What to do instead · reverse Stimpunks × More Realms L★S The habits Trace it to the primary. The book, the paper, the talk. Aggregators and summaries are leads, not citations. Cite the source you actually read. If you haven't opened it, it doesn't go in the references. Read your own siblings. Check what you've already claimed about the same thing. When one source falls, re-check its relatives. Errors travel with their quotes. Quote or paraphrase — never dress one as the other. Verbatim and in marks, or in your own words with the idea attributed. Say what's still open. “Leading hypothesis, not a settled result” costs one sentence. Log the correction in public. With a date, and the name of whoever caught it. Measure rather than assume. A stated principle nobody checks is a wish. Five we got wrong The forest is wired together. Elders feeding shaded seedlings through the fungal network — in three of our pieces. Karst, Jones & Hoeksema (2023) find no published evidence for the elder-feeds-offspring claim. Mode 06. “We are star stuff harvesting sunlight.” Sagan never wrote it. Two real sentences in Cosmos ch. 9, welded into a better one. Mode 01. Orion's Belt is scattered in depth. Hipparcos figures for stars Hipparcos measured badly. VLTI and Gaia put all three at one depth — siblings from one cloud. Mode 02. Neurodiversity was coined by one author in 1998. Developed collectively by the online Autistic community; reached print via Harvey Blume, who said so (Botha et al., 2024). Mode 04. Disgust is learned. Ours, and wrong as we stated it. Distaste is present at birth. Caught by Helen Edgar ; the zine gained a spread. Mode 06. Not: Not “do your own research.” Tracing a claim moves toward the evidence and ends somewhere checkable. That phrase moves away from it and ends where nothing can be checked at all. Not science literacy as a gate. Nobody owes anybody a reading list before they're allowed to speak about their own life. Not the pleasure of the debunk. A Myth! headline is exactly as smooth and retellable as the thing it debunks. Not contempt for the people who repeat the story. We repeated it. In three pieces. Where we started The skeleton you were promised This whole collection opens with a bone. Bone Song starts where you'd expect: your calcium was forged in stars, and the skeleton it built is piezoelectric. Press on it and it makes voltage. Iwao Yasuda found that in the 1950s. Your bones are listening to how you move. That's the founding image here. Star-forged mineral, laid down in a living lattice, humming quietly under load. And then the ocean says: sure. Or don't. There is a whole class of vertebrates — sharks, rays, skates, the strange deep chimaeras — that never turns up to the bone. Same phylum. Same backbone-having club. No true bone anywhere in the body. Not a lesser version of yours. A different answer to the same question, and it has been working for a very long time. two vertebrates, two skeletons us mineralised bone press → voltage piezoelectric shark soft core cartilage + tiles bends, then springs no true bone both are vertebrates · neither is the draft same club, different build yasuda 1954–1957 · dean & summers 2006 Skipped Bone · Stimpunks
A mosaic where the bone would be

What's in there instead A mosaic where the bone would be "Cartilaginous" makes it sound floppy. It isn't. A shark's skeleton is cartilage with a mineral crust laid over it — thousands of small blocks, packed edge to edge like paving, sitting on top of an uncalcified core. The blocks are called tesserae, from the word for mosaic tiles, and that is exactly what they look like. Mason Dean and Adam Summers, reviewing the tissue in 2006, describe a skeleton whose mineralisation comes in distinct types — areolar, globular, prismatic — arranged differently depending on the animal's age, its species, where in the body you're looking, and how it feeds. The skeleton is tuned to the life. And the design does something bone can't. A tiled surface over a soft core bends further before it breaks, then springs back. It's lighter than bone. It doesn't need marrow cavities or a blood supply threaded all the way through. None of that is a workaround. It's a different set of trade-offs, chosen — over deep time — by an enormous number of successful animals. You were taught one skeleton and told it was the skeleton. There are others, and they are not rough drafts. tessellated cartilage, in section uncalcified cartilage core tesserae — mineral tiles, laid edge to edge the seams between tiles are where it flexes stiff enough to bite · springy enough to swim areolar · globular · prismatic — three ways to mineralise dean & summers 2006 · zoology a mosaic, tuned to the life it carries Skipped Bone · Stimpunks
They didn't miss it. They let it go

The part that changes the story They didn't miss it. They let it go For most of a century the shark was taught as the before picture. Cartilage first, bone later — sharks as a living snapshot of the stage vertebrates passed through on the way to becoming us. Primitive. Ancestral. Not there yet. The fossils stopped cooperating. In 2020 Martin Brazeau and colleagues described Minjinia turgenensis, an Early Devonian fish from Mongolia on the placoderm grade — close to the common ancestry of all jawed vertebrates — and it is full of endochondral bone. The kind sharks don't have. Which flips the sequence. If the shared ancestor already had bone, then the shark's bonelessness isn't something it never got round to. It is something its lineage gave up. A derived condition. A loss. We have run into this exact shape before, one zine ago. The crab body plan was gained five times and lost seven — leaving turned out to be the commoner event. Here it is again in the skeleton: subtraction is not the same as never having arrived. And whatever they traded away, they have been fine. The chondrichthyan record runs back to the early Silurian — call it 440 million years, on scales and teeth at first. Four mass extinctions. Still here. The animal you were told hadn't got there yet had been there, and chose otherwise. who had bone, and when shared ancestor HAS BONE Minjinia turgenensis early Devonian bony fishes → us kept the bone sharks & rays let the bone go loss derived, not primitive · brazeau et al. 2020 nature ecology & evolution, 2020 the before picture was never before Skipped Bone · Stimpunks

The word doing the damage "Primitive" is a verdict Watch how it works. Primitive has a technical meaning — a trait resembling an ancestral state — and it carries a second meaning it never declares: unfinished. lesser. earlier on the way to better. Both meanings ride in the same word. So a real observation ("this trait resembles the ancestral condition") arrives already sentenced. And here the technical meaning was also wrong. The shark skeleton isn't ancestral. It's a later change. The word was carrying a verdict it hadn't earned, about a fact that wasn't a fact. Our field guide to nervous systems flagged the same habit in neuroscience — jellyfish nets called primitive, worm brains called simple. Same move, different tissue. It's the move that gets made about us, too. Low-functioning. Developmentally delayed. Behind. Every one of them a measurement with a destination smuggled inside it, and the destination is always somebody else. one word, two cargoes "primitive" what it declares resembles the ancestral state what it smuggles unfinished · lesser · behind and for the shark skeleton: the declared meaning was false too a sentence, passed before the evidence the verdict inside the description low-functioning · delayed · behind Skipped Bone · Stimpunks
Then someone decided it was a cure

The turn Then someone decided it was a cure Here is what happened next to the skeleton we've just spent five pages admiring. Somewhere along the way a claim got loose: sharks don't get cancer. Cartilage has no blood vessels of its own; tumours need a blood supply to grow; therefore — the reasoning went — a shark must be carrying something that stops them. Grind it up. Take it as a powder. It became an industry. Capsules, powders, whole shelves of them, sold to people who had just been given the worst news of their lives and were looking anywhere at all. Notice the shape of the claim, because it is the important part. The animal is no longer an animal. Once you've decided a body contains the answer to your problem, the body stops being a life with its own reasons and becomes a supply. And then there's the small matter of whether it was true. the chain of reasoning cartilage has no vessels true so sharks don't get cancer false so grind them into pills didn't work one true premise does not carry a conclusion a body that contains an answer stops being read as a life the premise, the leap, the shelf an animal becomes a supply Skipped Bone · Stimpunks

The record Sharks get cancer They always did. Somebody just had to go and count. In 2004 Gary Ostrander and colleagues went through the literature and the Registry of Tumors in Lower Animals and found 42 documented tumours in cartilaginous fishes — across at least 21 species, in nine families and seven orders. Twenty-four in sharks, sixteen in skates and rays, two in chimaeras. Tumours of the nervous system, the gut, the skin, the blood-forming tissue, the reproductive organs, the endocrine system — and of the skeleton itself. At least fifteen were malignant, invading normal tissue. Their paper's title says the quiet part: Shark Cartilage, Cancer and the Growing Threat of Pseudoscience. Then it was tested properly. Charles Loprinzi and colleagues ran a randomised trial in patients with advanced cancer and reported in 2005: no difference in survival, no difference in quality of life, and side effects bad enough that people struggled to keep taking it. So: the premise was false, the product did nothing, and the animals were killed anyway. 42 documented tumours ≥ 21 species · 7 orders 0 benefit to survival or quality of life The claim was never checked because it was useful. That is usually the reason. 42 tumours, by group sharks 24 skates & rays 16 chimaeras 2 at least 15 malignant · invading normal tissue ostrander et al. 2004 · cancer research the count that was there all along nobody had asked Skipped Bone · Stimpunks
A body read as a cure gets harvested

The pattern underneath A body read as a cure gets harvested This is the sentence the zine exists for, so here it is plainly. The shark was not harmed because anyone hated it. It was harmed because somebody decided its body contained something useful, and once that decision is made, everything else follows without anyone needing to be cruel on purpose. You stop asking what the animal is doing with its own skeleton. You start asking what the skeleton can do for you. And then you go and get it. It is the same operation when it's aimed at people. We know this frame very well: the search for the cause, so there can be a cure. The interest in Autistic people that arrives only as what are they good at, could we use that. The inspiration story where a disabled life is raw material for somebody else's lesson. The research funding that goes to prevention rather than to the things we've actually asked for. All of it starts the same way — not with hatred, with usefulness. A body is read for what can be extracted, and the reading feels like appreciation right up until the moment it costs you something. Being valued for what can be taken out of you is not the same as being valued. two ways of looking at the same body read for what's in it the useful part leaves the body supply read as a life the useful part is doing a job here a life the difference is not kindness · it is direction extraction begins as appreciation and then it comes to collect Skipped Bone · Stimpunks
What the skeleton is actually for

Back to the animal What the skeleton is actually for It's for the shark. That's the whole answer, and it's worth sitting with, because it is the answer that got skipped. The tiled cartilage is doing a job every second of that animal's life. It holds a jaw that has to bite without shattering. It carries a body through water with the springy recoil that makes the swimming cheap. It grows with the animal, tuned — species by species, region by region, feeding style by feeding style — to the exact loads that particular life puts on it. It is not a message to us. It is not a resource with an animal wrapped round it. It is a body, solving the problem of being that body, in a way that has held up across four mass extinctions. Your skeleton is doing the same thing. Yasuda's finding wasn't that your bones are useful to somebody — it's that they're listening, minute by minute, to the life you are actually living. Two different mineral answers. Both of them the same star-forged calcium. Neither of them owed to anyone. one element, two skeletons calcium · forged in stars bone makes voltage under load tesserae bends, then springs back each one for the body that's wearing it the same element, twice neither of them owed to anyone Skipped Bone · Stimpunks

Held with care What we are not saying There are several wrong turns available here, and a few of them are flattering. Naming them. Notsharks are better. We're not swapping which skeleton wins. Bone is extraordinary. Tesserae are extraordinary. There is no podium. Notlosing a trait is secretly superior. "They gave up bone" is a fact about history, not a moral. Loss isn't noble. It's just not the failure it was read as. Notmedicine is the enemy. The people who counted the tumours and ran the trial are the medicine. Pseudoscience is what failed the patients here, and it failed the sharks too. Notanyone who took the pills was a fool. They were frightened people who had been lied to by an industry. The blame sits with whoever sold it. Notdisabled people are like sharks. We are not making anyone an animal metaphor. The shared thing is the frame — a body read for what can be taken out of it — not the bodies. Notbiology proving a politics. A rhyme, not a proof. That vertebrates built two skeletons is not why difference deserves welcome — it would deserve welcome in a universe that only ever made one. what we are not building not a podium side by side bone tesserae others no ranks a rhyme, not a proof the universe doesn't pathologize its own variation no podium, no ranks two answers, both standing Skipped Bone · Stimpunks
You don't owe anyone a reason

Closer to home You don't owe anyone a reason Everything in this zine turns on one question, and it's a question that gets asked about people constantly. What is it for? Asked of a shark's skeleton, it produced a shelf of pills that didn't work and a lot of dead animals. Asked of a person, it produces the same shape: what are you good for, what does your difference get us, where's the upside. You've probably been handed the flattering version. Autistic people are so detail-oriented — brilliant for quality assurance. It sounds like praise. It's a receipt. It says the welcome is conditional on the yield, and quietly hands you the bill if the yield stops. So here is the plain form of the refusal, which is the same one we'd make on the shark's behalf if it could be bothered to care what we think: The skeleton is for the animal. Your mind is for you. Not a resource. Not a lesson. Not a supply. A body doing the work of being itself, which is the only justification anything in this universe has ever had, and it has always been enough. Four hundred million years of no bone at all, and nobody down there is apologising. The tiles aren't a rough draft of a spine. The Skeleton That Skipped Bone is Zine No. 32 in the Stimpunks Star Stuff series, and a deliberate companion and counter-song to Bone Song (1) — which opens this collection on piezoelectric bone, and which this zine answers with a vertebrate that has none. It is also a second visit to the argument in Five Times a Crab, Seven Times Not (31): that a lineage leaving a trait is a different fact from a lineage never having arrived at it. It extends the naming of buried verdicts begun in A Field Guide to Nervous Systems (FG 5) and The Lines We Drew (9). It was written for a young person in our community whose special interest is sharks. It is theirs. Sources & notes. On the tissue: Dean, M. N. & Summers, A. P. (2006). On the loss of bone: Brazeau, M. D., Giles, S., Dearden, R. P., Jerve, A., Ariunchimeg, Y., Zorig, E., Sansom, R., Guillerme, T. & Castiello, M. (2020). On the age of the group: the chondrichthyan fossil record reaches the early Silurian (~440 Ma), though the earliest material is scales and teeth rather than skeletons; Doliodus problematicus (Early Devonian, Canada) is the oldest known largely intact shark. On the cure claim: Ostrander, G. K., Cheng, K. C., Wolf, J. C. & Wolfe, M. J. (2004). Shark cartilage, cancer and the growing threat of pseudoscience. Evaluation of shark cartilage in patients with advanced cancer: A North Central Cancer Treatment Group trial. Cancer, 104(1), 176–182 — no difference in overall survival or quality of life, with adverse effects driving poor compliance. Piezoelectric bone is Iwao Yasuda's (1954–1957), as set out in Bone Song. Held honestly. The secondary-loss reading of the chondrichthyan skeleton is the direction the current evidence points, and it is a live area rather than a closed one — Brazeau and colleagues present Minjinia as reviving and supporting that view, not as settling it. "No true bone" means no endochondral bone: chondrichthyans do mineralise, extensively, and the tesserae are real mineral; some rays carry bone-like tissue in dermal denticles and thorns, which is an active question in the literature. The reasons a lineage would shed bone are not established here and we have not claimed any. We have not put a number on how many sharks the cartilage trade killed, because we could not verify one in a primary source; what is documented is that the premise was false and the product did not work. And the ethics do not come from the biology. That the universe built more than one skeleton is not why a person deserves welcome — as about.html puts it, we are noticing a rhyme, not collecting a proof. The star stuff is Carl Sagan's, and the SN 1006 remnant on every Stimpunks page. Calcium from a dying star, spent two ways. The universe doesn't pathologize its own variation. exchange fungus plant L★S · 001 The Underground Exchange Fungi + plant roots · mutualism ~90% of land plants partner with fungi Fungal threads sheath and enter plant roots, trading the minerals and water they are good at gathering for the sugars the plant makes in the light. Underground, those threads reach far past anything a root could manage alone. mutualismthe wood wide webredistributionno one alone ▸ Field notes Field notes · Fungi + plant roots · mutualism Around nine in ten land plants live in partnership with mycorrhizal fungi. The fungus threads far further through the soil than any root could, gathering water and scarce minerals; the plant pays in sugar it makes from sunlight. Neither is doing charity — each is handing over what it has plenty of for what it lacks. Fungal threads do connect many plants at once, and the popular name for that is the "wood wide web" (Simard) — a sunlit elder feeding a seedling shaded on the forest floor. Be careful with this one: the root-to-fungus trade above is settled, but the forest-wide version is not. Reviewing the field studies, Karst, Jones & Hoeksema (Nature Ecology & Evolution 7, 2023) found the evidence too thin to say shared networks are widespread or that they reliably help seedlings, and found no published evidence that elder trees preferentially feed their own offspring through them. The lesson we keep is the smaller, sturdier one: not charity from the strong, but partners each handing over what they have plenty of. It is really a partnership: a fungus that builds the structure and holds water, and an alga or cyanobacterium that makes food from light. Together they colonise bare rock, deserts, and tundra where neither could live alone. In 2016 Toby Spribille found that many lichens include a second fungus too — not two partners but a small consortium. Where does one partner end and the other begin? In a lichen, the question quietly stops making sense — interdependence isn't a bridge between separate selves; sometimes it is the self. Why a council The cosmos convenes Carl Sagan said it plainly: the calcium in our bones, the iron in our blood, forged in stars that died before the Earth was born. But the same is true of the soil under the city, the water in the river, the beaver and the cuckoo and the meadow. Every being at the table is star stuff. The Council of All Beings is a ritual from deep ecology, developed by Joanna Macy and John Seed: for an afternoon, humans set down the human mask and speak on behalf of another being — a mountain, a wolf, a river. Read cosmically, it isn't make-believe. It's the universe convening with itself, in all the forms it has learned to take. And that reframes everything downstream. You cannot rank what you are made of. Kinship here is not a metaphor — it's an inventory of shared atoms. The council is the universe convening with itself — the same star stuff, gathered in all the forms it has learned to take. one forge C · O · H Ca · Fe human beaver cuckoo river meadow same forge, different form every seat is star stuff The Council of All Beings · Stimpunks

justice count recognition be heard participation exist & act capabilities fair share distribution four questions for every being the agenda of a real council The seating chart Mere service providers The trouble is the seating chart we inherited. Modern planning treats the more-than-human world as a set of service providers — nature valued for what it yields to us, a resource rather than a relation. Repeated everywhere, that one move is a root of the socioecological crisis (Harms et al., 2025). Multispecies justice turns the resource back into a party with standing. It asks four plain questions of any being: can it count (recognition), can it be heard (participation), can it exist and act (capabilities), does it get a fair share (distribution)? These aren't abstractions. They're the agenda for a council that actually means to seat everyone. The Council of All Beings · Stimpunks
Difference in how, not just what

Ethodiversity Difference in how, not just what Biodiversity counts the kinds of life. But a subtler variety is nested inside it: not just what lives, but how it lives. Ombre Tarragnat calls this ethodiversity — the variety of "ways of being and behaving" across all animals — extending a term coined in ecology by Adolfo Cordero-Rivera. The migratory route, the dialect of a birdsong, the nocturnal life, the whole existential style of a creature. Its shadow is ethonormativity: the unwritten rule about which behaviours are allowed to count as acceptable. The horse who refuses the rider, the cat who won't be petted — abandoned, or worse, for departing from the expected script. A grid laid over a field that was already full of variation. So justice has to protect more than a list of species. It has to protect their ways of being. Star stuff varies in matter — and in manner. The council seats not just the beaver, but the beaver's way of being a beaver. The cosmos varies not only in what it makes, but in how its creatures live. Speak as the soil, the river

the table SOIL BEAVER CUCKOO RIVER MEADOW a role card for every voice you argue the world from there Participation · the method Speak as the soil, the river How do you give a being a seat when it can't pull up a chair? You speak as it. In multispecies role-play — the method behind the guide Speaking as a River — people take the part of the soil, the beaver, the cuckoo, the meadow, and argue the world from there. One role card simply reads: "You are the Soil — without you, nothing works here." Good councils run on a few principles (after Artmann): each being is a relating subject with agency, not an object; each has a right to its own voice; each has value in itself, not only in use; and the exchange is reciprocal — giving and taking on equal terms, the old hierarchy set down. It's a rehearsal for a wider "we" — a room where the beaver's right to stay is something you answer to, not around. The Council of All Beings · Stimpunks

The hard part Who speaks, and how A borrowed voice carries a real hazard: speaking for a being can slide into speaking over it. A human voicing the river is, honestly, a human guess — shaped by human wants. Philosophical ethology offers a discipline for it. Vinciane Despret asks that we pose the questions that matter to the animal, not only to us; Jakob von Uexküll called each creature's lived world its Umwelt — the meadow a tick senses is not the meadow you see. The task is to enter that world, as far as you can, before you presume to represent it. Listen long. Represent second. Notventriloquism — a borrowed voice is a responsibility, not a costume. TE AWA TUPUA the river · a legal person the water runs through us all standing, not service the river flows through the room Distribution · standing A real seat, not a favour The ritual points toward real governance. Under Rights of Nature, some rivers and forests now hold legal standing. Aotearoa New Zealand recognised the Whanganui River as a legal person — Te Awa Tupua — with appointed guardians who speak in its name. Projects like the Interspecies Council rehearse the same shift: governing with the more-than-human world, not merely about it. And the river was never only "out there." In Astrida Neimanis's hydrofeminism, we are all bodies of water — rain, river, and blood passing through one another. The water in you has been the sea; it will be the cloud. This isn't charity extended outward — it's the cosmos, made of one shared stuff, learning to govern itself with care. The Council of All Beings · Stimpunks

Coda Already in flow Not every convening needs a chair. The council seats us — star stuff at a table, taking turns to speak. But water never waited for an invitation to convene. It was already in flow before anyone sat down: sea to cloud, cloud to rain, rain to river, river to blood, blood to rain again — one long convening that never adjourns. Maybe that's the truer shape of the thing. Not a table with seats around it, but a flow with all of us already in it — no head of the table, no order of speaking, just the same water finding its way through every body it passes. The council asks us to notice who's missing from the table. The flow asks something simpler: notice you were never outside it. We are star stuff, and we are the water that carries it. The message keeps arriving after the sender is gone. In the spring of 1006, people across the world recorded a brilliant new star in the south. Inheritance Their ending, our beginning A star's death is not only a loss. It is a dispersal. The heavy elements a star forges — the calcium, the iron — are flung out when it dies, drift for ages, and gather again into planets, and bodies, and us. We are made of dead stars. Not as a metaphor: the atoms in our bones were forged in stars that died before the Earth existed. Their ending is the reason we are here to look up at all. Ancestors work the same way. What they made — the free spaces, the strategies, the words — scattered outward when they were gone, and gathered into us. We don't start the fire. We catch its light. The Dead Stars Still Reach Us is the tenth zine in the Stimpunks series, and the one about ancestry — the astronomy underneath our writing on memory and lineage. The astronomy is real, and worth stating precisely. Light travels at a finite speed, so we always see a star as it was when its light departed, never as it is now. It's often said that "the stars you see are already dead" — in truth, most naked-eye stars are still shining, because they sit tens to hundreds of light-years away, far less than a star's lifetime. The deeper, exact point is that we can never see any star's present, so we live by light from sources we cannot check — and some of them, especially distant ones, are indeed already gone. SN 1006 is the vivid case: observers worldwide recorded the supernova in the spring of 1006 CE; the star lay roughly 7,200 light-years off, so the explosion itself happened millennia before anyone on Earth saw it, and only its expanding remnant — and its scattered elements — remain (this is the "Liberating Star Stuff" image Stimpunks keeps). Betelgeuse, about 550 light-years away, will end as a supernova; if it exploded today we would not know for roughly five centuries, and it may already have gone. The ancestry is drawn from our own writing. The Highlander Folk School crosswalk reads the school (founded 1932 by Myles Horton; Septima Clark's citizenship schools; Rosa Parks, 1955; Aldon Morris's "movement halfway house") as ancestry rather than parallel — via Nico Slate's 2022 history. How knowledge grows The garden, not the stream Most of the web is a social stream: a feed of dated posts, sorted by an algorithm, urgent for a day and then washed away. A post starts decaying the moment it's published. You don't return to it; you scroll past it. A garden is the older idea. Mike Caulfield drew the line: the garden is the web as space, an arrangement you can walk. It's evergreen — you keep tending and refining the notes — and richly cross-linked, so that, as Maggie Appleton puts it, every walk creates new paths. You add things not in sequence but so they can form future, unpredicted relationships. The Star Stuff site is a garden. So is the whole knowledge garden it grew from. Not a feed to keep up with — a landscape to wander. A stream tells you what's new. A garden lets you wander what's true. hierarchy subjects → articles rhizome sideways, not up grown from lived experience a mesh, not a ladder roots down in real life Lived experience Grown from the ground up An encyclopedia grows downward from the top: subjects, then categories, then articles, handed down by an authority. A garden grows the other way. Ours climbs up from the soil of lived experience — from what a body knows, to a word for it, to a pattern, a recipe, an environment, a system. And it doesn't grow in straight lines. Its shape is a rhizome and a mycelial network (after Deleuze & Guattari): ideas spread sideways and underground, throwing up shoots where they connect, refusing the neat trunk-and-branches of the tree. Knowledge grown up from the ground of real neurodivergent and disabled life — not lowered down onto it. An encyclopedia is handed down from the top. A garden grows up from the ground. The cosmic turn Star stuff, knowing itself Here is the reason it's a garden and not a vault. Carl Sagan said we are a way for the cosmos to know itself. A knowledge garden is that sentence built into a thing you can walk through — and the method it uses is the cosmos's own. A star forges the elements in its core and then, dying, scatters them — a supernova is a seed-head bursting (the image on every Stimpunks page, SN 1006, is literally liberated iron). That scattered stuff settles into life; life grows minds; minds grow gardens of meaning that go to seed and grow new minds. Nucleosynthesis, then the periodic table — the first seed catalogue — then us. So the universe doesn't know itself as stored data. It knows itself as a garden — by growing, connecting, and seeding, over and over. The reflex It arrives before you do You know the feeling. It gets there ahead of you. Something on a screen, something in a jar, something in a documentary about the deep sea — and before a single thought has formed, the whole body has already voted. The face does its thing. The shoulders go up. Ugh. No. Get it away. And it doesn't feel like an opinion. That's the important part. It feels like perception — like you have simply noticed a property the thing has, the way you'd notice that it was blue. It isn't. There is no gross in the animal. There is no gross anywhere in the ocean. Gross is a reading, produced by a particular frame, in a particular animal, at a particular moment in its history — and this zine is about who ends up on the wrong side of it.
