Before we go any further Two icks, not one There is a distinction the research makes, and an earlier version of this zine walked straight past it. It matters enormously, so it goes here, before the argument. Paul Rozin's own framework separates two things that both feel like "ew." Distaste is sensory. It is a response to the actual properties of a thing — bitter, sour, slimy, sticky, cold and wet in the wrong way. And it is there from the beginning. Put something bitter on a newborn's tongue and you get the gape face: mouth open, upper lip pulled back, nose wrinkled, brow down. It is highly conserved across species. It has been observed in humans in utero. And then the finding that settles how deep it runs. In 1973 Jacob Steiner published observations of the gustofacial response in anencephalic newborns — infants born without most of the higher brain. They make the face too. The response does not require a cortex. It isn't a judgement, it isn't an attitude, and it cannot be a prejudice, because there is nothing there to hold one. Disgust proper is a different animal. Rozin calls it ideationally based and contamination-sensitive: you don't have to taste a cockroach to be disgusted by one. It attaches to ideas about things — where they have been, what they touched, what they count as. This zine is about the second one. Everything that follows — the borders, the projections, the sorting of bodies — is the ideational kind doing political work. The sensory kind is not a prejudice and never was. You were never a blank slate. You arrived with a body that already had positions on the world, and that gape is older than our species — history, carried in you. Which is, after all, the premise of this entire collection. The correction on this spread is Helen Edgar's, who taught children with profound and multiple learning disabilities for twenty years and pointed out that the first version of this zine presumed a thinking response to the ick — and that the babies and the young people she has worked with plainly have one without it. two responses, both called "ew" distaste the gape face present at birth no cortex needed disgust where has it been? ideational contamination-sensitive develops later not a prejudice never was does border work this zine is about this one rozin · steiner 1973 · gustofacial response distaste is bodily · disgust is ideational only one of them can be a prejudice The Ick · Stimpunks

Where it came from The second one gets taught The gape was there at birth. The contamination logic was not, and small children are famously unbothered by it. Paul Rozin and April Fallon, in a 1987 paper that still anchors the field, treat disgust as a food emotion at root — revulsion at the prospect of taking something into the mouth. Its objects are overwhelmingly of animal origin. And crucially, this kind develops, arriving across a child's first eight years or so rather than being present at the start. They also describe what it runs on. Disgust obeys the laws of sympathetic magic — including the law of contagion, under which contact transfers an essence. A cockroach touches your sandwich; the sandwich is now inedible. Not partly inedible where the legs went. All of it. Forever. Sit with that, because it's the whole argument in one move: the reaction is out of all proportion to any physical fact. No amount of chemistry explains the whole sandwich. What's operating is a rule about categories and contact — and rules about categories are things a culture teaches you. Which means the border can be redrawn. People do it constantly, in both directions, without noticing. Somebody, somewhere, feeds their child something you would gag on, and their child grows up finding it delicious and finding your dinner revolting. Both of you think you are perceiving. the law of contagion edible one touch ALL of it inedible and it arrives on a schedule birth ~4 yrs ~8 yrs unbothered fully installed rozin & fallon 1987 · it was taught a rule about categories not a measurement of danger The Ick · Stimpunks

Exhibit one The worm with no mouth In 2004 Greg Rouse, Shana Goffredi and Robert Vrijenhoek named a genus that shouldn't work. Osedax — the name means bone-devourer — lives on whale skeletons on the deep sea floor. The adult females have no mouth and no gut at all. What they have instead is a root system: a branching, blood-supplied network that grows down into the bone, carrying symbiotic bacteria that break the bone down from inside. The animal doesn't eat. It roots, like something between a worm and a small tree, into the skeleton of something enormous that died above it. And the males never grow up. Dozens of them — tiny, paedomorphic, arrested partway through development — live inside the female's own tube, doing the one job they are there for. Every clause of that is a small horror in English, and not one of it is a problem. It is a lineage that found a food source nobody else could reach, and built a body that could get at it. Read from inside, it's just competent. You are not looking at a violation. You are looking at somebody's job. What it costs to never let go

Exhibit two What it costs to never let go The deep-sea anglerfish is the one everybody has heard about, usually told as a joke. A male, far smaller than the female, finds her in the dark, bites on, and fuses. Tissues join. The two circulatory systems merge into one. He never leaves. It is the only case in nature of two vertebrates becoming, permanently, a single joined body. Here is the part that isn't a joke, and it is the reason this zine exists. In 2020 Jeremy Swann, Stephen Holland, Malte Petersen, Theodore Pietsch and Thomas Boehm looked at the genomes and found what the fusion cost. Species whose males attach temporarily have lost functional aicda — the gene behind antibody maturation. Species whose males attach permanently go further, some losing functional rag genes altogether, which abolishes the somatic shuffling of antigen receptors that is the defining hallmark of adaptive immunity. Your immune system's entire job is telling you from not-you, and rejecting the not-you. So: To be permanently joined to another body, they gave up the machinery that draws the line between self and other. They did not solve rejection. They dismantled the thing that rejects. The border you are so sure of is a piece of equipment. It can be traded. Somebody did. attachment, and what it costs temporary lost: aicda no antibody maturation permanent lost: aicda + rag no receptor shuffling — adaptive immunity gone the immune system's job: self | not-self to stay joined, they gave up the line swann, holland, petersen, pietsch & boehm 2020 science, 2020 · immunogenetics of sexual parasitism the price of never letting go The Ick · Stimpunks
A body that becomes a town

Exhibit three A body that becomes a town Nothing triggers the reflex like a corpse. So let's take the biggest one there is. A whale dies and sinks. Down there, food arrives as a slow drizzle of scraps from far above — and now, all at once, forty tonnes of it lands in one place. Craig Smith and Amy Baco, reviewing the whole field in 2003, put the scale plainly: the sediment beneath a sunken carcass gets an initial pulse of organic matter equivalent to roughly 2,000 years of the normal background supply. Then a town builds itself, in three overlapping stages. Months to years. The mobile scavengers — sleeper sharks, hagfish, rat-tails — strip soft tissue at 40 to 60 kilograms a day. Months to years. Enrichment opportunists move onto the enriched sediment and the exposed bones: dense assemblages of polychaetes and crustaceans, up to 40,000 animals per square metre. Decades. The sulphophilic stage. Bone lipids break down without oxygen and give off sulphide; bacteria make a living out of the sulphide; a large, trophically complex community assembles on top of that. Smith and Baco report a mean of 185 macrofaunal species on a large skeleton at this stage — higher local diversity than any other hard surface in the deep sea. Across the world's whale falls, 407 species. Twenty-one of them are known from nowhere else on Earth. The thing you were taught was the end of a body is, down there, one of the most generous events that ever happens. 185 mean macrofaunal species on one large skeleton 21 species known from nowhere else one carcass, three stages, decades 1 · mobile scavengers sleeper sharks · hagfish · rat-tails — 40–60 kg/day months–years 2 · enrichment opportunists polychaetes · crustaceans — up to 40,000 per m² months–years 3 · sulphophilic bone lipids → sulphide → chemoautotrophs mean 185 macrofaunal species DECADES ≈ 2,000 years of background food, at once smith & baco 2003 decay is a construction schedule the richest hard surface down there The Ick · Stimpunks
What the ick was actually measuring

The turn What the ick was actually measuring Go back over the three of them and ask what they had in common. It wasn't danger — none of them can hurt you. It wasn't dirt — the deep sea is one of the cleanest places on the planet. What they share is distance from one particular body plan. Mouths belong on faces. Bodies end at the skin. The dead are separate from the living. Eating is done with a gut. These aren't laws of nature. They are the specifications of one animal, generalised into a template — and the ick is what fires when something falls outside it. That template has two settings, and this collection has been picking at both: Anthronormative — the assumption that the human arrangement is the correct arrangement for a body. Neuronormative — the assumption that one kind of mind is the correct kind, and other kinds are that kind gone wrong. Same machine, two dials. Both take a local arrangement and file everything else as a deviation from it. distance from a template one template Osedax anglerfish whale fall the ick tracks radius · nothing else anthronormative one right body neuronormative one right mind same machine, two dials a local arrangement, promoted to a standard The Ick · Stimpunks
The same reflex, aimed at us

Where it lands The same reflex, aimed at us Now the part this zine was actually written for. That reflex — the one that fires at a rooted worm and a fused fish — does not stay in the ocean. It gets pointed at people, and it does an enormous amount of work. It fires at a feeding tube. At drooling. At an adult in incontinence pads. At a stim that isn't the socially cleared kind — the loud one, the wet one, the one with hands. At a communication device that speaks in a voice somebody decided was unpleasant. At bodies that need help with the parts of being alive that everyone has agreed to pretend are private. Nobody says disgusting out loud. They don't have to. The reflex does its work in the face, in the half-step back, in the seat that stays empty, in the invitation that doesn't come, in the tone of the assessment paperwork. Martha Nussbaum gave this its name in 2004: projective disgust. We take what we cannot stand about being animal — that we leak, decay, depend, and die — and we load it onto a group of people, who then function as a buffer between us and our own bodies. Push them out and the animal facts feel further away. Which is why the ick is not a matter of taste, and why we are not asking anyone to find worms charming. Disgust is how a border gets enforced without anyone having to defend it. It doesn't argue. It just refuses, and then it acts hurt if you ask it to explain. The reflex that ruled out the bone-eating worm is the reflex that empties the seat next to us. It never learned there was a difference. projective disgust, in one move what we can't stand about being animal: leaking · decaying · needing · dying loaded onto a group of people who then sit between us and the facts push them out → the animal feels further away it was never about them nussbaum, hiding from humanity, 2004 a buffer, made of people the ick is doing somebody's laundry The Ick · Stimpunks
Weird we took. Gross we haven't

Two words, two jobs Weird we took. Gross we haven't There's a word next door to this one, and it has already been reclaimed. In Wyrd & Weird, Helen Edgar follows weird back to Old English wyrd — becoming, fate, a web held from every side — and shows Autistic and disabled communities running the drift backwards, taking the word up as a name rather than a verdict. Weird is ours now. People wear it. Gross has not been taken, and it works differently. Weird is a judgement about categories: you don't fit the box. It can be answered with pride, because pride is also a claim about where you belong. Gross isn't a claim at all. It's a body refusing another body. You can't be proud at it, because it doesn't stay to listen — it has already turned away. So this one doesn't get reclaimed. It gets disarmed: shown to be learned, shown to be arbitrary, shown to be doing political work it never admitted to. You don't march under it. You just stop letting it decide who's in the room. two words, two jobs weird a claim about categories "you don't fit" answerable → RECLAIMED worn as a name gross a body refusing another body "get it away" unanswerable → DISARMED shown for what it is you can march under one of these the other you just take the keys off no. 28 took the first one this one gets disarmed instead The Ick · Stimpunks

Held with care What we are not saying This argument has several cheap versions. Naming them so we don't get mistaken for one. Not"actually it's beautiful." That just swaps one aesthetic verdict for another and keeps the judge's chair warm. The worm doesn't need to be pretty. It needs to be left alone. Not"gross but useful to humans." Hagfish slime is being studied for fibres; whale-fall bacteria for enzymes. Fine — but usefulness is the extraction frame, and the zine before this one is about where that leads. Notyour sensory aversion is a prejudice. If a texture, a smell, a sound or a wet thing on your hands sends you through the roof — that is distaste, it is bodily, and none of this argument is pointed at it. Autistic and otherwise neurodivergent sensory responses are real, they are not bigotry, and you do not owe anybody an apology or an exposure programme for them. Nota blank slate. We are not claiming you arrived with no positions on the world. You arrived with a nervous system that had plenty, and the oldest of them are older than our species. What is learned is the contamination logic laid over the top, not the body underneath it. Notdisgust is never useful. It plainly has a job — some of it tracks real contamination. The claim is narrower: its objects are learned, it overshoots wildly, and it should never be trusted as evidence about a person. Notyou're bad for feeling it. It was installed in you before you could consent. Nobody is guilty of a reflex. You are only answerable for what you do in the two seconds after. Notdisabled people are deep-sea creatures. We are not anyone's metaphor. The shared thing is the reflex and the border it draws — not the bodies on either side of it. Notbiology proving a politics. A rhyme, not a proof. That the ocean is full of arrangements we find upsetting is not why people deserve welcome. They would deserve it in an empty universe. the two seconds after the reflex not yours to choose not yours to be blamed for treat it as evidence → the seat stays empty treat it as weather → you stay in the room nobody is guilty of a flinch everyone is answerable for what comes next a rhyme, not a proof the flinch is not the failure what you do next is The Ick · Stimpunks

Look again Nothing down there has changed Go back to the worm. It is still rooted in the bone. It still has no mouth. The males are still small and still in her tube. Not one fact about it has moved since page four. If it reads differently now — and it might — then the thing that changed was on this side of the glass. That's the whole demonstration. The verdict was never in the water. It was in the frame, that part of the frame was learned, and a learned thing can be widened. Your body may still not want to touch it. That's allowed, and it always was — that part isn't the frame, it's you, and it has a history in it older than our species. Not wanting to touch something is not the same as ruling it out of the world. The whole argument is the gap between those two. And widening it is not a favour you do the deep sea. The deep sea is fine. It's a favour you do yourself, and everyone who has ever been on the far side of somebody's flinch — which, at some point, is everybody. Because here is the thing the reflex is actually protecting you from, and it's not the worm: you are an animal. You leak, you decay, you need enormous amounts of help, and one day you will be food for something. Every one of those is also true of the whale, and the whale's version fed a town for thirty years. The atoms doing all of this were made in stars. That part is true of the worm, the anglerfish, the whale, and you — the same calcium, the same carbon, the same everything, arranged into a few thousand ways of being alive, not one of which is the correct one. The Ick Is a Border is Zine No. 33 in the Stimpunks Star Stuff series. It is a house zine and a deliberate companion to Wyrd & Weird (28), Helen Edgar's guest zine on weird — the word this community did reclaim. Weird is hers and the reclamation is hers; this zine takes the neighbouring word, gross, which works differently and is disarmed rather than worn. It extends Every Nervous System (27) and The Council of All Beings (25) into the territory of disgust, and continues the account of constructed lines begun in The Lines We Drew (9). Written after The Skeleton That Skipped Bone (32), for the same young person, whose marine biology special interest is the reason both exist. Corrected after publication — and the correction is the important part. The first published version of this zine argued that the ick is learned, full stop. Helen Edgar, who taught children with profound and multiple learning disabilities for twenty years, read it and pointed out that it presumes a cognitive, intellectualising response — and that pre-term babies, and the young people she has worked with, plainly have an ick without one. She is right, and the literature is unambiguous. Rozin's own framework separates distaste — a chemosensory rejection tied to a thing's actual properties, producing the highly conserved "gape face," present at birth and observed in utero — from disgust proper, which Rozin describes as ideationally based and contamination-sensitive, and which you can feel about a cockroach without tasting one. The strongest evidence for how deep the first one runs is Jacob Steiner's (1973) observations of the gustofacial response in anencephalic newborns, who produce it without most of a higher brain: the response does not require a cortex, and therefore cannot be an opinion. Spread 3 now makes that distinction before the argument starts, and the argument is explicitly scoped to the ideational kind. Helen's second point is the one that goes deepest and is now in the zine's own voice: we are not blank slates — that is the point of star stuff; we have history in us. A response conserved across species and present before birth is exactly that history, and the earlier draft was, in effect, arguing against this collection's own premise. Autistic and otherwise neurodivergent sensory aversion is distaste, not prejudice, and spread 11 now says so in a refusal. Sources & notes. Nussbaum, M. C. (2004). Hiding from Humanity: Disgust, Shame, and the Law. One axis, and we put ourselves at the top of it

The ladder One axis, and we put ourselves at the top of it Ask how smart an animal is and you have already agreed to something: that smart is a quantity, that it runs along one axis, and that every mind can be given a place on it. The axis needs a yardstick, so we have built several. Absolute brain mass. Brain mass against body mass. The encephalisation quotient. Cortical surface. Neuron counts. These are real measurements, taken carefully by careful people, and none of them is the problem. The problem is the ordering. A measurement tells you how much of something there is. It does not tell you that more of it is better, or that the creature with the most of it is the one the others are failing to be. And the ordering came first. We had the ladder long before we had the instruments, and then we went looking for the instrument that would show us on the top rung — which is a different activity from measuring. us apes monkeys the rest … more the shape of the assumption one axis · one winner a ladder, not a measurement The Layer We Call Essential · Stimpunks
Then somebody counted the pilot whale

The count Then somebody counted the pilot whale Neuron number is the yardstick that feels least arguable. Cells are countable. You can do the stereology and get a figure, and the figure does not care what you were hoping for. In 2014, Mortensen and colleagues did the counting on the neocortex of the long-finned pilot whale — a dolphin, despite the name. They found roughly 37.2 billion neocortical neurons, alongside some 127 billion glial cells. That is, in the paper's own words, almost twice as many neocortical neurons as humans. The first animal ever counted with more neocortical neurons than us, and it is a mid-sized dolphin that most people have never heard of. 37.2 ×10⁹ neocortical neurons long-finned pilot whale ≈ 2× the human count mortensen et al. 2014 Neuron density is lower in the whale; the total is higher because the brain is bigger. Both facts are in the paper, and both are worth keeping. 37.2 pilot whale ≈ half human neocortical neurons ×10⁹ the countable yardstick and it does not favour us mortensen et al. 2014 The Layer We Call Essential · Stimpunks
The measurement lost. The ranking survived it.

The part nobody quotes The measurement lost. The ranking survived it. Here is the sentence in that same paper. The absolute number of neurons in the human neocortex, the authors conclude, is not correlated with the superior cognitive abilities of humans — at least not compared with cetaceans — as had previously been hypothesised. Read it slowly. The yardstick was neuron count. The count came back against us. And the conclusion drawn is not perhaps the ranking is wrong. It is the count must not be the right yardstick. To be fair to the authors: as a narrow claim about neuroscience that is entirely defensible, and probably correct. Neuron number alone plainly does not explain human cognition. They are reporting an honest negative result. But look at what stayed fixed while everything else moved. Human superiority is not the thing being tested here. It is the thing the test is being fitted to. Which tells you something useful: the ranking was never resting on the count. So no count could ever disturb it. Another yardstick will be found, and if that one comes back wrong too, another will be found after it. the evidence whale us moved and yet the ranking us didn't it was never resting on the evidence a fixed point, dressed as a finding the yardstick is replaceable the conclusion is not The Layer We Call Essential · Stimpunks
The input layer our textbooks call canonical is simply not there

No fourth layer The input layer our textbooks call canonical is simply not there Open a neuroscience textbook at the cortical column and you will find six layers, with layer IV as the front door: the granular layer where signals from the thalamus arrive before anything else happens to them. The cetacean neocortex does not have one. Not reduced in places — the whole sheet is agranular. The lamination, as the literature describes it, runs: a thick cellular layer I; a densely packed layer II whose neurons send dendrites up into layer I; a wide pyramidal layer III; an absent or underdeveloped layer IV; a magnocellular layer V of large pyramidal cells; and a heterogeneous layer VI. So where does the input go? The current reading is that layer I takes the job — that it is the main target for incoming subcortical neurons precisely because layer IV is absent, with layer II then relaying that information down to the lower layers. The front door moved upstairs. The result, in the words of the review that lays this out, is a very different connectivity scheme compared to more commonly studied species, like rats and macaque monkeys. Sit with that phrase — more commonly studied species. The canonical column is canonical because of who we happened to put on the microscope. Rats and macaques are the baseline for reasons of husbandry and history, not because evolution nominated them. And in layer V of the anterior cingulate, anterior insular and frontopolar cortices, the humpback whale turns out to carry large spindle cells — von Economo neurons — similar in shape and distribution to those described in hominids. Hof and Van der Gucht call it a likely case of parallel evolution. Same cell type, arrived at separately, in a cortex with no fourth layer to build it on. primate IIIIII IV VVI in front door: IV cetacean I IIIII IV VVI in relay front door: I IV: absent the job moved two routes into a cortex absent ≠ missing ≠ lacking hof & van der gucht 2007 · marino et al. 2008 The Layer We Call Essential · Stimpunks
Difference read as deficit, in Biological Reviews, in 2006

The live argument Difference read as deficit, in Biological Reviews, in 2006 In 2006 Paul Manger published a long paper arguing that cetacean brains got big to make heat — thermogenesis against a cooling ocean — rather than to think. He argued further that cetaceans are considerably less intelligent than generally supposed. One of his three claims was this: there is no neural basis for complex cognition in cetaceans. Among the evidence offered were the indistinct lamination, the pyramidalised layer II, and the absence of layer IV. In 2008, sixteen authors replied. Those features, they answered, are one aspect of an unusual combination of conservative and derived traits — and cetacean brains, having diverged from our common ancestor more than 95 million years ago and arrived at high encephalisation entirely independently, in all likelihood represent a non-primate route to neuroanatomical (and cognitive) complexity. A brain organised unlike ours was read as a brain insufficient for mind. The reply did not say the difference wasn't real. It said the difference wasn't a deficit. You know this argument. It is the one made about us, in clinics and classrooms, in the same century. Here it is being had by neuroscientists, about whales, in a review journal — and the shape of the inference is identical. one observation no layer IV manger 2006 no neural basis for cognition marino et al. 2008 the input moved to layer I same slide different baseline the inference is a choice one fact, two readings deficit or design the data did not decide it The Layer We Call Essential · Stimpunks
We are not telling you who won

Held with care We are not telling you who won It would be easy, and dishonest, to leave Manger as the villain of this zine. So: his thermogenesis hypothesis was a serious proposal, published in a serious journal, and it has not simply evaporated. Later work has found real thermogenic signatures in cetacean brains — uncoupling proteins expressed in cortical neurons and in glia, an increased density of noradrenergic boutons. A brain in cold water may well be doing heat work and thought work. Organs are not single-purpose. The reply from Marino and colleagues is also not neutral ground. It is an argued position by researchers with a stake in cetacean cognition, and calling a paper a claim in search of evidence in your own title is not a gesture of detachment. So we are not handing you a verdict. What we are pointing at is narrower and, we think, harder to wriggle out of: the direction the inference travelled by default. Given a cortex organised unlike the ones we had studied, the available readings included this brain is built differently and this brain is built worse. The second was reached quickly, defended at length, and required no additional evidence to feel reasonable — because the ladder was already there to catch it. That is the part that recurs. It recurs in the lines we drew around normal, and it is the mechanism the difference-first frame exists to interrupt. Not who was right about whales. Which reading you get for free. obs unlike ours built worse no extra evidence required built differently argued for at length both available one is downhill the gradient under the argument a rhyme, not a proof what you get for free is the finding The Layer We Call Essential · Stimpunks
They had to borrow from music, because the shelf didn't fit

Rubato They had to borrow from music, because the shelf didn't fit Sperm whales talk in codas — short patterned bursts of clicks. For decades the Eastern Caribbean repertoire was described as around 21 discrete coda types. A modest vocabulary. Roughly what you would expect from a lesser mind. In 2024, a team analysed 8,719 codas from at least 60 whales recorded between 2005 and 2018, and found the repertoire was not a list at all. It has four features that combine freely: rhythm and tempo, which hold steady regardless of context, plus two they named rubato and ornamentation, which shift with the conversation going on around them. Combine those four and you get roughly 143 combinations actually in use — nearly an order of magnitude past the old count. Notice the naming. Rubato and ornamentation are borrowed from music, because the categories on the shelf did not have a slot for what the whales were doing. The vocabulary had to be built before the structure could be seen. Which is the quiet lesson of the whole zine. When your instrument has no category for a thing, the thing reads as absence. Twenty-one types was never what the whales had. It was what we could hear. rhythm tempo faster, same shape rubato stretched ornament +1 extra was: 21 types is: ≈143 combinations four features, freely combined context-sensitive · context-free sharma et al. 2024 The Layer We Call Essential · Stimpunks
Fifteen mothers out of a hundred and forty-one

Only some of them Fifteen mothers out of a hundred and forty-one In Shark Bay, Western Australia, some bottlenose dolphins break a marine sponge off the seafloor, wear it over the closed beak, and use it to probe the sediment for fish. It is called sponging. Not the dolphins. Some. Krützen and colleagues found it in 15 of 141 known mothers, and mitochondrial DNA put its transmission almost entirely down a single matriline — mother to daughter, learned rather than inherited. And spongers live differently. Compared with non-spongers in the same water, they are more solitary, work the deep channels, dive for longer, and spend more of the day foraging. So inside one population, sharing one gene pool and one bay, there is a minority with a different sensory route to food, a different social pattern, and a different shape of day — passed along a family line, by learning. We have a word for a profile with peaks and troughs rather than a single level: the spiky profile. And a word for surfacing and diving by capacity — dolphining, which we named after them before we knew this. 141 known mothers 15 spongers · one matriline variation inside one population not a species difference krützen et al. 2005 · mann et al. 2008 The Layer We Call Essential · Stimpunks

The question, straight Is there neurodiversity among whales? We went looking, and here is the honest answer: there is no cetacean autism literature. No whale ADHD, no dolphin dyslexia, no diagnostic framework of any kind applied to a cetacean. We found none, and we are not going to invent one to make this zine land better. That absence is worth stating plainly, because the temptation runs the other way. It would be easy to write whales are neurodivergent too, and it would be false, and it would borrow legitimacy from a clinical apparatus we spend the rest of our time arguing with. But the question has a real answer, once you notice that the neurodiversity paradigm was never about diagnoses. It is about variation within a population, and whether the population is built so that variation survives. At that level the record is not empty at all. It is fifteen mothers out of a hundred and forty-one, with a traced inheritance route. It is 143 combinations where we had heard 21. It is a cortex with no fourth layer, working. The frame that lets us say this without diagnosing anybody is ethodiversity — Ombre Tarragnat's extension of the neurodiversity paradigm, by way of ethology, to beings with nervous systems. It takes the part that travels (variation is normal, and it is not a defect) and leaves behind the part that shouldn't (the clinic, the diagnosis, the deficit). You do not need to find an Autistic whale. You need to stop requiring a diagnosis before variation counts. Not: whales are smarter than us. That is the same ladder with a new occupant. We are not trying to win the ranking; we are declining it. Not: dolphins are Autistic. We do not diagnose across species to borrow standing. No such literature exists and we are not manufacturing it. Not: a superpower. 37.2 billion neurons is not a gift narrative, and neither is anybody's spiky profile. Not: nature proves the ethics. Difference would deserve welcome in a universe that made exactly one shape. The whales are a rhyme, not a warrant. And: we notice we are doing it too. This zine spends eleven spreads using cetacean minds as material for a human argument. Their minds are not evidence for our politics first. They are theirs first. observed variation diagnosis required? no such literature ethodiversity tarragnat it counts no clinic needed two routes from the same observation one needs a diagnosis first the paradigm never did The Layer We Call Essential · Stimpunks
A body shaped differently, travelling with whales

Eight days off Pico A body shaped differently, travelling with whales In 2011, off the island of Pico in the Azores, two researchers watching sperm whales found something else in the group: an adult male bottlenose dolphin whose spine curved so severely that his rear half held an S shape. Over eight days he travelled with the whales, foraged with them, and played with the adults and their calves. When he rubbed his body against them, the rubs were sometimes returned. A dolphin with a spine that didn't work like other dolphins' spines was moving with a slower species that had room for him in it. Two things this is not. First, it is not an adoption. The paper is titled Repeated Non-Agonistic Interactions — careful, unglamorous, exactly as far as the evidence goes. "Adopted" is the press's word, not the researchers'. Second, we do not know why. The suggestion that other dolphins had harassed him and he sought refuge is a plausible guess offered to reporters — not a finding. It may be that a curved spine made sperm whale pace easier to keep than dolphin pace. We don't know. What is in the record is eight days, and the rubs coming back. That is enough. It does not have to mean anything about us to be worth knowing. sperm whales S-curved spine rubs returned calf days recorded together 8 — and the rubs came back azores, 2011 non-agonistic, repeatedly wilson & krause 2013 The Layer We Call Essential · Stimpunks
Douglas Adams got there first, and then the joke came due

So long Douglas Adams got there first, and then the joke came due In 1979, in The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy, Douglas Adams made this exact joke and made it better. On Earth, he wrote, humans had always assumed they were the most intelligent species on the planet — whereas in fact they were the third. Mice first. Dolphins second. Look at the mechanism. He does not overturn the ranking. He keeps its form perfectly intact and moves us down two rungs, and the whole apparatus collapses into absurdity, because a ladder that puts mice on top was never measuring anything. The dolphins, knowing what was coming, left. Their last message, mistaken for a stunt: So long, and thanks for all the fish. Then the bill arrived. In 1988 Adams travelled with the zoologist Mark Carwardine to find endangered species for Last Chance to See, and one of them was the baiji, the Yangtze river dolphin — a freshwater cetacean going deaf and blind in a river turned into an industrial corridor. In December 2006, a six-week survey of the Yangtze ended without a single sighting. Turvey and colleagues published it as, possibly, the first human-caused extinction of a cetacean species. A species actually said so long. Not as a punchline. The ranking was never a description of the world. It was a permission slip — and the thing it gave us permission to do, we did. adams, 1979 1 · mice 2 · dolphins 3 · us same ladder, obviously absurd baiji · lipotes vexillifer drawn as an outline, which is all there is left to draw 1979 the joke 1990 last chance 2006 survey: none so long — and it wasn't a joke 1979 → 2006 the punchline, collected turvey et al. 2007 The Layer We Call Essential · Stimpunks

Look up The hunter everyone learns Here is Orion, the way we are all taught to see it: two shoulders, two feet, and the three perfect stars of the belt. A hunter, mid-stride, raising his club against the winter sky. Almost every culture that has watched this patch of sky has drawn something here — a hunter, a shepherd, a giant, a canoe. We are pattern-hungry animals. Our eyes reach for a shape and our minds hand us one, fast, before we've decided to look. Then we forget we did it. The line stops feeling like a choice and starts feeling like a fact of the sky. That forgetting is the whole subject of this zine. 250 500 750 1000 1250 light-years you are here the belt, all three ~1,250 ly Rigel Saiph Betelgeuse Bellatrix ~860 ly ~650 ly ~550 ly ~250 ly the hunter, in depth the belt is one shelf — the figure spans five Now step to the side There is no hunter The three belt stars really are together — all near 1,250 light-years, all members of the same association, born from the same cloud. The figure is stitched from stars spread across a thousand light-years, which have nothing to do with each other but the direction we happen to look. And our own numbers moved. For years these three were published at 690, 740 and 2,000 light-years — a satellite's parallax, misread on bright double stars. Better instruments brought them home to the same shelf. Even the line we drew in depth turned out to be ours. The line was never out there. It was in the seat we happened to be sitting in. The stars are just… where they are, indifferent to the figure we hung on them. The pattern was never in the sky. It was in the vantage point — and the vantage point got mistaken for a law. The bell curve is a vantage point

The same trick, on us The bell curve is a vantage point The curve that sorts us into normal and abnormal began in astronomy. It was the "error curve" — the math for how repeated measurements of a star's position scatter around its true one. In the 1800s, Adolphe Quetelet — an astronomer — turned that instrument on people, and invented l'homme moyen, the average man. What had described the error in a measurement now described the ideal human, with everyone else scattered around it as deviation. Francis Galton took the next step, reading the curve as a ranking, and built eugenics on it. So the tool that mapped the indifferent stars got turned on our minds — and the average, a made-up midpoint, was handed to us as the shape we were supposed to be. "normal" everyone else = "deviation" born as the curve for measurement error a midpoint, drawn as an ideal the same line we hung on the stars The Lines We Drew · Stimpunks

It doesn't. Homosexuality was a diagnosis until the field voted it out in 1973. Asperger's was added in 1994 and dissolved into the autism spectrum in 2013. The people didn't change between editions. The line did — drawn, erased, and redrawn by a committee holding a pen. A border that can be revised was never the sky. It was always a decision about where to point. Notthat nothing is real. Distress is real; support is real. The border drawn around them is the made thing. Notthat our line is truer than theirs. It's that theirs was never the stars either. Believed, and nameable The words to name it Philosopher Miranda Fricker names two quiet harms. Testimonial injustice: being disbelieved about your own experience because of who's speaking. The Lines We Drew is the ninth zine in the Stimpunks series, and the companion argument to Field Guide No. 1 — where that guide redraws the constellations, this one is about why redrawing is legitimate at all. The astronomy moved, and this page moved with it. An earlier version of this zine said the belt was a line-of-sight accident — Alnitak ~740 light-years, Mintaka ~690, Alnilam ~2,000, "nearly three times farther." That was wrong, and we have corrected it. Those were Hipparcos-era parallaxes, and Hipparcos measured these bright, distant, multiple O and B stars badly: its parallax for Mintaka (212 ± 30 pc) is about half the figure that spectroscopy, cluster membership and Gaia DR3 now agree on, and both Hipparcos reductions of Alnilam proved incorrect. Current distances put all three at essentially the same depth — Alnitak 1,260 ± 180 ly (387 ± 54 pc), Alnilam 1,250 ± 26 ly (384 ± 8 pc, from VLTI interferometry: Oplištilová, Brož, Hummel, Harmanec & Barlow, "VLTI observations of the Orion Belt stars: I. ε Orionis," Astronomy & Astrophysics 704, A204, 2025), and Mintaka ~1,240 ly (381 ± 8 pc, Gaia DR3). All three belong to the Orion OB1b association, and the ε Ori paper places its star at that association's median distance: they are siblings from one cloud, not strangers in a row. APOD, cited in our earlier draft, likewise gives the three as a group "about 1,500 light-years away" — it never supported the numbers we hung on it. The depth is real; it is just in the figure rather than the belt. Bellatrix lies 250 ± 10 ly away, Betelgeuse about 548 (uncertain by as much as 100), Saiph 650 ± 30, Rigel about 863, and the belt near 1,250 — so the hunter is assembled from stars strung across roughly a thousand light-years. We think the correction improves the zine. A page arguing that confident lines get mistaken for facts of the sky had drawn one of its own, in depth, from superseded data — and better instruments moved it. That is the argument arriving uninvited, and it now runs on the spread. The lineage from stars to people is real and well documented. The bell curve entered science as the astronomer's "law of error": in his Theoria Motus (1809), Gauss used it to model how imperfect measurements scatter around a celestial body's true position — the same method that recovered the lost asteroid Ceres — with Legendre and Laplace close behind. Adolphe Quetelet, who directed the Brussels observatory, carried that error law from the sky to the census in his Essai de physique sociale (1835), inventing l'homme moyen, "the average man" — and, crucially, treating the average not as merely typical but as an ideal from which real people "deviate." Francis Galton kept Quetelet's curve but flipped its meaning: in Hereditary Genius (1869) he ranked human ability along what he called the "law of deviation from the average" and graded groups above and below the line. He coined the word eugenics later, in Inquiries into Human Faculty and Its Development (1883), where a footnote to the introduction proposes it for "the science of improving stock." His protégé Karl Pearson gave the field its machinery — the standard deviation (1894) and the correlation coefficient — in the Mathematical Contributions to the Theory of Evolution series, and was later appointed the first Galton Professor of Eugenics at University College London (1911–1933); the mathematics came first, the chair after. The statistical sense of the word "normal" arrives in the 1870s alongside all of this — used apparently independently by C. S. Peirce (1873), Galton, and Wilhelm Lexis (1877), with "normal distribution" settling into place in Pearson's writing by 1897. The sleight of hand was never the curve — some traits really are close to normally distributed — but the leap from deviation-as-measurement-error to deviation-as-human-defect, and the mistaking of a made-up midpoint for a law about how a person ought to be. Robert Chapman's Empire of Normality (2023) follows this same thread forward, into psychiatry and capitalism. On Chapman's account, Galton reframed the statistical centre as mere mediocrity rather than an ideal — so that deviation above it read as superiority and deviation below as defect — founding the frame that, carried through Kraepelin into the DSM, the neurodiversity movement later arose to name and refuse. That frame's name — the pathology paradigm, and its counterpart the neurodiversity paradigm — is Nick Walker's, articulated in "Throw Away the Master's Tools: Liberating Ourselves from the Pathology Paradigm" (written 2011; published 2012 in Loud Hands: Autistic People, Speaking; revised 2013), not Chapman's; Chapman works with the terms rather than coining them. The "normal" mind, in other words, has a history — and a contestable one. The border really does move: the American Psychiatric Association removed homosexuality from the DSM beginning in 1973; Asperger's disorder was added in DSM-IV (1994) and merged into Autism Spectrum Disorder in DSM-5 (2013). "Epistemic injustice," with its testimonial and hermeneutical forms, is Miranda Fricker's (2007). "Neurodiversity" is not one person's coinage, though it is often credited to Judy Singer (1998). Botha, Chapman, Giwa Onaiwu, Kapp, Stannard Ashley & Walker, "The neurodiversity concept was developed collectively: An overdue correction on the origins of neurodiversity theory" (Autism, 2024), show that "neurological diversity" and "neurodiversity" reached print in 1997 and 1998 in the work of journalist Harvey Blume, who attributed them to the online Autistic community — and that the concept and its theory were developed collectively by neurodivergent people. We follow that correction here. The neurodivergent / neurodivergence coinage is Kassiane Asasumasu's (2000), as logged for Zine No. 3; the paradigm's articulation is Nick Walker's and the wider community's. The reading is ours: that the constructed line was never the sky, and so is ours to redraw. Further reading: Robert Chapman, Empire of Normality (Pluto, 2023); Stephen Stigler, The History of Statistics (1986); Theodore Porter, The Rise of Statistical Thinking (1986); Ian Hacking, The Taming of Chance (1990); Lennard Davis, Enforcing Normalcy (1995); Sarah Chaney, Am I Normal? (2022); and, for a general reader, Todd Rose, The End of Average (2016). Online: Fergus Murray, "Weird vs. Normal" (Weird Pride Day). Primary sources: Quetelet's Essai de physique sociale (1835) and Galton's Hereditary Genius (1869). Tidal force The near body wins The tide is the ocean answering to the sky. The Moon pulls hardest on the water directly beneath it, a little less on the rock of the Earth, less still on the far ocean — and that difference in pull, stretched across the planet, lifts a bulge on each side. Two bulges, turning under us: two high tides a day. Here is the strange part. The Sun is 27 million times more massive than the Moon, and it hauls on the Earth with over 170 times the raw force. Yet the Moon runs the tide. Tidal force falls off not with distance but with distance cubed — so the small, close body overwhelms the vast, far one. Distance matters more than mass. You are pulled most by what is nearest — not by what is largest. The Sun is 27 million times heavier. The Moon still owns the tide. Nearness beats mass. Phase transitions Water doesn't get gradually stiffer Cool a glass of water and it does not slowly thicken toward solid. It stays liquid, liquid, liquid — and then, at a single temperature, it flips all at once into ice. Not a gradual stiffening; a sudden change of state. It is the same H₂O on both sides — the very same molecules, only rearranged. Physicists call this a phase transition: a substance holding steady until a threshold in its conditions is crossed, then reorganising completely — solid, liquid, gas — with nothing added and nothing taken away. Nothing about the water got better or worse. It crossed a line. Nothing about the water changed. It crossed a line. state colder → liquid ice 0°C not a ramp — a cliff the flip happens all at once The Same Water · Stimpunks

pressure temperature → solid liquid gas one substance, many states the conditions decide The phase diagram The conditions, not the substance Whether that water shows up as ice, liquid, or steam depends entirely on the conditions around it — temperature and pressure. Scientists chart it on a phase diagram: a map with a region for each state and lines where one becomes another. Read it and the point lands quietly. Ice is not defective water; steam is not water trying harder. There is no best state and no failed state — only one substance, and the conditions it happens to be in. So if you want a different state, you change the conditions, not the substance. We said this once about rooms and minds. Here it is again, about states. Ice isn't broken water. It's water somewhere colder. The Same Water · Stimpunks

Fluctuating capacity Why could you do it yesterday? Here is the question so many of us brace for: why could you do it yesterday and not today? However kindly it's meant, it lands like a charge of inconsistency — as if yesterday proved today is a choice. The phase answer is simple. Capacity is a state, not a trait — and you were near a boundary. A little less sleep, one extra transition, a degree more noise, and the conditions tip. The same person crosses from managing to not managing, the way the same water crosses from liquid to ice on one degree of difference. Not unreliable. Not lazy. Not putting it on. The same you, in changed conditions. You are not inconsistent. Right at a phase boundary a substance turns turbulent and hypersensitive — tiny nudges cause wild swings, because it's poised between two states at once. For a monotropic mind a transition means tearing attention out of one deep channel and re-forming it in another — and done suddenly, or piled up, it can pull the mind past what it can hold. So the fix isn't a sturdier person. It's a better crossing — built with warning, with a way back, with time. Broken thresholds, not broken people. Broken thresholds, not broken people. Weather-bodies Held past the point, slow to return Two more facts, because they name things that get misread. A smooth universe is a dead one

The cosmic scale A smooth universe is a dead one The early universe was almost perfectly uniform. Its oldest light — the cosmic microwave background — is smooth to about one part in a hundred thousand. Almost. Those faint differences, tiny ripples of denser and thinner, were the seeds. Gravity pulled the denser spots together, and over billions of years they grew into everything: stars, galaxies, planets, you. A perfectly uniform cosmos would have stayed a featureless fog forever — nothing to see, no one to see it. Structure exists because sameness broke. And the elements you are built from? Sameness is a single point of failure

monoculture blight one clone · one blight · total collapse polyculture many kinds · same blight · it holds variety is the resilient bet uniformity is efficient, and brittle The living scale Sameness is a single point of failure Nearly every banana shipped worldwide is a Cavendish — a sterile clone, grown from cuttings, all but genetically identical. One vast monoculture. It wasn't always. The export banana was the Gros Michel, until a fungus — Panama disease — wiped it out commercially by the 1960s. The industry survived only by switching to the Cavendish, which happened to resist that strain. Now a new strain, Tropical Race 4, is spreading, and the Cavendish has no defense. One clone, one blight from collapse. Biodiversity is the opposite bet: ecologists find more varied systems tend to be more resilient — when nothing is identical, no single shock takes it all. Monoculture is the engineered thing. Cavendish Space is our answer to it — caves, campfires, and watering holes for dandelions, tulips, and orchids alike. The Universe Runs on Difference · Stimpunks

The spikes are the default state of matter: variety, the thing that actually makes something new. The peaks are real. So are the troughs. The cosmic microwave background is uniform to about one part in 100,000; those faint density differences grew under gravity into all large-scale structure — galaxies, clusters, us (COBE, WMAP, Planck). The Cavendish banana is a sterile clone grown as a near-global monoculture; its predecessor, the Gros Michel, was driven to commercial extinction by Panama disease (Fusarium wilt, Race 1) by the 1960s, and the Cavendish now faces the same fate from Tropical Race 4. Biodiversity is generally associated with greater resilience (the "insurance" effect); the Irish potato famine is the classic monoculture catastrophe. The concepts are the community's own: the spiky profile (named by Damian Milton, building on Francesca Happé's work) and the competency network — "a map of the gifts people bring to each other" — drawing on Lori Hogenkamp, the NeurodiVenture model at Autistic Collaboration, Temple Grandin, and adrienne maree brown; Carol Black on cognitive diversity; and ethodiversity — the variety of ways of being across human and nonhuman animals — coined in ecology by Adolfo Cordero-Rivera and brought into neurodiversity studies by Ombre Tarragnat's more-than-human, more-than-neurological turn. Cavendish Space is a Stimpunks concept. The reading — that uniformity is the engineered thing and difference is the default — is ours. The elements in you were difference forged in stars. Too Good to Check How a story gets smoother than the science, and what reading the primary source puts back. Six ways a fact goes wrong, and seventeen worked corrections — most of them ours, published, dated, and fixed in public. Everybody knows the forest is wired together. Fungal threads under the soil, trees trading sugar and warnings across a shared network, an old tree in the sunlight feeding a seedling stuck in the shade. It is one of the loveliest facts of the last thirty years, and we put it in three pieces without checking it. We should not have. In 2023, Karst, Jones and Hoeksema went through the citation record and found the evidence insufficient that these common mycorrhizal networks are widespread in forests, insufficient that transfer through them reliably helps seedlings, and — this is the part that stung — no published evidence at all that mature trees preferentially feed their own offspring. The trade between a root and its fungus is settled science and always was. The forest-wide story is a different claim, and it had been growing by citation rather than by evidence. We corrected it on 3 August 2026 , across No. 5 , No. 26 , and Field Guide No. 6 . And the reason it got past us is not that we were careless. It is that it rhymed with everything we believe . A collection arguing for interdependence and mutual aid met a finding that said the forest is a mutual-aid society, and did not ask it a single hard question. A story that fits gets less scrutiny, which is exactly when it needs more. This page is about that failure and its relatives. It is written from inside the problem rather than above it: nearly every example below is one we shipped, or nearly shipped, and had to go back and fix. That is the only honest place to write it from. It is also the reader-facing front door to our fact-check ledger and our public changelog , which have been quietly accumulating this material for a year.

Why the smooth version wins Misconceptions do not spread because people are stupid. They spread because the retellable version out-competes the accurate one , and the competition is not close. A paper is hedged, conditional, and boring on purpose. It says in this system, under these conditions, we observed . The retelling drops the conditions, because the conditions are what make it hard to remember. Each hop smooths a little more: the hedge goes, then the sample size, then the species, then the name of the person who found it. What arrives at the other end is a clean sentence that anyone can repeat and nobody can source. The trap underneath is that repetition feels like verification . When you have met a claim in six places, it has the texture of a well-established fact — but if all six were downstream of the same press release, you have met it once, six times. Our own house rule exists because of this: aggregators and summaries are leads, not citations . A quote site, an encyclopedia, our own glossary, an AI summary — any of them can point you at a source. None of them can be one. The citation trail, and the hop that never happens A left-to-right chain of five boxes: the paper, the press release, the popular article, the summary, and our page. Arrows run rightward between them. Only the first arrow touches the evidence; the rest copy the copy. A dashed arc runs from our page all the way back to the paper, labelled as the one hop that actually checks anything. THE PAPER hedged, dated PRESS RELEASE hedge drops THE ARTICLE verb gets livelier THE SUMMARY name falls off YOUR PAGE stated as fact four hops. only the first one ever touched the evidence. THE ONE HOP THAT CHECKS ANYTHING meeting a claim in six places is not six confirmations if all six are downstream of the same release Figure 1 · Every arrow feels like corroboration from inside the chain. Only the dashed one leaves it.
Six ways a fact goes wrong

Six ways a fact goes wrong Sorting a year of our own corrections, they fall into six shapes. The value of a taxonomy over a list of trivia is that you can point it at a claim nobody has written about yet — including one of your own.

01 The quote nobody said The most quotable version of a thought is usually not the one a person actually produced, because people speak in clauses and circumlocutions and the culture files off the corners afterwards. What circulates is a compression — accurate in spirit, unfindable in the text. “We are star stuff harvesting sunlight” is Sagan's most-shared line and he never wrote it. Searching all thirteen chapters of Cosmos turns up two real sentences in chapter 9 — “Farming is simply the methodical harvesting of sunlight, using plants as grudging intermediaries. We are, almost all of us, solar-powered” and, separately, “We are made of starstuff” — which the internet welded into something better than either. We had it in No. 6 inside quotation marks with a citation. It is now marked as ours, with his two real sentences printed underneath. Brian Eno's definition of scenius has the same shape. The version everywhere — including in five places in our own knowledge garden — reads “the intelligence and the intuition of a whole cultural scene… the communal form of the concept of the genius.” That wording entered circulation through Kevin Kelly in 2008. Eno's own sentence, in A Year with Swollen Appendices (1996), does not have those articles in it. A small difference, and it means the line has been quoted as his for eighteen years in a form he did not write. And sometimes the wrong name is on it. “We are caught in an inescapable network of mutuality” shipped in our Symbioses field guide credited to James Baldwin. It is Martin Luther King Jr., Letter from Birmingham Jail , 1963. Helen Edgar caught it. The tell It is more quotable than anything anyone says out loud. Search the actual book, not the web.

02 The number that went stale A measurement can be wrong simply by being old. The literature moves; museum placards, planetarium scripts and popular astronomy do not, and the superseded value keeps circulating for decades with nothing to mark it as expired. No. 9 built a whole spread on Orion's Belt being an accident of sightline — Alnitak about 740 light-years out, Mintaka 690, Alnilam nearly 2,000, one star three times farther than its neighbours. Those are Hipparcos-era parallaxes, and Hipparcos measured bright, distant, multiple O and B stars badly. Current values from VLTI interferometry and Gaia put all three at essentially one depth, around 1,240–1,260 light-years, all of them in the Orion OB1b association. They are not a coincidence. They are siblings from one cloud. Two things should have caught it sooner, and both are worth stealing as habits. The zine's own colophon cited an astronomy-picture-of-the-day page that gives the three as a group at about 1,500 light-years and never supported our figures — we cited a source we had not read closely . And Field Guide No. 1 , the companion piece, already said it correctly. The collection had been contradicting itself in public for weeks. The tell You can find the figure repeated everywhere and dated nowhere. Check the source you cited actually gives your number.

03 The story told backwards Sometimes the facts survive the retelling and the emphasis does not, which inverts the meaning while leaving every individual sentence defensible. Everybody knows everything evolves into a crab. The paper behind that meme — Wolfe, Luque and Bracken-Grissom, 2021 — does say the crab-like body plan has arisen at least five times. It also says it has been lost at least seven times , that the reasons for the repetition “remain a mystery,” and that the authors do not know whether they are looking at true convergence or at deep homology. Three facts that cut against the meme, none of which travel with it. No. 31 is built on the ones that got left behind. Same shape in No. 32 : the shark's cartilage skeleton is routinely called primitive, as though bone had not been invented yet. Minjinia turgenensis , described in 2020, preserves endochondral bone deeper in the tree — so the chondrichthyan condition is a secondary loss . Derived, not primitive. The textbook reading is upside down, and the loaded word turns out to be factually wrong as well as rude. And in No. 35 : the turtle shell is not armour that evolved for protection. Broadened ribs came first as an adaptation for digging, and Lyson and colleagues note they “provide little protection” while costing the animal in locomotion and breathing. The protection is an exaptation — a later use for a structure built for something else. The tell The paper's own hedge is missing, and every fact that complicates the punchline dropped out together.

04 The credit that drifted Attribution decays toward tidiness. A collective becomes a founder; a documenter becomes a coiner; the person with the most citable book absorbs the idea of everyone around them. This one matters more than the others, because it is not only inaccurate — it takes something from people. The clearest case is in our own field. Neurodiversity was coined by Judy Singer in 1998 is repeated everywhere, including in places that should know better. Botha, Chapman, Giwa Onaiwu, Kapp, Stannard Ashley and Walker published the correction in Autism in 2024: the concept was developed collectively by the online Autistic community, and reached print in 1997 and 1998 through the journalist Harvey Blume, who attributed it to that community. Neurodivergent is Kassiane Asasumasu's, from 2000. The pathology paradigm is Nick Walker's, not Robert Chapman's, who works with the term. Crip time was documented by Zola and Gill, not coined by them. We had two of those wrong in No. 9 and No. 19 . It happens outside our field too, in both directions. Galton did not coin eugenics in Hereditary Genius (1869); he coined it in Inquiries into Human Faculty (1883), in a footnote. “Dirt is matter out of place” is credited to Mary Douglas so reliably that it reads as hers, and it appears unreferenced in Purity and Danger ; the earliest instance we could locate is an 1853 address by Lord Palmerston. “Turtles all the way down” is attributed to William James, whose 1882 essay uses rocks ; the turtle punchline was attached to him in a 1967 doctoral thesis. The tell One name sits where a community was, or a famous name sits where an obscure one belongs.

05 The press release, not the paper Between the finding and the public there is a layer whose job is to make the finding interesting, and it is very good at its job. Its output is not a lie; it is a livelier verb. While building No. 36 we nearly used the story of the bottlenose dolphin that adopted a sperm whale calf. The paper — Wilson and Krause, 2013 — reports “repeated non-agonistic interactions.” “Adopted” is the press's word, not the researchers'. And the explanation everyone repeats, that the dolphin had been harassed by its own kind, is a researcher's suggestion to reporters, not a finding in the paper. The zine says the motive is unknown, because it is. The costly version of this mode is shark cartilage. A popular book, a market, and decades of belief that sharks don't get cancer — against 42 documented tumours across at least 21 chondrichthyan species, and a clinical trial that found no difference in survival or quality of life. A false premise, industrialised. The tell The vivid verb is doing the work. Find the abstract and see which word the authors chose.

06 The finding that flatters you The last one is the wood wide web, and it is the dangerous one, because the others are accidents and this one is an appetite. Our worst instance was not a fact we imported but an argument we made. No. 33 argued that disgust is learned — a claim that suited us, since the zine is about how revulsion gets recruited into prejudice. Helen Edgar , who taught children with profound and multiple learning disabilities for twenty years, said plainly that this was wrong: pre-term babies have an ick without any capacity to have been taught one. She was right, and Rozin's own framework already carried the distinction we had collapsed. Distaste is chemosensory rejection, present at birth — Steiner's 1973 work found anencephalic newborns produce the gustofacial response, so it cannot be an opinion. Disgust proper is ideational and contamination-sensitive, and that is the only kind our argument was ever about. We added a spread rather than a footnote, because as published a reader with sensory processing differences could reasonably have understood the zine to be telling them their aversions were prejudice to get over. Aimed at our own community, that would have done harm. And Helen's underlying point is the better framing and now sits in the zine's voice: we are not blank slates — that is the whole point of star stuff. We have history in us. A response conserved across species and present before birth is that history. We had been arguing against this collection's founding premise without noticing. The tell You wanted it to be true before you read it. That is the moment to slow down, not speed up. Six failure modes and their tells A reference card of six boxes in two columns. One: the quote nobody said — more quotable than real speech. Two: the number that went stale — repeated everywhere, dated nowhere. Three: the story told backwards — the paper's hedge is missing. Four: the credit that drifted — one name where a community was. Five: the press release not the paper — the verb is livelier than the finding. That card exists as a two-sided printable sheet — the six modes and their tells on the face, the habits and the refusals on the reverse. Print it, pin it up, hand it to someone.

What actually works None of this needs a laboratory. It needs a handful of stubborn habits, each of which we adopted because something went wrong without it. Trace it to the primary. The book, the paper, the essay, the talk. Not a quote site, not an encyclopedia, not our own glossary, not a search summary. Those are leads. Cite the source you actually read. The Orion error survived because a colophon named a page that never said what we said. If you have not opened it, it does not go in the references. Read your own siblings. Field Guide No. 1 had the belt right while No. 9 had it wrong. Before shipping, check what the collection has already claimed about the same thing. When one source falls, re-check its relatives. One 2023 paper on mycorrhizal networks meant re-opening three pieces, not one. Errors travel with their quotes. Distinguish a quote from a paraphrase. Verbatim and in quotation marks, or in your own words with the idea attributed. Never dress the second as the first. Say what is still open. “This is the leading hypothesis, not a settled result” costs one sentence and is the difference between a claim and an overclaim. Log the correction in public, with a date and a name. A living document that never shows a correction is just a document making a claim about itself. Measure rather than assume. The same discipline applies to the artifact and not only to its facts — we discovered 44 of our pages printed blank because “prints fine” had been a belief and not a measurement. A stated principle nobody checks is a wish.

Not “do your own research” There is a version of everything above that curdles, and it is worth naming precisely, because it wears the same clothes. “Go to the primary source” is one short step from “do your own research,” a phrase that has been thoroughly captured and now mostly means trust no one who knows more than you . The difference is not attitude, it is direction. Tracing a claim moves toward the evidence and ends somewhere checkable, with a citation you can hand to someone else. The captured version moves away from it and ends in a place where nothing can be checked at all, because every institution that could check it has been disqualified in advance. One of them can be wrong and be shown to be wrong. The other cannot, which is the whole appeal. Debunking has its own failure mode, and it is the mirror image of the one this page is about. Carol Black's essay Science / Fiction describes it exactly: the reverse strategy of asserting “there is scientific consensus where there is no such thing, that an open, ongoing area of scientific inquiry has reached a settled conclusion,” and that anyone disagreeing is “as irrational and ‘anti-science’ as a climate denier.” Her worked example is the wave of LEARNING STYLES ARE A MYTH headlines, which take a narrow experimental result about one simplistic model and inflate it into a verdict on how human beings learn. A debunking can be a misconception. The Myth! headline is as smooth and as retellable as the thing it debunks, which should make you just as suspicious of it.

The refusals Not: Not “do your own research.” Tracing a claim toward its evidence is the opposite move from refusing everyone who has any. Not science literacy as a gate. Nobody owes anybody a reading list before they are allowed to speak about their own life. Not the pleasure of the debunk. If correcting people feels good, that is the appetite from mode six wearing a lab coat. Not contempt for the people who repeat the story. We repeated it. In three pieces. Not a claim to be finished. This page will need corrections, and the ledger it links to has open items in it today. Not certainty as the goal. The goal is knowing which things we have checked and which we haven't, and saying so out loud.
The primary source for a life

The primary source for a life Here is why a fact-checking page belongs in a collection about belonging. The deficit story told about neurodivergent and disabled people has exactly the citation structure described above. It is smooth, endlessly retellable, and repeated until repetition passes for evidence. Its hedges have fallen off. Its credit has drifted onto the people who wrote about us rather than the people who are us. And it flatters the teller, which is why it gets so little scrutiny from the people doing the telling. Autistic people lack empathy is the wood wide web of our field: a claim that grew by citation, and that Damian Milton's double empathy problem (2012) corrected by going back and looking — the breakdown is mutual, a difference in shared understanding between two parties rather than a deficit in one of them. Neurodiversity was coined by one author in 1998 is the credit that drifted, and it took a 2024 paper by six researchers to put a community's name back on its own idea. The primary source for an Autistic life is an Autistic person. That is not a metaphor and it is not a softening. It is the same rule as the rest of this page, applied where it costs something. Miranda Fricker's testimonial injustice names what happens when it is broken — a speaker's account is discounted because of who is speaking — and disability studies has had the shorter version since long before the philosophy arrived: nothing about us without us . Going to the source, here, means asking the person, and then believing the answer enough to let it change what you were going to write. Which is precisely what happened with the disgust zine. The correction came from a member of our own community with two decades of direct experience, arriving after publication, contradicting the argument we had just made. That is a primary source. We rewrote the piece.

Tending the garden No. 18 describes this project as a knowledge garden: evergreen, cross-linked, grown rather than filed. Gardens have weeds. The interesting property of a garden is not that nothing unwanted grows in it — it is that someone walks the beds , and a bed nobody walks looks perfectly healthy from the path right up until it isn't. So the corrections run both ways, which is the cosmic connections point. Checking the scenius quote for No. 31 found the altered wording in five places on stimpunks.org and in none of them the sentence Eno wrote — an error discovered here that has to be fixed upstream. Fact-checking one of Helen's zines surfaced a citation-year discrepancy that neither site can settle alone. This traffic is the part that makes a web of sites worth more than three sites. Two places hold the record. The fact-check ledger is the working file — every piece, every check, every open item, in the detail needed to re-derive a decision a year later. The changelog is the public version: what we got wrong, what's right, who caught it. Neither is an embarrassment to be managed. They are the only thing that makes the rest of the collection worth believing. These are not the seventeen most important misconceptions in circulation — they are seventeen we can show our full working on, which is a different and much narrower claim. A page about verification has no business asserting anything it hasn't verified. Several rows rest on findings that are themselves live rather than closed. The secondary-loss reading of the chondrichthyan skeleton is where current evidence points, not a settled matter. Rozin and Fallon's is one theory of disgust among several, and that some disgust tracks real pathogen risk is not disputed. Karst and colleagues' paper is an argued position in an active dispute, not a final verdict — which is exactly the hedge the popular version dropped, so we are not dropping it in the other direction either. And the ledger has open items right now. A Carol Black quotation in No. 8 is marked plausible rather than verified. A Deleuze line reaching No. 29 by way of a paywalled article still needs primary confirmation. Five instances of the altered Eno wording remain live on stimpunks.org. Publishing the open items is part of the method, not a lapse in it. None of this makes us reliable. It makes us checkable , which is the only thing anyone can honestly offer. Read the receipts, follow them back, and tell us where we're wrong — open an issue or write to us. Two of the corrections on this page exist because somebody did. The forest is not wired together the way we wanted it to be. Fungus and root still trade, nine in ten land plants still depend on the arrangement, and the ordinary version is astonishing on its own. The Ones That Went Around the Moon

the far sideout, and backsept 1968 · before us L★S · 001 The Ones That Went Around the Moon Steppe tortoise · Testudo horsfieldii 15–21 Sept 1968 · and came back Two Soviet steppe tortoises rounded the far side of the Moon on Zond 5 and returned alive — the first living things to do it, two months before any human. first around the MoonZond 5, 1968came homelost 10% of body weight ▸ Field notes Field notes · Steppe tortoise · Testudo horsfieldii Zond 5 lifted off from Baykonur on 15 September 1968 carrying wine flies, mealworms, plants, seeds, bacteria — and two steppe tortoises. Three days later it passed about 1,950 km above the far side of the Moon, swung around, and started home. On 21 September a guidance error put it into the Indian Ocean instead of Soviet territory, and a recovery ship went and got it. The tortoises were alive. They had lost roughly ten per cent of their body weight and were otherwise in good health. Apollo 8 would not carry humans around the Moon for another three months. We are opening a field guide with this because of what the collection is called. Sagan's line is that the calcium in your bones was made in dying stars — that you are, physically, star stuff. In September 1968 some of that star stuff, in the shape of two undramatic land reptiles from the Central Asian steppe, went out past the Moon, looked at the back of it, and came home to be weighed. This is one well-documented case, monitored for two decades, and it is not a general licence. But it is a real answer to a real question, and the question is the one this guide has been circling since spread one: what do you do when the thing that was holding a system together is gone? Sometimes the answer is that the job is more portable than the animal — and somebody else, from another ocean entirely, can be supported to do it. Which is, more or less, what accommodation is. A textbook line about an entire order fell over, and nothing about the animals had changed. What changed was that somebody brought a hydrophone and stayed long enough. It is not established what any particular call means, and we are not going to translate them for you. But the shape of the error is worth carrying out of the water. An absence of communication is a claim about a listener at least as often as it is a claim about a speaker. Non-speaking is not non-thinking; unrecorded is not absent; "doesn't communicate" has meant "doesn't communicate in the channel I was monitoring" often enough that it should never again be the first conclusion. That is a rhyme with what our community knows, and we are calling it a rhyme, not a proof. The turtles are not a metaphor. They are just, once again, the thing that was there before we were paying attention.
