Still here from before your country was

The animal Still here from before your country was Somewhere in the Arctic dark right now, four hundred metres down, there is a shark that was already alive when Napoleon was. The Greenland shark, Somniosus microcephalus. It lives in water near freezing — down to about −1.8 °C — and has been recorded to depths of around 2,647 metres. It grows less than a centimetre a year. In 2016 Julius Nielsen and colleagues published the ages of 28 of them in Science. The results were not what anyone expected. A life span of at least 272 years. The largest animal in the study, five metres long, came out at 392 ± 120 years old. That makes it the longest-lived vertebrate known — longer than the bowhead whale, longer than anything else with a backbone. And the number that this zine is really about, the one that stopped everybody: They don't reach sexual maturity until roughly 156 years old. A century and a half. They read it in the eye

How anyone could possibly know They read it in the eye You cannot age a Greenland shark the usual way. It has no bone to lay down rings in — see the zine before last — and its vertebrae are too poorly calcified to count. So the researchers used the one tissue in a vertebrate body that never updates itself. At the very centre of the eye lens is a core of crystallin proteins laid down before the animal is born, and then left alone. No turnover. No replacement. Whatever carbon was around when that lens formed is still sitting there, decades or centuries later. The eye carries its own birth certificate. Then the second trick, and it is a strange one. Between the mid-1950s and the early 1960s, atmospheric nuclear testing spiked the amount of radiocarbon in the atmosphere worldwide — a sharp, dated, globally shared marker scientists call the bomb pulse. It works out to a timestamp printed across the whole planet. Find that spike in the lens core, and you know the animal was born after it. Don't find it, and you know it was born before — and how much ¹⁴C is there tells you roughly how long before. The oldest animals in the study were born before the pulse. Before the industrial revolution finished. Some of them, before the United States. "Late" is a comparison, not a measurement

It has not fallen off a track. It is exactly on time — for a Greenland shark. The word late only means something once you've picked a calendar, and the calendar always comes from somewhere. Pick a herring's, and every Greenland shark that ever lived is a catastrophic failure. Pick the Greenland shark's, and the herring is gone before the shark has opened its eyes properly. Neither calendar is the true one. There isn't a true one. There are just organisms and the rates they run at, and a ruler somebody laid alongside them afterwards. We do this to people constantly, and we do it with enormous confidence. Delayed. Behind. Not age-appropriate. Should have been doing this by now. Each one sounds like an observation about a child. Every one of them is a comparison to a schedule, and the schedule was made by averaging other people. Our zine on the invention of "normal" is about where those averages came from and what they were built to do. This is the same argument, in an animal that makes it impossible to miss. This is not a zine about slow being beautiful

The turn — and this one is not comfortable This is not a zine about slow being beautiful It would be easy to stop here, and it would be a lie. Read the last line of Nielsen's abstract. Having established the longest vertebrate life span ever measured, the authors do not celebrate. They raise concerns about species conservation. Here's why. An animal that takes about 156 years to reproduce even once has almost no capacity to replace losses. Kill a thousand of them and you are not waiting a decade for the population to recover — you are waiting longer than the modern world has existed. Every Greenland shark caught as bycatch today is an animal whose replacement will not be mature until well after everyone reading this is dead. They were hunted for liver oil for a long time, in very large numbers. They still turn up in trawls. The IUCN lists the species as Vulnerable. So slowness is not a superpower. It is a strategy with a bill attached. It is superbly adapted to an environment that stayed roughly the same for millions of years, and it is nearly defenceless against one that changes in decades. And that is the honest shape of the thing, for sharks and for us. A pace is not good or bad on its own. What follows from that The environment decides Put the last three spreads together and you get a single claim, and it is the one this whole collection keeps arriving at. A ruined cornea is a disaster in bright water and nothing at 400 metres. A 156-year childhood works fine in an ocean that holds still and is fatal in one full of trawlers. Every one is a fact about the shark and the world it is in — and when the outcome is bad, the thing that changed was almost never the animal. Disabled people have a name for this. It's the social model of disability: the distinction between a body's actual condition and the disabling produced by environments and expectations built as though that condition didn't exist. Stairs disable a wheelchair user. Open-plan offices and fluorescent light disable us. The pace of a school day disables a kid who needs longer. Which turns the question around. Not how do we get this child up to speed — but what is this environment demanding, who chose that, and what would it cost to stop? The defence of the clock Better get used to it Ask for a slower pace and you will meet one particular answer so often that it has an acronym. Alfie Kohn named it in Education Week in 2005: what he calls the BGUTI principle — Better Get Used To It. You have heard every version. Homework in the early years because there's homework later. Grades young because there are grades eventually. Sitting still now because a job will demand it. No accommodation at school because the real world won't accommodate you. The logic is always the same: life will be hard later, so hardship now is preparation. Kohn's sentence about this is the one that belongs in this zine, and it is exact: Almost by definition, the BGUTI defense ignores developmental differences. Alfie Kohn, "Getting Hit on the Head Lessons," Education Week, 7 September 2005 It has to ignore them, or it stops working. The whole argument treats the timetable as the fixed thing and the child as the adjustable thing. But if children arrive at things at genuinely different rates — and they do — then "everyone gets this at this age" guarantees that some of them are being handed something they cannot yet use. BGUTI doesn't overlook developmental difference by accident. It cannot survive noticing it. And the claim underneath is not even true. Kohn again: people don't really get better at coping with unhappiness because they were deliberately made unhappy when they were young. Early adversity is not a vaccine. It mostly just teaches you that adults will do this to you. This is where behaviorism does its worst work. A model that watches compliance and reaches for consequences has no way to represent a child who needs longer — so needing longer shows up as refusing, and refusing gets a consequence. The consequence never changes the pace. It only adds fear to it. Nobody asked the shark to hurry

Closer to home Nobody asked the shark to hurry If you have been on the receiving end of a developmental timetable, you already know the whole of this zine in your body. The chart on the wall at the clinic. The milestone that didn't get met. The report that said working below age-related expectations. The reading level, the year group, the "should be able to by now." The particular quiet of being the last one still doing the thing everybody else finished. None of that measured you. All of it measured a gap between you and an average — and the average was assembled from other people, for reasons that had a lot to do with sorting and not much to do with you. Some things do take you longer. That's true and it doesn't need softening. What isn't true is the part that got smuggled in with it: that taking longer is a defect, that the schedule is a law of nature, and that being behind on it means being behind at living. There is an animal in the Arctic that spends a century and a half growing up, and no one has informed it that this is a delay. It is not lagging. It is not a slow version of a faster animal. It is simply what it is, at the rate it does it, and it was doing that before every schedule any of us has ever been measured against was invented. You are made of the same star stuff as that shark: the same carbon, the same calcium, forged in the same kind of dying star. Two arrangements of it, running at completely different speeds, and the universe has never once indicated a preference. Take the time it takes. Then ask who built the clock, and whether it can be moved. You were never late. You were being timed by somebody else's watch. two questions you can ask a schedule "why am I behind?" assumes the clock · looks for the fault in you "who set this clock?" makes the schedule a decision · decisions can change only one of these has an answer you can act on change the question and the fault moves off you Two Hundred Years · Stimpunks

The three of them One clade, three refusals This is the last of three zines built out of one young person's special interest, and they turn out to make one argument in three moves. No. 32 refused the word primitive. Sharks didn't fail to invent bone — their lineage had it and let it go. What was read as an earlier stage was a later change, and the reading was a verdict wearing a description's coat. No. 33 refused the word gross. Disgust isn't information about an animal; it's information about a frame, learned young, and it does border work on bodies — theirs and ours. No. 34 refuses the word late. There is no lateness without a calendar, and someone always brought the calendar. Three words that feel like observations and are all three verdicts. Primitive. Gross. Late. Each one describes a relationship between a thing and a standard, while sounding like a fact about the thing. And the sharks did not know they were carrying any of it. They were only ever doing the thing they do — slowly, in the cold, in the dark — while a species with a very short life and a very fast clock swam past and filed them. The animal is never the argument. The ruler is always the argument. three words that hide a standard primitive → sounds like: a stage is: a ranking gross → sounds like: a property is: a border late → sounds like: a time is: a comparison each one needs a standard to mean anything and somebody always brought the standard nos. 32 · 33 · 34 one argument, three words Two Hundred Years · Stimpunks

5 Underground Under ground on mycelial networks, decomposition, and the quiet dark where we do our realest work — the below to Bone Song's above L★S Love You Down To Your Star Stuff · open edition ·
The oldest anarchist in the room

The mycelial network The oldest anarchist in the room Beneath the forest floor runs a living web of fungal threads — mycelium — laced through the soil and trading nutrients with the roots it meets. That trade is well established; how far the shared networks reach, and how much moves tree to tree through them, is still argued over by the people who dig them up. It has no head office. It grows in every direction at once, feeds its neighbors, and asks no one's permission. Its intelligence is distributed: problems get solved, paths get reinforced, weak connections fade — all with no commanding center telling each thread what to do. We know this shape, because it is how we try to hold each other. A competency network — everyone knowing something, sharing it with whoever needs it. Mutual aid — resources moving to where the need is greatest, not up a hierarchy to be rationed back down. Zero hierarchy is not a slogan we impose on the network. It is the shape the network takes when we stop forcing it into a chain of command. The mycelium never needed a manager. Neither, it turns out, do we — we need interdependence, which is a very different thing. no center trade distributed network · no commanding center hyphae · nodes · nutrient trade · reinforcing paths Underground · Stimpunks
Nothing is wasted. Only waiting to be metabolized.

star · C forged falls soil uptake the loop carbon: forged above, metabolized below star → soil → hyphae → uptake → and back Decomposition · bricolage Nothing is wasted. Only waiting to be metabolized. Decomposition has an image problem. We hear the word and think of rot and loss. But fungi reframe it: they break the toughest structures — rock, oil, a fallen tree — back down into materials life can use again. Rock becomes soil. A dead trunk becomes a nursery. The star-forged carbon of Bone Song does not stop at the skeleton. It falls, becomes soil, is taken up by the network, and passed along — star stuff all the way down, and up again through the ground. Then comes the leap from biology to politics: we can enlist those powers on the hard structures too. The pathology paradigm that files us as broken. The deficit framing. The systems built hostile toward the people who most need them. We do not argue with the rock. We grow into its cracks and, over time, turn it into ground. Composting is not destruction. It is how a commons renews itself. Underground · Stimpunks

The poem Beneath the forest, a network with no name is doing the work. No head office. No throne. No plan on file. It grows in every direction at once, feeds its neighbors, and breaks the dead down into the living — underground, unseen, asking no one's permission. We know this shape. It is how we try to hold each other: no one at the center, resources moving to wherever the need is, everyone teaching, everyone learning, growth in every direction at once. Decomposition is not the end. Rock becomes soil. A fallen tree becomes a nursery. Nothing is wasted here — only waiting to be metabolized into whatever comes next. The carbon in you was forged in a star. It fell. It became soil. The network took it up and passed it on, and some of it became you. Star stuff, all the way down, and up again through the ground. The realest work happens in the dark, where no one is watching, where the metrics never reach. Do not mistake invisibility for absence. The network is busiest exactly where you cannot see it. We are not admiring a clever organism. We are kin, recognizing a relative. We look for ourselves in the fungi and we find us there: mischief with a purpose, refusing the world as given, making new possibilities while composting the old. We love you down to your star stuff — and up again through the soil. To the thread. To the trade. To the dark. To the network that occasionally surfaces and is busiest when it does not. L★S. Underground · Stimpunks
The work that changes everything is the work no one is watching

The quiet and the dark The work that changes everything is the work no one is watching In a world of influencers and incessant self-promotion, mycelial networks engineer whole ecosystems in the quiet and the dark. The most transformative work is often the most invisible. There is deep resonance here for anyone told to be louder, more visible, more legibly productive to count. So much of what holds us together is quiet crip labor — unglamorous, unposted, done where the metrics never reach. Unmasking is often a retreat from the stage lights into a truer, quieter mode. Monotropism — sinking all the way down into a single interest — needs exactly what the mycelium thrives in: undisturbed, unhurried, unsurveilled depth. This is what a cave is for. We do not mistake invisibility for absence. Mischief · punk Fungi gleefully defy well-established assumptions, making new possibilities while decomposing old ones. Mycologists call this punk science. Read the description back without the word fungi and it is a description of us: crossing boundaries, refusing the world as given, rooting the work in creativity. To neuroqueer a space is a punk act. To imagine a livable, interdependent future built by and for the people this world discards is punk aimed at the horizon. Nota tidy metaphor for teamwork. This is kinship and a critique of hierarchy, not a synergy poster. Notyour pain was worth it because it composts. Composting does not justify the harm — the hostile structure should never have been built. Notbe invisible and grateful. Quiet crip labor deserves resourcing, not romanticized erasure. Nota substitute for redistribution. Loving the network does not feed anyone; mutual aid does. We are not a hierarchy that occasionally cooperates. We are a network that occasionally surfaces. Underground is the fifth zine in the Stimpunks series — the below to Bone Song's above. It is offered freely, to be printed and folded and handed to someone who needs it. It draws on two Stimpunks pieces, "A Mycelium and a Rhizome" and "The Mycelial Worldview Is Punk," and on the sources they build from: the MOTH collective's essay "Punk Law: Lessons from Fungi," Toby Kiers and SPUN on "punk science," and the documentary Allpa Ukundi, Ñukanchi Pura (Kichwa for "underground, around, and among us"), made with the Kichwa people of Sarayaku in the Ecuadorian Amazon together with the Fungi Foundation and SPUN. The rhizome comes from Deleuze & Guattari; the neurodiversity paradigm language from Nick Walker and the Autistic community of InLv; the cosmology from Carl Sagan. The Stimpunks synthesis is our own extension, not a claim made by those authors. On the science: mycorrhizal symbiosis — fungi and roots trading nutrients — is well established. The popular "wood wide web" picture of forests wired together, with elder trees feeding seedlings through shared fungal networks, is contested; see Karst, Jones & Hoeksema, "Positive citation bias and overinterpreted results lead to misinformation on common mycorrhizal networks in forests" (Nature Ecology & Evolution 7, 2023). We keep the kinship and drop the overclaim. A rhyme, not a proof. The underground has been among us all along. The mycelial worldview is punk, and punk is a Stimpunks worldview. We Are All Star Stuff Zine No. 4 · In progress Open call for contributors The first three zines in this series made arguments. This one holds space for something different: the actual voices of the people the series is for. Zines No. 1, 2, and 3 built the framework — the piezoelectric bones, the cosmology of care, the neurodiversity paradigm. They explained why you are made of star stuff and why that matters. We Are All Star Stuff is the zine that asks: what does that mean to you? We're collecting short pieces — a few sentences to a few paragraphs — from Autistic, ADHD, dyslexic, disabled, and otherwise neurodivergent people, and from the family members, educators, and community members who love them. No expertise required. No particular format. Just your honest answer to the question of what it means to be loved down to your star stuff, or to love someone that way. This zine will be offered freely, the same as the rest of the series — print-at-home, shareable, open edition. Every contributor will be credited exactly as they choose: full name, first name only, initials, role, or anonymous. 11 Guest Zine Why Difference Comes First Inspired by our collaborative Stimpunks work, and my own neuroqueering Deleuze project, I've been thinking about the connections in-between — physics, philosophy, my own life as an Autistic person. This is me following that thread. Helen Edgar · Autistic Realms · More Realms L★S Love You Down To Your Star Stuff · guest edition ·

Two · I'm not a fixed thing I'm not a fixed thing A little while back I wrote about something called relational quantum mechanics — a way of thinking about physics where tiny particles don't have fixed qualities all on their own. They only become something in relation to whatever's around them (Rovelli, 1996). I'm not a physicist — it's one idea among several, and physicists argue about it. As a multiply neurodivergent person, that's always been closer to how I experience myself — not as a fixed, separate thing moving through the world, but as something that shows up through my relationships and encounters with everything around me (Edgar, 2026a). I'm still working through what that means. Physics, philosophy, and my own life keep circling the same ideas about being interconnected, unfixed, always transforming. Why Difference Comes First · Helen Edgar

Three · my monotropic galaxy My monotropic galaxy The oldest light we can see is called the cosmic microwave background — it's the afterglow of the Big Bang, and it's almost perfectly smooth. It only varies by about one part in 100,000 across the whole sky — almost uniform, but only almost. Those tiny variations — slightly denser here, slightly thinner there — were the beginning of everything. Gravity pulled the denser bits together, and over billions of years they became stars, galaxies, planets, you, me, all of it. If the universe really had been perfectly uniform, it would have stayed a flat, empty fog forever. Nothing to see, no one to see it. Structure only exists because that near-sameness broke. That's the same shape I recognise in my own monotropic attention — energy pulled gravitationally into a few bright points, rather than spread out in an even, undifferentiated glow. And yet it's exactly that unevenness, that refusal to flatten, that so many of us — anyone who's ever been called too much, not enough, or too different — have been measured against. the "almost" is where everything comes from almost uniform · not quite the tiny unevenness seeds the stars Why Difference Comes First · Helen Edgar

Four · neuronormative time Measured against neuronormative time I've spent a lot of my life being measured against a flat line. Nobody always said it in those words, but that's what was happening — a standard chart, a "typical" way of communicating or paying attention or experiencing the world, treated as the baseline everyone should be smoothed toward. And me, positioned as the deviation that needed explaining, or fixing, or at least accounting for. That flat line was never just about behaviour — it was also about time: a single approved tempo, a single approved rhythm, everyone expected to arrive and finish and transition together, in step with a clock that was never actually neutral. So there's something that genuinely steadies me in learning that the universe itself never once managed that. what was already there, moving the "typical" baseline you = "deviation" a straight line, laid over what was already moving the grid comes after the field, not before Uniformity was never the achievement. It's the thing that would have stopped everything before it even started. Why Difference Comes First · Helen Edgar
There is no normal or baseline

Five · no normal or baseline There is no normal or baseline Gilles Deleuze, working with Félix Guattari, made a version of this same argument. Deleuze noticed that a lot of Western thinking treats difference as secondary — judged by how much it resembles some ideal, some average, some "normal" category. All of that quietly assumes the baseline came first, and difference is just a deviation from it. The baseline is the thing that got built. The idea of normality is what has shaped our capitalist society (Chapman, 2023) and is what we are judged against (Deleuze, 1994). Difference is what's actually there, first — and identity is what eventually forms out of it, temporarily and locally, the way a crystal settles out of a solution along the gaps and spaces in between — the places where those of us most marginalised live, and where we build our own networks, our own solidarity. This is where Deleuze and Guattari's idea of smooth space becomes useful (Deleuze & Guattari, 1987). Smooth space is full of local, variable difference — it hasn't had a fixed grid laid over it yet. Striated space is what happens when that grid arrives: when a field gets measured, divided, standardised. Difference doesn't get smoothed into existence by that process. Smoothing is what a system does afterward, only if it insists on it — striation laid over what was already smooth. Nothing gets smoothed into existence. Smoothing is what happens to something afterward — only if a system insists on it. Why Difference Comes First · Helen Edgar

Six · smooth ≠ flat Smooth doesn't mean flat Smooth space isn't empty of movement — it's just ungridded. It cuts against how regulation usually gets talked about, as though it means being still, quiet, zen: a flat line of its own. But smooth space is defined by what it lacks — a grid — not by what it's doing. It can be full of movement and still be smooth — which is closer to how neurodivergent regulation actually works: through stimming, through bodily autonomy, through movement rather than stillness. That's closer to what I recognise when I try to describe my own attention — my porousness to my environment, the way my sensory system stays open to everything around it, the way time folds back on itself instead of running in a straight line. Not flat. Not gridded. Full of shape that never quite resolves into one measurable thing. SMOOTH · ungridded STRIATED · gridded smooth is not empty · it's ungridded the fog was neither — a field before either one Why Difference Comes First · Helen Edgar

Seven · ethodiversity What ethodiversity means This is where Ombre Tarragnat's work on ethodiversity has become important to me. Ethodiversity is the variety of ways of being and behaving, across humans and other animals — and Tarragnat is precise about where it actually lives: not inside any one person, but as a property of the relationships between us, the way biodiversity belongs to a whole ecosystem, not to any single creature in it (Tarragnat, 2025). Ethonormativity, in their framing, is the unwritten rule about which ways of being are allowed to count as normal in a given room. Put next to Deleuze, I don't think it's a stretch to say ethonormativity simply is that grid — applied to how we're allowed to behave. A fixed grid laid over a field that was already full of variation before the grid ever showed up. Ethonormativity reaches further than neuronormativity, though. Neuronormativity is about which neurotypes get treated as the default — Autistic brains judged against non-Autistic ones, for instance. Ethonormativity is the wider grid underneath that: it governs which ways of being and behaving, across every species, get to count as acceptable at all. It holds neuronormativity inside it, but it isn't limited to brains, or even to humans (Tarragnat, 2025). Ethonormativity simply is that grid — a fixed grid laid over a field that was already full of variation before the grid ever showed up. Why Difference Comes First · Helen Edgar

Eight · a constellation of intensities A constellation of intensities I recognise that grid in every space I've ever masked in — education, the workplace, wherever something that was moving gets asked to hold still long enough to be measured. And I recognise its absence, with real gratitude, in the spaces I'm part of — NeuroHub Community and David Gray-Hammond, Stimpunks: an Autistic rhizome, a mycelial network of care, non-hierarchical, no fixed centre, connecting wherever it meets (Deleuze & Guattari, 1987). I used to think the shape of my own mind was something like a spiky profile — a way of picturing uneven ability across different areas, real peaks and real troughs, instead of one flat line running across the whole of who you are. At least it's truer than a flat line. But a profile still measures. It still needs axes, still has edges — and that's exactly where I want to push further, past even the spiky profile. What I actually recognise, when I try to map myself, isn't a chart at all. It's a constellation of intensities: a galaxy, always in relationship with itself, always in motion, never finished (Edgar, 2026b). Some stars I've lived in for decades. Others I've only just learned to name. None of them sit on an axis. They just belong to the same galaxy — we are all made of stardust. flat line a grid spiky profile still axes, still edges a constellation no axis · in motion flat line → spiky profile → no chart at all even the spiky profile is still a grid A profile still measures. It still needs axes, still has edges. What I actually recognise, when I try to map myself, isn't a chart at all. Why Difference Comes First · Helen Edgar
The universe doesn't do flat lines

Nine · permission The universe doesn't do flat lines I still don't have this fully settled or finished. But every time I follow this thread — from the sky, down through physics and philosophy, into the actual shape of my own attention — I end up in the same place. Not a tidy conclusion. More like a kind of permission. The universe doesn't do flat lines. It never really tried to. It went straight from near-uniform fog to unrepeatable structure, without ever pausing at sameness for its own sake. I think that's worth remembering, gently — the next time any of us is asked to explain why we don't match the line. We are all star dust. We are neuroqueering the spiky profile: no edges, limitless ways of being. Why Difference Comes First · Helen Edgar

still being woven 28 Wyrd Wyrd & Weird on the old word for fate, and the newer word we made of it Helen Edgar · Autistic Realms · a becoming, not a verdict L★S Love You Down To Your Star Stuff · open edition ·

Before the insult The word before the insult Long before "weird" meant strange, it meant becoming. In Old English, wyrd comes from weorþan — "to happen, to occur, to become" (Stone, 2022). It wasn't a synonym for doom, and it wasn't a script waiting to be read out. It was the word for the process by which anything at all comes into being. A person's wyrd wasn't what had been written about them. It was what they were still becoming. The same root gives us a second thread worth holding onto: Old English wyrd is twined with the ancestors of modern "worth" (Stone, 2022). Becoming and worth, tangled in the same word, from the start. "Weird" isn't the opposite of normal. It's the oldest word we have for becoming. one root, two threads weorþan "to become" wyrd becoming worth value becoming & worth, from the start tangled in one word Wyrd & Weird · Helen Edgar

an account, not a plot Urð has come to be Verðandi becoming Skuld what is owed the well beneath Yggdrasill what is, what becomes, what is owed The well beneath the tree Worth, not written Norse tradition keeps fate's three keepers at a well beneath the world tree, Yggdrasill — Urð, Verðandi, and Skuld. Popular retellings gloss them as past, present, and future. That's tidy, and it isn't quite right (Stone, 2022). Verðandi comes from verða, "to become." Skuld means "debt" or "tax." Urð may share a root with worth, or with a word meaning "to turn." Read plainly, together they describe not a plot but an account: what has come to be, what is happening now, and what is owed simply for having lived (Stone, 2022). A life's wyrd was never a plot laid down before you were born. It was the worth a life comes to have, built thread by thread in the living of it. — reading Stone (2022), pp. 36–37 Wyrd & Weird · Helen Edgar

Weaving, not writing The web, not the line Fate's keepers — the nornir, the Moirai, the Weird Sisters — are pictured again and again as spinners and weavers, working at a loom whose cloth is called, in one Old English poem, "the web of man" (Stone, 2022). Notice the shape of that image. Fate was never drawn as a single straight line running from birth to death. It was drawn as cloth — many threads, crossing, holding each other's weight, none of them load-bearing alone. A single thread can be cut. A web asks a different question: whose hands are helping hold it up? A line has one direction. A web holds weight from every side. a line one cut ends it a web holds from every side cloth, not a single strand many hands, many threads Wyrd & Weird · Helen Edgar

the three who spun it picked up again, as a name nornir · Moirai · the Weird Sisters impossible to write out How the word survived Weird Sisters, reclaimed Wyrd stayed alive in English through women who unsettled people. Medieval, mostly Christian, writers kept the word for fate but let the goddess behind it quietly fade (Stone, 2022). By Shakespeare, they were the three Weird Sisters of Macbeth, drawn from Holinshed's Chronicles (1587) — feared, consulted, impossible to write out of the story. A small honest note: Shakespeare's First Folio actually prints "weyward sisters." "Weird" is Holinshed's own word for them, fixed in place by later editors — which, if anything, makes the thread back to wyrd even more direct. Centuries on, "weird" drifted again — from fate-word, to uncanny, to a casual insult for anything too strange to sit comfortably in the room. Autistic and disabled communities didn't start that drift. But plenty of us have chosen to run it backward: to pick "weird" up again as a name, not a verdict. That's not just cheek. It's etymologically honest. We're not turning a slur into a compliment — we're giving an old, powerful word its meaning back. Wyrd & Weird · Helen Edgar

Held with care What wyrd is not Reclaiming a word means being clear about what we are not saying with it. Nota script written before you arrived, with no part in it for you to weave. Notdoom. Skuld's debt is the cost of having lived — not a punishment for how you lived it. Nota synonym for wrong, broken, too much, or not enough. Notsomething done to you alone. A web has many hands on it. many hands on it no thread load-bearing alone a web, not a single strand whose hands help hold it? Wyrd & Weird · Helen Edgar

still on the loom unfinished — and that is the design the cloth is still being made nobody is finished The root, again Becoming, together Weorþan — the root under wyrd — never meant "to be." It meant "to become." The self it describes isn't a fixed thing waiting at the end of a life; it's a self still happening, still owed, still worth building (Stone, 2022). That's a strange kind of comfort, if you've ever been told your difference makes you incomplete, or unfinished, or not-yet-normal. Under the old word, nobody is finished. Becoming was never a flaw in the design. It was the design. Nobody is finished. Becoming was never the flaw. It was the design. Wyrd & Weird · Helen Edgar

7 Never One Thing You Were Never One Thing on endosymbiosis, the cell as a truce, and interdependence written into the body L★S Love You Down To Your Star Stuff · open edition ·

Endosymbiosis The stranger that stayed More than one and a half billion years ago, a free-living bacterium ended up inside a larger cell — and was not digested. It stayed. It became the mitochondrion, the part that powers almost everything you do. And it never quite stopped being itself: it still keeps its own loop of DNA, its own ribosomes, and it divides on its own schedule. New mitochondria come only from old ones. Every complex cell you have carries that ancient merger, trillions of times over. You are not a single thing that happens to contain parts. You are the parts, still in their long agreement. host cell nucleus mitochondrion its own DNA a cell that is also a settlement host cell · engulfed bacterium · genome retained You Were Never One Thing · Stimpunks

lichen fungus + alga = one : gut microbiome ≈ 38 trillion : 30 trillion microbe : human cells mycorrhiza plant root + fungus the merger was never a one-off symbiosis, woven through the tree of life Cooperation, over and over Not a footnote. An engine. The mitochondrion was not a fluke. The green in every leaf — the chloroplast — came from a separate merger, when a cell took in a photosynthesizing cyanobacterium and kept it. A lichen is a fungus and an alga living as one body. Most land plants feed through fungi laced into their roots. And your own gut carries roughly as many bacterial cells as human ones — about thirty-eight trillion to thirty. Cooperation is not a footnote to competition. It is one of the engines that built complex life at all. We are not individuals who sometimes team up. We are teams that learned to say I. You Were Never One Thing · Stimpunks

The poem More than a billion years ago, one small cell ended up inside another and was not digested. It stayed. It became the mitochondrion — the thing that powers you now — and it never stopped being itself. Its own loop of DNA. Its own clock. A guest that became a home. You are not one thing. You are a truce so old it forgot it was ever two, kept alive in every cell, trillions of times over. This is not a metaphor we reached for. It is the blueprint. The body is a settlement. The self is a collaboration that learned to answer to one name. So when they told you to stand on your own, to need no one, to be independent or be nothing — they were telling a story over a body that had already decided otherwise, a billion years before you were born. You were never one thing. You were never alone in there. We love you down to the merger, down to the two that became you, down to the star stuff that both of them were made of. L★S. You Were Never One Thing · Stimpunks
Autonomy was never the same as being alone

The reframe Autonomy was never the same as being alone Disability justice values interdependence over independence. Your own cells settle the argument. "Independence" was always a story told over a body that is itself a collaboration — a merger it never dissolved. Needing support is not a failure of selfhood. Selfhood is need met by need. The mitochondrion did not lose itself by depending on the cell, and the cell did not lose itself by depending back. That mutual keeping is what made something new possible. You Were Never One Thing is the seventh zine in the Stimpunks series, and a companion to Bone Song — Bone Song was the skeleton; this is the cell. The science is established. Mitochondria descend from once-free-living bacteria (alphaproteobacteria) that took up residence inside an ancient host cell — most likely an archaeon — more than one and a half billion years ago; the exact timing is still debated. Mitochondria keep their own DNA and divide on their own schedule. Chloroplasts arose from a separate endosymbiosis of cyanobacteria. The gut carries roughly as many bacterial cells as human cells — about 38 trillion to 30 trillion (Sender, Fuchs & Milo, 2016), correcting the old 10:1 figure. Serial endosymbiotic theory was given its modern form by Lynn Margulis (as Lynn Sagan) in "On the Origin of Mitosing Cells" (1967), reviving earlier proposals by Mereschkowsky and Wallin; phylogenomics has since confirmed its core. The reading — interdependence over independence, autonomy was never the same as being alone — is ours. The atoms of both ancient partners were forged in stars.
